question: Find the product of the three complex cube roots of $-1-i\sqrt3$.
solution:
Let $w=-1-i\sqrt3$. The cube roots of $w$ are exactly the roots of the polynomial $z^3-w$, and there are three of them, all distinct since $w\ne0$. By Vieta's formulas, the product of the roots of $z^3+0z^2+0z-w$ is $-(-w)=w$. So the product is
\[\boxed{-1-i\sqrt3}.\]

\emph{Check with polar form.} $|w|=\sqrt{1+3}=2$ and $w$ lies in the third quadrant with argument $240^\circ$, so $w=2(\cos240^\circ+i\sin240^\circ)$. By De Moivre's theorem the cube roots are
\[\sqrt[3]{2}\,\bigl(\cos\theta_k+i\sin\theta_k\bigr),\qquad\theta_k=80^\circ+120^\circ k,\quad k=0,1,2.\]
Their product has modulus $\left(\sqrt[3]{2}\right)^3=2$ and argument $80^\circ+200^\circ+320^\circ=600^\circ$, which is $240^\circ$ after subtracting $360^\circ$. So the product is again $2(\cos240^\circ+i\sin240^\circ)=-1-i\sqrt3$.

question:
Solve the system
\[\begin{cases}2^{x}-3^{y-1}=5,\\ 2^{x+1}+8\cdot3^{y}=712\end{cases}\]
for real numbers $x$ and $y$.
solution:
Put $a=2^x>0$ and $b=3^y>0$. Then $3^{y-1}=\dfrac b3$ and $2^{x+1}=2a$, so the system becomes linear:
\[a-\dfrac b3=5,\qquad 2a+8b=712\iff a+4b=356.\]
Subtracting the first equation from the second gives $4b+\dfrac b3=351$, i.e. $\dfrac{13b}{3}=351$, so $b=81$ and $a=5+\dfrac{81}{3}=32$.

Since $2^x=32$ and $3^y=81$, and exponential functions are one-to-one, $x=5$ and $y=4$.

(Check: $32-27=5$ and $64+8\cdot81=64+648=712$.) The solution is $\boxed{(x,y)=(5,4)}$.

We use the product formula $\varphi(x)=x\prod_{p\mid x}\left(1-\dfrac1p\right)$, the product being over the distinct primes $p$ dividing $x$ (an empty product is $1$). Hence
\[\dfrac{x}{\varphi(x)}=\prod_{p\mid x}\dfrac{p}{p-1}.\]

\textbf{(a)} Every factor $\dfrac{p}{p-1}$ is greater than $1$. So $\dfrac{x}{\varphi(x)}\ge1$, with equality exactly when $x$ has no prime factor, i.e. $x=1$. The smallest value is $\boxed{1}$, attained only at $x=1$. (For $x\ge2$ the value is larger than $1$, although it can be very close to $1$: for a prime $p$ it is $\dfrac{p}{p-1}$.)

\textbf{(b)} Let $n\ge2$ and $x=n!$. The primes dividing $n!$ are exactly the primes $p\le n$, so, summing geometric series,
\[\dfrac{x}{\varphi(x)}=\prod_{p\le n}\dfrac{1}{1-\dfrac1p}=\prod_{p\le n}\left(1+\dfrac1p+\dfrac1{p^2}+\cdots\right)\ge\prod_{p\le n}\left(1+\dfrac1p+\cdots+\dfrac1{p^m}\right),\]
where $m$ is chosen with $2^m>n$. Expanding the last product gives the sum of $\dfrac1k$ over all integers $k$ whose prime factors are at most $n$ and appear with exponents at most $m$; by unique factorisation each such $k$ appears exactly once. Every $k$ with $1\le k\le n$ is of this kind (a prime power $p^e$ dividing $k$ satisfies $2^e\le p^e\le n<2^m$). Therefore
\[\dfrac{x}{\varphi(x)}\ge1+\dfrac12+\dfrac13+\cdots+\dfrac1n.\]
The harmonic sums are unbounded: for each $j\ge1$,
\[\dfrac{1}{2^{j-1}+1}+\cdots+\dfrac{1}{2^j}\ge2^{j-1}\cdot\dfrac{1}{2^j}=\dfrac12,\qquad\text{so}\qquad1+\dfrac12+\cdots+\dfrac{1}{2^j}\ge1+\dfrac j2.\]
Hence for $x=\left(2^j\right)!$ we get $\dfrac{x}{\varphi(x)}\ge1+\dfrac j2$, which exceeds any given bound for large $j$. So $\dfrac{x}{\varphi(x)}$ has minimum $1$ and no maximum. $\blacksquare$
note: The post asks for the "range" of x/phi(x) and defines phi(n) as the number of integers less than n coprime to n, which would give phi(1) = 0. The record uses the standard definition and asks for the minimum (1, only at x = 1) and a proof that the ratio is unbounded. Checked numerically: the ratio for n! exceeds the harmonic sum H_n for n up to 30.

solution:
\textbf{(a)} By the definitions,
\[4^{\dfrac12}=\sqrt4=2,\qquad\sqrt[4]{16}=2,\qquad8^{\dfrac23}=\left(\sqrt[3]{8}\right)^2=2^2=4,\qquad16^{-\dfrac34}=\dfrac{1}{\left(\sqrt[4]{16}\right)^3}=\dfrac{1}{8}.\]
In particular $4^{\dfrac12}=2$, not $\pm2$: like $\sqrt4$, the power $4^{\dfrac12}$ names one number, the positive square root.

\textbf{(b)} Factor:
\[x^4-16=\left(x^2-4\right)\left(x^2+4\right)=(x-2)(x+2)\left(x^2+4\right).\]
Since $x^2+4>0$ for real $x$, the real solutions are $x=2$ and $x=-2$.

The symbol $\sqrt[4]{16}$ is defined to be one particular number (the positive one), so that expressions such as $\sqrt[4]{16}+1$ have a single value. The equation $x^4=16$ asks instead for \emph{every} number whose fourth power is $16$, and there are two: $\sqrt[4]{16}$ and $-\sqrt[4]{16}$. In the same way $\sqrt4=2$, while $x^2=4$ has the two solutions $\pm2$.

\[\boxed{\text{(a) }2,\ 2,\ 4,\ \dfrac18;\qquad\text{(b) }x=2\text{ or }x=-2}\]
note: The post asks whether 4^(1/2) and the fourth root of 16 mean only the positive value. The record states the standard definition and asks for evaluations and for the real solutions of x^4 = 16.

question:
Prove that for every integer $n\ge2$,
\[\left(\dfrac{n+1}{2}\right)^n>n!.\]
solution:
Apply the AM-GM inequality to the $n$ positive numbers $1,2,\dots,n$:
\[\dfrac{1+2+\cdots+n}{n}\ge\sqrt[n]{1\cdot2\cdots n}.\]
The left side is $\dfrac{1}{n}\cdot\dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}=\dfrac{n+1}{2}$. Equality in AM-GM holds only when all the numbers are equal, which is not the case for $n\ge2$ (since $1\ne2$). Hence
\[\dfrac{n+1}{2}>\sqrt[n]{n!},\]
and raising both (positive) sides to the $n$th power gives $\left(\dfrac{n+1}{2}\right)^n>n!$. $\blacksquare$

question:
For positive integers $a>b$, the numbers
\[a^2-b^2,\qquad2ab,\qquad a^2+b^2\]
form a Pythagorean triple, since $\left(a^2-b^2\right)^2+(2ab)^2=\left(a^2+b^2\right)^2$. (One way to see this: $(a+bi)^2=\left(a^2-b^2\right)+2abi$ and $\left|(a+bi)^2\right|=|a+bi|^2=a^2+b^2$.) A triple is called \emph{primitive} if the greatest common divisor of its three numbers is $1$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] A student claims that \emph{every} Pythagorean triple of positive integers is of this form, with the legs $a^2-b^2$ and $2ab$ in some order. Show that the claim is false.
\item[(b)] The student also claims that if $\gcd(a,b)=1$, the triple is primitive. Show that this is false too, and prove the corrected statement: if $\gcd(a,b)=1$ and $a$, $b$ have opposite parity, then the triple is primitive.
\end{enumerate}
solution:
\textbf{(a)} The triple $(9,12,15)$ is a counterexample: $81+144=225$. In the claimed form one leg is $2ab$, which is even, so $2ab=12$ and $ab=6$. With $a>b$ this gives $(a,b)=(6,1)$ or $(3,2)$, which produce the triples $(35,12,37)$ and $(5,12,13)$, not $(9,12,15)$. So $(9,12,15)$ is not of the form. (Every triple is a multiple of a triple of the form, e.g. $(9,12,15)=3\cdot(3,4,5)$ with $(a,b)=(2,1)$, but the multiples are missed.)

\textbf{(b)} Take $a=3$, $b=1$, which are coprime: the triple is $(8,6,10)$, and all three numbers are even. So $\gcd(a,b)=1$ is not enough.

Now let $\gcd(a,b)=1$ with $a$, $b$ of opposite parity, and suppose a prime $p$ divides all three numbers. Then $p$ divides $\left(a^2+b^2\right)+\left(a^2-b^2\right)=2a^2$ and $\left(a^2+b^2\right)-\left(a^2-b^2\right)=2b^2$. Since $a$ and $b$ have opposite parity, $a^2-b^2$ is odd, so $p\ne2$. Hence $p\mid a^2$ and $p\mid b^2$, so $p\mid a$ and $p\mid b$, contradicting $\gcd(a,b)=1$. So the greatest common divisor of the triple is $1$ and the triple is primitive. $\blacksquare$

(The parity condition is needed: if $a$ and $b$ are both odd, all three numbers are even, as in the counterexample.)
note: The post claims that all Pythagorean triples have the form a^2 - b^2, 2ab, a^2 + b^2 and that gcd(a, b) = 1 gives a primitive triple. Both claims are false (counterexamples (9, 12, 15) and a = 3, b = 1 giving (8, 6, 10)); the record asks for the counterexamples and proves the corrected statement (a, b coprime of opposite parity). Checked by search over small a, b.

question:
Consider the cubic equation
\[x^3+100x^2+19x+13251234=0.\]
Show that it has exactly one real root $r$, and find the integer $n$ with $n<r<n+1$.
solution:
Let $f(x)=x^3+100x^2+19x+13251234$.

\textbf{No root with $x>-100$.} For $x\ge0$ every term is nonnegative and the constant is positive, so $f(x)>0$. For $-100\le x<0$ we have $x^3+100x^2=x^2(x+100)\ge0$ and $19x\ge-1900$, so $f(x)\ge13251234-1900>0$.

\textbf{At most one root with $x\le-100$.} For $y<x\le-100$,
\[f(x)-f(y)=(x-y)\left(x^2+xy+y^2+100(x+y)+19\right)=(x-y)\bigl(x(x+100)+y(y+100)+xy+19\bigr).\]
Here $x(x+100)\ge0$ and $y(y+100)\ge0$ (each a product of two non-positive numbers), and $xy>0$, so $f(x)>f(y)$. Thus $f$ is strictly increasing on $(-\infty,-100]$ and has at most one root there.

\textbf{Locating the root.}
\[f(-275)=-20796875+7562500-5225+13251234=11634>0,\]
\[f(-276)=-21024576+7617600-5244+13251234=-160986<0.\]
Since $f$ is continuous, it has a root between $-276$ and $-275$, and by the above this is its only real root $r$ (numerically $r\approx-275.07$). So $n=\boxed{-276}$.

(There is a general formula for cubics, Cardano's formula, but for an equation like this one it is usually more practical to locate the real roots as above and then approximate them numerically. Integer roots, if any, would divide $13251234$, and the computation shows there is none.)
note: The post asks how to solve cubic equations such as this one. The record works the poster's example: there is exactly one real root, between -276 and -275 (about -275.068), found by bounding and sign changes; checked with sympy.

question: Four nonnegative integers $a_1,a_2,a_3,a_4$ have sum $101010$, and no carrying occurs when they are added in base $10$. How many ordered quadruples $(a_1,a_2,a_3,a_4)$ are possible?
note: Source as given in the thread title (BdMO 2021 divisional round, Problem 5). Checked by brute force over the digit splits.

The original figure is missing; it is reconstructed from the text. External tangency at A puts E, A, F on a line, the arcs centred at A force AD = AB = 2, and the congruent arcs give angles EAD = BAF = 45 degrees. The question diagram shows only the given figure; the result matches choice (A).

question:
Arjun, Beth, Bela, Jenn and Mira play a game. Each of them chooses a number from $1$ to $10$ inclusive, and a player gets a point if nobody else chooses the same number. At the start, Arjun announces that he will choose $1$, and he does. The other four players cannot discuss a strategy: each of them chooses independently at random, all four using the same probabilities $p_1,p_2,\dots,p_{10}$ for the numbers $1,2,\dots,10$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Explain why these four players should never choose $1$, i.e. why $p_1=0$ for a sensible strategy.
\item[(b)] Assume $p_1=0$. Which statement is true? Prove your answer.

(A) Arjun has a higher expected number of points than each of the others.

(B) Arjun has a lower expected number of points than each of the others.

(C) Everyone has the same expected number of points.
\item[(c)] Find each of the other players' expected number of points if they choose uniformly at random from $2,3,\dots,10$.
\end{enumerate}
solution:
\textbf{(a)} Arjun always chooses $1$, so a player who chooses $1$ never gets a point. Choosing some other number instead can only help: a player's expected score is $\sum_k p_k q_k$, where $q_k$ is the probability that nobody else chooses $k$, and $q_1=0$. So moving the probability $p_1$ onto other numbers never lowers the expected score, and a sensible strategy has $p_1=0$.

\textbf{(b)} With $p_1=0$, nobody else ever chooses $1$, so Arjun gets a point every time: his expected score is $1$.

Consider Beth (the others are the same). She chooses $k\in\{2,\dots,10\}$ with probability $p_k$, and then scores exactly when the other three random players all avoid $k$ (Arjun's $1$ never equals $k$), which has probability $(1-p_k)^3$ by independence. So her expected score is
\[\sum_{k=2}^{10}p_k(1-p_k)^3\le\sum_{k=2}^{10}p_k=1.\]
Equality would need $(1-p_k)^3=1$, i.e. $p_k=0$, for every $k$ with $p_k>0$, which is impossible because the $p_k$ add up to $1$. So each of the others has expected score less than $1$, and the answer is $\boxed{\textbf{(A)}}$.

\textbf{(c)} With $p_k=\dfrac19$ for $k=2,\dots,10$, the expected score is $9\cdot\dfrac19\left(\dfrac89\right)^3=\boxed{\dfrac{512}{729}}\approx0.70$.
note: The post says the others use "the optimal strategy taking into account Arjun's announcement", which is not defined. The record assumes the four use the same random strategy (as they cannot coordinate) and never pick 1, and proves (A) for every such strategy; the uniform strategy is worked as an example.

question:
Arjun and Beth will each come to my house at a time chosen uniformly at random between 3 pm and 4 pm. I also have a meeting with two other people, who will each arrive at a uniformly random time between 3 pm and 4 pm; the meeting starts as soon as both of them have arrived. All four arrival times are independent. What is the probability that at least one of Arjun and Beth arrives before the meeting starts?

$\textbf{(A) }\dfrac13\qquad\textbf{(B) }\dfrac12\qquad\textbf{(C) }\dfrac23\qquad\textbf{(D) }\dfrac56\qquad\textbf{(E) }\dfrac{23}{24}$
solution:
With probability $1$ the four arrival times are distinct, and since the four times are independent and identically distributed, all $4!=24$ orders of arrival are equally likely.

The event fails exactly when both Arjun and Beth arrive after both meeting participants, i.e. when the two participants are the first two to arrive. That happens in $2!\cdot2!=4$ of the $24$ orders. So the probability is
\[1-\dfrac{4}{24}=\boxed{\textbf{(D) }\dfrac56}.\]
note: Story shortened. The post labels the last choice (C) a second time; it is relabelled (E). Checked by enumerating the 24 orders and by simulation.

question: A picometer is a trillionth of a meter, and the diameter of a hydrogen atom is $240$ picometers. Annabelle's height increased by $1$ inch during a non-leap year, and $1$ inch equals $2.54$ centimeters. On average, by how many hydrogen-atom diameters did Annabelle's height increase each second? Express your answer as a decimal to the nearest tenth. (A calculator may be used.)
solution:
One inch is $2.54\text{ cm}=2.54\times10^{-2}$ m, and one hydrogen diameter is $240\times10^{-12}\text{ m}=2.4\times10^{-10}$ m. A non-leap year has $365\cdot24\cdot3600=31536000=3.1536\times10^7$ seconds. So the average growth per second, in hydrogen diameters, is
\[\dfrac{2.54\times10^{-2}}{\left(2.4\times10^{-10}\right)\left(3.1536\times10^{7}\right)}=\dfrac{2.54\times10^{-2}}{7.56864\times10^{-3}}\approx3.356,\]
which is $\boxed{3.4}$ to the nearest tenth.
note: Checked with exact fractions (79375/23652, about 3.3560).

question: Right triangle $ABC$ has $AC=3$, $BC=4$ and a right angle at $C$. Let $v_1$ be the midpoint of $AB$ and $v_2$ the midpoint of $v_1B$, and for $n\ge3$ let $v_n$ be the midpoint of $v_{n-1}v_{n-2}$. Compute the integer closest to the area of triangle $v_{4912}AC$.
note: Checked with exact fractions for the first terms and the closed form.

question:
Consider the following five statements.
\begin{itemize}
\item[(A)] At least one of statements C, D and E is true.
\item[(B)] None of the statements below this one (C, D and E) is true.
\item[(C)] All of the statements above this one (A and B) are true.
\item[(D)] All of the statements below this one (that is, E) are true.
\item[(E)] Statement A is true.
\end{itemize}
Find every way of declaring each statement true or false so that every statement is true exactly when what it says holds. Can the question ``which statement is true?'' be answered uniquely?
solution:
Write the conditions as equivalences. Statement D says E is true, so D and E have the same truth value; E says A is true, so E and A have the same truth value. Hence A, D and E are all true or all false.

\textbf{Case 1: A, D, E true.} B says that C, D, E are all false; since D is true, B is false. C says that A and B are both true; B is false, so C is false. Finally A says that one of C, D, E is true, which holds (D is true). Everything is consistent.

\textbf{Case 2: A, D, E false.} A is false, so none of C, D, E is true; in particular C is false. Then B (``C, D, E are all false'') is true. C (``A and B are true'') is false since A is false, consistent with C false. Everything is consistent.

So there are exactly two consistent assignments:
\[\boxed{\text{A, D, E true and B, C false;}\quad\text{or B true and A, C, D, E false.}}\]
The question ``which one is true?'' has no unique answer: B alone, or A, D and E together.
note: The post asks "Which one is true?", but two truth assignments are self-consistent ({A, D, E} or {B} true). The record asks for all consistent assignments. Checked over all 32 assignments.

question: An equilateral triangle and a square have equal areas. Let the side length of the triangle be $t$ and the side length of the square be $s$. Let $n$ be the smallest positive integer such that $\left(\dfrac{s}{t}\right)^n$ is a rational number, and write $\left(\dfrac{s}{t}\right)^n=\dfrac pq$ with $p$ and $q$ relatively prime positive integers. Find $n+p+q$.

A positive integer $r$ has more positive divisors than every positive integer less than $r$. Write
\[r=2^{e_1}\cdot3^{e_2}\cdot5^{e_3}\cdot7^{e_4}\cdot11^{e_5}\cdots,\]
where $e_i$ is the exponent of the $i$th prime $p_i$ (all but finitely many $e_i$ are $0$). Prove that if $n>m$, then $e_n\le e_m$.
solution:
The number of divisors of $r$ is
\[\tau(r)=(e_1+1)(e_2+1)(e_3+1)\cdots.\]
Suppose, for contradiction, that $e_n>e_m$ for some $n>m$, so $p_n>p_m$. Let $r'$ be the number obtained from $r$ by swapping the exponents of $p_m$ and $p_n$:
\[r'=r\cdot\dfrac{p_m^{\,e_n}\,p_n^{\,e_m}}{p_m^{\,e_m}\,p_n^{\,e_n}}=r\left(\dfrac{p_m}{p_n}\right)^{e_n-e_m}.\]
Then $r'$ is a positive integer, and $r'<r$ because $\dfrac{p_m}{p_n}<1$ and $e_n-e_m\ge1$. But $\tau(r')=\tau(r)$, since the product $(e_1+1)(e_2+1)\cdots$ only has two of its factors interchanged. So $r'<r$ has as many divisors as $r$, contradicting the property of $r$. Hence $e_n\le e_m$ whenever $n>m$. $\blacksquare$
note: Checked on all numbers up to 10^5 with more divisors than every smaller number.

question: The three roots of $144x^3-210x^2+91x-10$ are the probabilities of three independent events. The probability that exactly two of these events happen can be written as $\dfrac mn$ for relatively prime positive integers $m$ and $n$. Find $m+n$.
solution:
First, the roots are genuine probabilities:
\[144x^3-210x^2+91x-10=(3x-2)(6x-1)(8x-5),\]
so the roots are $a=\dfrac23$, $b=\dfrac16$, $c=\dfrac58$, all between $0$ and $1$.

By independence, the probability that exactly two events happen is
\[ab(1-c)+ac(1-b)+bc(1-a)=(ab+bc+ca)-3abc.\]
By Vieta's formulas, $ab+bc+ca=\dfrac{91}{144}$ and $abc=\dfrac{10}{144}$, so the probability is
\[\dfrac{91}{144}-\dfrac{30}{144}=\dfrac{61}{144}.\]
Since $61$ is prime and does not divide $144$, $m+n=61+144=\boxed{205}$.

question: Today I was muted in a chat room. On any day following a day on which I was muted, I am muted with probability $\dfrac12$; on any day following a day on which I was not muted, I am muted with probability $\dfrac15$. As $k$ grows, the probability that I am muted $k$ days from now converges to $\dfrac mn$, where $m$ and $n$ are relatively prime positive integers. Find $m+n$.
solution:
Let $a_k$ be the probability that I am muted $k$ days from now, so $a_0=1$. Conditioning on day $k$,
\[a_{k+1}=\dfrac12a_k+\dfrac15(1-a_k)=\dfrac15+\dfrac{3}{10}a_k.\]
The fixed point $L$ satisfies $L=\dfrac15+\dfrac3{10}L$, so $L=\dfrac27$. Subtracting,
\[a_{k+1}-\dfrac27=\dfrac3{10}\left(a_k-\dfrac27\right),\qquad a_k-\dfrac27=\left(\dfrac3{10}\right)^k\cdot\dfrac57\to0.\]
So $a_k\to\dfrac27$ and $m+n=\boxed{9}$.
note: Story shortened; the percentages 50% and 20% are written as 1/2 and 1/5.

question: Call a nonnegative integer \emph{nice} if the sum of its digits equals its cube root, and \emph{nontrivial} if it has more than one digit. Find the two smallest nontrivial nice numbers.
solution:
If $N$ is nice, its cube root is its digit sum $k$, an integer, so $N=k^3$ and the digit sum of $k^3$ is $k$.

Since a number and its digit sum leave the same remainder modulo $9$, we need $k^3\equiv k\pmod9$. Cubes modulo $9$ are $0,1,8,0,1,8,0,1,8$ for $k\equiv0,1,\dots,8$, so $k^3\equiv k$ only for $k\equiv0,1,8\pmod9$. A nontrivial $N$ has $N\ge10$, so $k\ge3$, and the candidates in increasing order are $k=8,9,10,17,\dots$:
\begin{itemize}
\item $k=8$: $8^3=512$, digit sum $5+1+2=8$. Nice.
\item $k=9$: $729$, digit sum $18$. Not nice.
\item $k=10$: $1000$, digit sum $1$. Not nice.
\item $k=17$: $17^3=4913$, digit sum $4+9+1+3=17$. Nice.
\end{itemize}
The two smallest nontrivial nice numbers are $\boxed{512\text{ and }4913}$ (written with four digits, $0512$ and $4913$).
note: The post asks for the answers as 4-digit strings with leading zeros (0512, 4913); the record asks for the numbers. Checked by listing k^3 for k up to 60.

question: Call a nonnegative integer \emph{nice} if the sum of its digits equals its cube root. Prove that every nice number is congruent to $0$, $1$ or $8$ modulo $9$.
solution:
If $N$ is nice, its cube root equals its digit sum, which is a nonnegative integer $k$; so $N=k^3$ is the cube of an integer. Write $k=3j$, $k=3j+1$ or $k=3j-1$. Then
\[(3j)^3=27j^3\equiv0,\qquad(3j\pm1)^3=27j^3\pm27j^2+9j\pm1\equiv\pm1\pmod9.\]
So $N\equiv0$, $1$ or $-1\equiv8\pmod9$. $\blacksquare$

question: Sabrina has $2^{100}$ unit cubes. Using all of them, she builds a solid rectangular box, each of whose edge lengths must be at least $512$. How many different boxes can she make, if boxes whose edge lengths are the same numbers listed in a different order (length, width, height) are counted as different?
note: Checked by direct enumeration of exponent triples.
Checked by testing every integer k from 0 to 100.

question:
Let $f(n)$ be the number of positive divisors of $n$. Find the smallest positive integer $n>1$ such that
\[f(f(f(f(f(n)))))\ne2.\]
solution:
Write $f^j$ for $f$ applied $j$ times. For $m\ge2$ we have $f(m)\ge2$, with $f(m)=2$ exactly when $m$ is prime. So for $n\ge2$ all iterates are at least $2$, and $f^5(n)\ne2$ exactly when $f^4(n)$ is \emph{composite}.

Let $B_j$ be the set of $n\ge2$ with $f^j(n)$ composite. Then $B_0$ is the set of composite numbers, with least element $4$, and for $j\ge1$, $n\in B_j$ exactly when $f(n)\in B_{j-1}$. Let $D(k)$ be the least positive integer with at least $k$ divisors. If $n\in B_j$, then $f(n)\ge\min B_{j-1}$, so $n\ge D\left(\min B_{j-1}\right)$. We use
\[D(4)=6,\qquad D(6)=12,\qquad D(12)=60,\qquad D(60)=5040,\]
justified below. Then:
\begin{itemize}
\item $\min B_1=6$: $n\ge D(4)=6$, and $f(6)=4$ is composite.
\item $\min B_2=12$: $n\ge D(6)=12$, and $f(12)=6\in B_1$.
\item $\min B_3=60$: $n\ge D(12)=60$, and $f(60)=12\in B_2$.
\item $\min B_4=5040$: $n\ge D(60)=5040$, and $f(5040)=60\in B_3$.
\end{itemize}
Indeed $f(5040)=60$, $f(60)=12$, $f(12)=6$, $f(6)=4$, $f(4)=3\ne2$. The answer is $\boxed{5040}$.

\textbf{The values of $D$.} The numbers $2,\dots,5$ have at most $3$ divisors and $f(6)=4$; the numbers below $12$ have at most $4$ divisors and $f(12)=6$. For the other two, note that moving the exponents of $n$ onto the smallest primes, in non-increasing order, does not increase $n$ and keeps the number of divisors. So it suffices to consider $n=2^a3^b5^c7^d\cdots$ with $a\ge b\ge c\ge d\ge\cdots$.
\begin{itemize}
\item $D(12)=60$: suppose $f(n)\ge12$. With four or more primes, $n\ge2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7=210$. With exactly three primes, $2\cdot2\cdot2=8<12$ forces $a\ge2$, so $n\ge4\cdot3\cdot5=60$. With at most two primes, $(a+1)(b+1)\ge12$ and $a\ge b$ give $n\ge\min\left(2^{11},\ 2^5\cdot3,\ 2^3\cdot3^2,\ 2^3\cdot3^3\right)=72$ (for $b=0,1,2$ and $b\ge3$). And $f(60)=12$.
\item $D(60)=5040$, where $5040=2^4\cdot3^2\cdot5\cdot7$ has $5\cdot3\cdot2\cdot2=60$ divisors. Suppose $f(n)\ge60$.
\begin{itemize}
\item Six or more primes: $n\ge2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13=30030$.
\item Exactly five primes: if $b=1$, then $f(n)=16(a+1)\ge60$ gives $a\ge3$ and $n\ge8\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11=9240$; if $b\ge2$, then $a\ge2$ and $n\ge4\cdot9\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11=13860$.
\item Exactly four primes: if $c\ge2$ then $n\ge4\cdot9\cdot25\cdot7=6300$. If $c=d=1$, then $(a+1)(b+1)\ge15$: $b=1$ needs $a\ge7$ ($n\ge13440$), $b=2$ needs $a\ge4$ ($n\ge5040$), and $b\ge3$ gives $n\ge8\cdot27\cdot35=7560$.
\item Exactly three primes: if $c\ge2$, then $(a+1)(b+1)(c+1)\ge60$ gives $n\ge\min(2^6\cdot9\cdot25,\ 2^4\cdot27\cdot25,\ 2^4\cdot81\cdot25,\ 8\cdot27\cdot125)=10800$. If $c=1$, then $(a+1)(b+1)\ge30$ gives $n\ge\min(2^{14}\cdot15,\ 2^9\cdot45,\ 2^7\cdot135,\ 2^5\cdot405,\ 2^5\cdot1215)=12960$.
\item At most two primes: $n=2^a3^b\ge2^{a+b}$, and by AM-GM $\dfrac{(a+1)+(b+1)}{2}\ge\sqrt{(a+1)(b+1)}\ge\sqrt{60}>7.7$, so $a+b\ge14$ and $n\ge2^{14}>5040$.
\end{itemize}
So $f(n)\ge60$ implies $n\ge5040$.
\end{itemize}
note: Checked by computing f five times for every n up to 6000 (the first n is 5040) and by checking that no n below 5040 has 60 or more divisors.

question: The distance between Arlington and Pittsburgh is $477$ miles. At the same moment, one driver leaves each city and drives towards the other city along the same straight road at $50$ miles per hour. Also at that moment, a bird leaves Pittsburgh and flies towards the driver coming from Arlington. Whenever the bird reaches one of the drivers, it immediately turns around and flies towards the other driver. Because of the wind, the bird flies at $70$ miles per hour when flying in the direction from Pittsburgh towards Arlington, and at $60$ miles per hour when flying in the direction from Arlington towards Pittsburgh. To the nearest mile, how far does the bird fly before the two drivers meet?
solution:
Suppose the bird is with the Pittsburgh driver and the drivers are $D$ miles apart.
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Towards Arlington.} The bird and the Arlington driver close the gap at $70+50=120$ mph, so this leg takes $\dfrac{D}{120}$ hours and the bird flies $\dfrac{70D}{120}=\dfrac{7D}{12}$ miles. Meanwhile the drivers close $100\cdot\dfrac{D}{120}$ miles, so they are now $\dfrac D6$ apart.
\item \textbf{Back towards Pittsburgh.} The closing speed is $60+50=110$ mph, so this leg takes $\dfrac{D}{660}$ hours and the bird flies $\dfrac{60D}{660}=\dfrac{D}{11}$ miles. The drivers are then $\dfrac D6-\dfrac{100D}{660}=\dfrac{D}{66}$ apart, and the bird is again with the Pittsburgh driver.
\end{itemize}
So each round trip, starting from a gap $D$, covers $\dfrac{7D}{12}+\dfrac{D}{11}=\dfrac{89D}{132}$ miles and shrinks the gap to $\dfrac D{66}$. Starting from $D=477$, the total distance is a geometric series:
\[\dfrac{89\cdot477}{132}\left(1+\dfrac1{66}+\dfrac1{66^2}+\cdots\right)=\dfrac{89\cdot477}{132}\cdot\dfrac{66}{65}=\dfrac{89\cdot477}{130}=\dfrac{42453}{130}\approx326.56.\]
(Check: the total time is $\dfrac{477\cdot66}{65}\left(\dfrac1{120}+\dfrac1{660}\right)=4.77$ hours, which is exactly when the drivers meet, $\dfrac{477}{100}$ hours after starting.)

To the nearest mile, the bird flies $\boxed{327}$ miles.
note: Checked by summing the legs with exact fractions.

question: Compute $420(20\cdot15)$.
solution: First $20\cdot15=300$, so the product is $420\cdot300=\boxed{126000}$.

question:
Simplify the product
\[6(x+3)\cdot5(x+3)\cdot4(x+3)\cdot3(x+3)\cdot2(x+3)\cdot1(x+3)\cdot0(x+3)\cdot(-1)(x+3)\cdots(-6)(x+3),\]
in which the coefficients run through $6,5,4,\dots,1,0,-1,\dots,-6$.
solution: One of the factors is $0(x+3)=0$, and a product with a factor $0$ is $0$. So the product equals $\boxed{0}$ for every value of $x$.

question: What is the value of $23+18+7+12+13+8+17+22$?
solution:
Group the terms into pairs with sum $30$:
\[(23+7)+(18+12)+(13+17)+(8+22)=4\cdot30=\boxed{120}.\]

question: Solve the equation $4x+12-x=-4x+16$.
solution:
Combine like terms: $3x+12=-4x+16$. Adding $4x-12$ to both sides gives $7x=4$, so $x=\boxed{\dfrac47}$.

(Check: both sides equal $3\cdot\dfrac47+12=\dfrac{96}{7}$ and $-\dfrac{16}{7}+16=\dfrac{96}{7}$.)

question:
Find $a$ and $b$ that satisfy both equations
\[5a+7=22,\qquad6b+10a=42.\]
solution: From the first equation, $5a=15$, so $a=3$. Then the second gives $6b+30=42$, so $6b=12$ and $b=2$. The answer is $\boxed{a=3,\ b=2}$.

question: The phrase MENTAL MATH is written with its usual space between the two words. In addition, you may insert a single space into some of the gaps between two consecutive letters of the same word (for example, M ENTAL MATH), using at most $2$ extra spaces in total. In how many different ways can the phrase be written, counting the way with no extra spaces?
solution:
MENTAL has $5$ gaps between consecutive letters and MATH has $3$, so there are $8$ gaps, and a way of writing the phrase corresponds to a set of at most $2$ of them. The number of ways is
\[\dbinom80+\dbinom81+\dbinom82=1+8+28=\boxed{37}.\]
note: The post ("ways to spell Mental-Math if you can put a space between the letters, 2 maximum") is ambiguous. Following its example "M ental Math", the record keeps the space between the words and allows at most two extra spaces inside the words, one per gap.

The post asks how many ways there are "to make a line from one point to another" without overlapping, counting CE and EC once; this is read as counting segments (28). Part (b), the number of distinct lines (20), is added because three marked points lie on each side.

question: Jonah has $10$ cards showing the numbers $3,8,13,18,23,28,33,48,53,68$, one number on each card. What is the least number of cards he can choose so that the numbers on them add up to $100$? Give one such choice.
solution:
Every number on the cards leaves remainder $3$ when divided by $5$. So the sum of $k$ cards leaves the same remainder as $3k$. For the sum to be $100$, a multiple of $5$, we need $5\mid3k$, i.e. $5\mid k$. Hence at least $5$ cards are needed, and $5$ cards suffice:
\[3+8+13+28+48=100.\]
The least number is $\boxed{5}$.
note: Each number is taken to be on exactly one card. Checked by searching all subsets (smallest size 5).

question:
Find all integers $x$ with
\[x^3+x+1\equiv0\pmod{13}.\]
solution:
A congruence modulo $13$ only depends on $x$ modulo $13$, so we look for residues. One root is $x\equiv7$: $7^3+7+1=351=27\cdot13$. Dividing by $x-7$:
\[x^3+x+1\equiv(x-7)\left(x^2+7x+11\right)\pmod{13},\]
since $(x-7)\left(x^2+7x+11\right)=x^3-38x-77$ and $-38\equiv1$, $-77\equiv1\pmod{13}$.

Because $13$ is prime, a product is $\equiv0$ only if a factor is. For the quadratic factor, multiply by $4$ (invertible modulo $13$) and complete the square:
\[4\left(x^2+7x+11\right)=(2x+7)^2-5.\]
So we would need $(2x+7)^2\equiv5\pmod{13}$. The squares modulo $13$ are $0,1,4,9,3,12,10$ (from $0^2,1^2,\dots,6^2$; the others repeat these), and $5$ is not among them. So the quadratic factor has no roots, and the solutions are exactly
\[\boxed{x\equiv7\pmod{13}}.\]
(For a small modulus one can also simply test all $13$ residues.)
note: The post asks how to solve polynomial congruences such as this one; the record solves the example. Checked over all residues.

question: There are $100$ lockers in a room, numbered $1$ to $100$, all closed. One hundred people enter the room one at a time. For $n=1,2,\dots,100$, the $n$th person changes the state of every $n$th locker, that is, of lockers $n,2n,3n,\dots$ (opening it if it is closed and closing it if it is open). Which lockers are open after everyone has passed through?
solution:
Locker $k$ is changed by person $n$ exactly when $n$ divides $k$; since every divisor of $k$ is at most $k\le100$, locker $k$ is changed once for each positive divisor of $k$. It ends open exactly when it is changed an odd number of times, i.e. when $k$ has an odd number of divisors.

The divisors of $k$ come in pairs $d\leftrightarrow\dfrac kd$. A divisor is paired with itself only when $d=\dfrac kd$, i.e. $k=d^2$. So $k$ has an odd number of divisors exactly when $k$ is a perfect square.

The open lockers are $\boxed{1,4,9,16,25,36,49,64,81,100}$, the ten perfect squares.
note: Checked by simulation.

question:
Let $x$ be a nonzero real number and $n$ an integer. Prove that
\[x^{2n}+\dfrac{1}{x^{2n}}\ge2,\]
and find when equality holds.
solution:
Let $y=x^n$, a nonzero real number (also for $n\le0$). Then $x^{2n}=y^2$ and
\[x^{2n}+\dfrac1{x^{2n}}=y^2+\dfrac1{y^2}=\left(y-\dfrac1y\right)^2+2\ge2,\]
since a square of a real number is nonnegative. $\blacksquare$

Equality holds exactly when $y=\dfrac1y$, i.e. $y^2=1$, i.e. $x^{2n}=1$. For $n=0$ this always holds; for $n\ne0$ it means $|x|^{2|n|}=1$, i.e. $|x|=1$. So equality holds exactly when $\boxed{n=0\text{ or }x=\pm1}$.
note: The post writes "for all integers n" without conditions on x; the record adds that x is a nonzero real number and asks for the equality cases.
The poster did not understand the proof without words (Nelsen) showing that the sum is 1/3; the record asks for the partial-sum proof and for an explanation of the picture.

question: How many $4\times4$ arrays are there in which every entry is one of $1,2,3,4$ and every row and every column contains each of $1,2,3,4$ exactly once?
solution:
\textbf{Reduced arrays.} First count the arrays whose first row is $1\,2\,3\,4$ and whose first column is $1,2,3,4$ (from top to bottom). The second row starts with $2$, and its other entries must avoid the entry above them, so it is $2\,1\,4\,3$, $2\,3\,4\,1$ or $2\,4\,1\,3$.
\begin{itemize}
\item Second row $2\,1\,4\,3$: the third row starts with $3$; its second entry avoids $2,1,3$, so it is $4$, and its last two entries are $1,2$ in either order. Both $3\,4\,1\,2$ and $3\,4\,2\,1$ work, and the fourth row is then forced ($4\,3\,2\,1$ or $4\,3\,1\,2$): $2$ arrays.
\item Second row $2\,3\,4\,1$: the third row starts with $3$; its last entry avoids $4,1,3$, so it is $2$; its third entry avoids $3,4,2$, so it is $1$; then its second entry is $4$. The fourth row is forced, $4\,1\,2\,3$: $1$ array.
\item Second row $2\,4\,1\,3$: similarly the third row must be $3\,1\,4\,2$ and the fourth row is $4\,3\,2\,1$: $1$ array.
\end{itemize}
So there are $4$ reduced arrays.

\textbf{All arrays.} Permuting the columns of an array, or permuting its rows, gives another valid array. Every valid array can be turned into a unique array with first row $1\,2\,3\,4$ by permuting columns ($4!$ choices of the first row), and then into a unique reduced array by permuting the last three rows ($3!$ orders of the first column below the top entry). Hence the number of arrays is
\[4!\cdot3!\cdot4=\boxed{576}.\]
note: The post's conditions b ("every row and column contain all the integers 1, 2, 3, 4") and c ("no row or column contains two of the same number") are equivalent for 4 entries; they are merged. Checked by enumerating all arrays of row permutations.

question: How many different $4\times4$ arrays whose entries are all $1$'s and $-1$'s have the property that the sum of the entries in each row is $0$ and the sum of the entries in each column is $0$?
solution:
Each row and each column must contain exactly two $1$'s (and two $-1$'s). So we count ways to choose two positions in each row for the $1$'s, with every column also receiving exactly two.

The first row can be chosen in $\dbinom42=6$ ways; by symmetry, suppose its $1$'s are in columns $1$ and $2$. For the second row:
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Same columns $\{1,2\}$} ($1$ way): columns $1,2$ are full, so rows $3$ and $4$ must both use columns $\{3,4\}$: $1$ completion.
\item \textbf{Columns $\{3,4\}$} ($1$ way): every column now has one $1$, so row $3$ can be any of the $6$ choices and row $4$ must be its complement: $6$ completions.
\item \textbf{One column in common} ($\{1,3\},\{1,4\},\{2,3\},\{2,4\}$: $4$ ways): say $\{1,3\}$. Column $1$ is full and column $4$ is empty, so rows $3$ and $4$ both contain column $4$ and not column $1$; one of them uses column $2$ and the other column $3$: $2$ completions.
\end{itemize}
So each first row has $1+6+4\cdot2=15$ completions, and the total is $6\cdot15=\boxed{90}$.
note: Checked by enumerating all 2^16 arrays.

question: The positive integer $m$ is a multiple of $101$, and the positive integer $n$ is a multiple of $63$. Their sum is $2018$. Find $m-n$.
solution:
Write $m=101a$ and $n=63b$ with positive integers $a,b$, so $101a+63b=2018$. Reduce modulo $63$: $101\equiv38$ and $2018=32\cdot63+2\equiv2$, so
\[38a\equiv2\pmod{63}\iff19a\equiv1\pmod{63},\]
dividing by $2$, which is invertible modulo $63$. Since $19\cdot10=190=3\cdot63+1$, this means $a\equiv10\pmod{63}$. Also $101a<2018$ gives $a\le19$, so $a=10$. Then $m=1010$ and $n=2018-1010=1008=63\cdot16$, and
\[m-n=\boxed{2}.\]
(A quicker way to see it: $2018=2\cdot1009$, and $1009+1=1010=10\cdot101$ while $1009-1=1008=16\cdot63$.)
note: Source confirmed from the official 2018 Purple Comet Middle School problems (Problem 5). The second problem of the post (multiples of 111 and 31 with sum 2017) is aliased to an earlier record. Checked by search.

question:
Is there anything ``bigger than infinity''? Mathematicians compare infinite sets as follows: a set $B$ is \emph{larger} than a set $A$ if there is no function from $A$ onto $B$, that is, no way of assigning to each element of $A$ an element of $B$ so that every element of $B$ is used.

Let $\mathbb{N}=\{1,2,3,\dots\}$ and let $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})$ be the set of all subsets of $\mathbb{N}$. Prove that there is no function $f:\mathbb{N}\to\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})$ onto $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})$. (So $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})$ is an infinite set larger than $\mathbb{N}$.)
solution:
Let $f:\mathbb{N}\to\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})$ be any function; each $f(n)$ is a subset of $\mathbb{N}$. Define
\[D=\{n\in\mathbb{N}:\ n\notin f(n)\}.\]
This is a subset of $\mathbb{N}$. We show that $D$ is not a value of $f$. Suppose $D=f(k)$ for some $k$.
\begin{itemize}
\item If $k\in D$, then by the definition of $D$, $k\notin f(k)=D$, a contradiction.
\item If $k\notin D$, then $k\notin f(k)$, so by the definition of $D$, $k\in D$, a contradiction.
\end{itemize}
Either way we get a contradiction, so $D\ne f(k)$ for every $k$, and $f$ is not onto. $\blacksquare$

(This is Cantor's diagonal argument: $D$ differs from the set $f(n)$ in whether it contains $n$. Repeating the construction gives larger and larger infinite sets, so there is no largest infinity.)
note: The post asks "Is there a number bigger than infinity?"; it is turned into Cantor's theorem that the set of subsets of N is larger than N.

question: A sequence has $a_1=2$ and $a_{n+1}=a_n+23$ for $n\ge1$. Find $a_{100}$.
solution:
Each step adds $23$, so the sequence is arithmetic with first term $2$ and common difference $23$, and $a_n=2+23(n-1)$. Hence
\[a_{100}=2+23\cdot99=2+2277=\boxed{2279}.\]

question:
Find all triples of integers $(x,y,z)$ with
\[x+y+z=xyz.\]
solution:
\textbf{One variable is $0$.} If, say, $z=0$, the equation becomes $x+y=0$. So every triple with one entry $0$ and the other two opposite, $(t,-t,0)$ in any order with $t$ an integer, is a solution (this includes $(0,0,0)$).

\textbf{No variable is $0$.} Replacing $(x,y,z)$ by $(-x,-y,-z)$ changes the sign of both sides, so it maps solutions to solutions. Hence we may assume that at least two of the variables are positive.
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{All three positive.} By symmetry let $x\le y\le z$. Then $xyz=x+y+z\le3z$, so $xy\le3$, and $(x,y)$ is $(1,1)$, $(1,2)$ or $(1,3)$. The first gives $2+z=z$, impossible; the second gives $3+z=2z$, so $z=3$; the third gives $4+z=3z$, so $z=2<y$, contradicting $y\le z$. So $\{x,y,z\}=\{1,2,3\}$, and indeed $1+2+3=6=1\cdot2\cdot3$.
\item \emph{Exactly two positive}, say $x,y>0>z$. Put $z=-w$ with $w>0$: then $x+y-w=-xyw$, i.e. $x+y=w(1-xy)$. The left side is positive, while $xy\ge1$ makes the right side at most $0$. No solutions.
\end{itemize}
Undoing the sign change adds the triples formed by $-1,-2,-3$.

\textbf{Answer.} The solutions are all permutations of $(1,2,3)$ and of $(-1,-2,-3)$, together with all permutations of $(t,-t,0)$ for integers $t$:
\[\boxed{(x,y,z)\in\{\text{perm. of }(1,2,3)\}\cup\{\text{perm. of }(-1,-2,-3)\}\cup\{\text{perm. of }(t,-t,0):t\in\mathbb{Z}\}}\]
note: "Integer roots" is read as integer solutions (x, y, z). Checked by brute force for |x|, |y|, |z| <= 30.

question:
Let $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ satisfy
\[f\left(x^2\right)=x\,f(x)\quad\text{for every real }x,\qquad\text{and}\qquad f(x)\ne0\text{ for }x\ne0,\]
so that $\dfrac{f\left(x^2\right)}{f(x)}=x$ for every $x\ne0$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Show that $f$ need not be of the form $f(x)=kx$.
\item[(b)] Prove that if $f$ is also continuous, then $f(x)=kx$ for some nonzero constant $k$.
\end{enumerate}
solution:
\textbf{(a)} Let $T=\left\{2^{\left(2^k\right)}:k\in\mathbb{Z}\right\}=\left\{\dots,\sqrt[4]{2},\sqrt2,2,4,16,256,\dots\right\}$ and define
\[f(x)=\begin{cases}2x,&|x|\in T,\\ x,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}\]
Then $f(x)\ne0$ for $x\ne0$. For a positive number $u$, $u\in T$ exactly when $u^2\in T$ (squaring replaces $2^{\left(2^k\right)}$ by $2^{\left(2^{k+1}\right)}$). So:
\begin{itemize}
\item if $|x|\in T$, then $x^2\in T$ and $f\left(x^2\right)=2x^2=x\cdot2x=x\,f(x)$;
\item if $|x|\notin T$ (including $x=0$), then $x^2\notin T$ and $f\left(x^2\right)=x^2=x\cdot x=x\,f(x)$.
\end{itemize}
So $f$ satisfies the conditions, but $f(1)=1$ while $f(2)=4$, so $f$ is not of the form $kx$.

\textbf{(b)} Putting $x=0$ gives $f(0)=0$. Replacing $x$ by $-x$ gives $f\left(x^2\right)=-x\,f(-x)$, so $x\,f(x)=-x\,f(-x)$ and $f(-x)=-f(x)$ for $x\ne0$: $f$ is odd.

For $x>0$ let $g(x)=\dfrac{f(x)}{x}$, which is continuous on $(0,\infty)$. The equation gives $g\left(x^2\right)=\dfrac{x\,f(x)}{x^2}=g(x)$, so $g(x)=g\left(\sqrt x\right)$ for $x>0$, and by repetition
\[g(x)=g\left(x^{\dfrac{1}{2^m}}\right)\quad\text{for every }m\ge1.\]
As $m\to\infty$, $x^{\dfrac{1}{2^m}}\to1$, so by continuity $g(x)=g(1)$. Hence $f(x)=kx$ for $x>0$, where $k=f(1)\ne0$. Since $f$ is odd and $f(0)=0$, also $f(x)=kx$ for $x\le0$. $\blacksquare$
note: The post asks whether f(x^2)/f(x) = x implies f(x) = kx. It does not in general (counterexample in (a)), but it does for continuous f (part (b)). The counterexample was checked numerically on random points and on points of T.

question: There are $5$ different pairs of gloves, and left and right gloves are distinguishable, so there are $10$ gloves in all. In how many ways can $4$ of the gloves be selected so that some $2$ of the $4$ form a pair? Count the selections directly (without complementary counting), and explain why a direct count giving $120$ is incomplete.
solution:
A selection of $4$ gloves containing a pair contains either exactly one complete pair or exactly two.
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Exactly one pair.} Choose the pair ($5$ ways), then $2$ of the other $8$ gloves that do not form a pair: $\dbinom82-4=24$ ways (the $4$ excluded choices are the remaining complete pairs). This gives $5\cdot24=120$ selections.
\item \textbf{Two pairs.} Choose $2$ of the $5$ pairs: $\dbinom52=10$ selections.
\end{itemize}
The total is $120+10=\boxed{130}$. A direct count of $120$ counts only the selections with exactly one pair and misses the $10$ selections made of two complete pairs.

(Check by complementary counting: there are $\dbinom{10}4=210$ selections, and $\dbinom54\cdot2^4=80$ of them contain no pair, one glove from each of $4$ different pairs; $210-80=130$.)
note: The poster obtained 120 directly and 130 by complementary counting; the record asks for the direct count (130) and for the missing case. Checked by enumerating all 210 selections.

solution:
\textbf{(a)} By assumption $a_1x_0+b_1y_0$ and $c_1$ are the same number, and $a_2x_0+b_2y_0$ and $c_2$ are the same number. Adding equal numbers to equal numbers gives equal results:
\[(a_1x_0+b_1y_0)+(a_2x_0+b_2y_0)=c_1+c_2,\quad\text{i.e.}\quad(a_1+a_2)x_0+(b_1+b_2)y_0=c_1+c_2.\ \blacksquare\]

\textbf{(b)} Adding $x+y=7$ and $x-y=1$ gives $2x=8$. The pair $(4,100)$ satisfies $2x=8$ but neither $x+y=7$ nor $x-y=1$.

\textbf{(c)} If $(x,y)$ solves the system, then by (a) it satisfies $2x=8$, so $x=4$, and then $y=7-x=3$. Conversely $(4,3)$ satisfies both equations ($4+3=7$, $4-3=1$). The solution is $\boxed{(x,y)=(4,3)}$.

Because of (b), adding equations only gives a \emph{necessary} condition; that is why the values found must be substituted back into the original equations.
note: The post asks why a pair that satisfies two equations also satisfies their sum; it is turned into a short exercise with the proof, a counterexample to the converse, and an elimination example.

question:
Solve the equation
\[x^4+ax^3+bx^2+ax+1=0\]
over the complex numbers, in terms of $a$ and $b$.
solution:
Since the constant term is $1$, $x=0$ is not a root, so we may divide by $x^2$:
\[x^2+\dfrac1{x^2}+a\left(x+\dfrac1x\right)+b=0.\]
Put $t=x+\dfrac1x$. Then $x^2+\dfrac1{x^2}=t^2-2$, so
\[t^2+at+(b-2)=0,\qquad t=t_{1,2}=\dfrac{-a\pm\sqrt{a^2-4b+8}}{2}.\]
For each value $t$, the equation $x+\dfrac1x=t$ is equivalent (for $x\ne0$) to $x^2-tx+1=0$, so
\[x=\dfrac{t\pm\sqrt{t^2-4}}{2}.\]
Conversely, every such $x$ is nonzero (the roots of $x^2-tx+1$ have product $1$) and satisfies the original equation, since the steps can be reversed. So the four roots (with multiplicity) are
\[\boxed{x=\dfrac{t\pm\sqrt{t^2-4}}{2},\qquad\text{where }t=\dfrac{-a\pm\sqrt{a^2-4b+8}}{2}}\]
(complex square roots are allowed). For example, $a=-10$, $b=26$ gives $t^2-10t+24=0$, $t=4$ or $6$, and the roots $2\pm\sqrt3$, $3\pm2\sqrt2$.
note: Checked symbolically: the product of (x^2 - t1 x + 1)(x^2 - t2 x + 1) is the quartic, with t1 + t2 = -a and t1 t2 = b - 2.

question: Prove that if $a$, $b$, $c$ are integers and $a^3+b^3+c^3$ is divisible by $9$, then at least one of $a$, $b$, $c$ is divisible by $3$.
solution:
We first find the cubes modulo $9$ of integers not divisible by $3$. Such an integer is $3k\pm1$, and
\[(3k\pm1)^3=27k^3\pm27k^2+9k\pm1\equiv\pm1\pmod9.\]
Suppose none of $a,b,c$ is divisible by $3$. Then each of $a^3,b^3,c^3$ is $\equiv\pm1\pmod9$, so their sum is congruent to one of
\[1+1+1=3,\quad1+1-1=1,\quad1-1-1=-1,\quad-1-1-1=-3\pmod9,\]
none of which is $0$. This contradicts $9\mid a^3+b^3+c^3$. Hence at least one of $a,b,c$ is divisible by $3$. $\blacksquare$

(With a square in place of the first cube the statement would be false: $a=4$, $b=c=1$ give $16+1+1=18$, divisible by $9$, while none of $4,1,1$ is divisible by $3$.)
note: The post writes "9/(a^2+b^3+c^3)", a garbled divisibility statement with a^2 in place of a^3. With a^2 it is false (a = 4, b = c = 1 give 18); the record proves the intended version 9 | a^3 + b^3 + c^3 and mentions the counterexample. Checked over all residues mod 9.

question: Compute $199-12$.

Find all real numbers $a$ such that the equation
\[(a^3-a)x^2+(a^2+a)x+a+1=0\]
(in the unknown $x$) has at most one real solution.
solution:
The coefficients factor as $a^3-a=a(a-1)(a+1)$, $a^2+a=a(a+1)$ and $a+1$.

\textbf{Degenerate cases.}
\begin{itemize}
\item $a=-1$: all three coefficients are $0$, the equation reads $0=0$, and every real $x$ is a solution. Not allowed.
\item $a=0$: the equation reads $1=0$: no solutions. Allowed.
\item $a=1$: the equation reads $2x+2=0$: exactly one solution. Allowed.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Quadratic case} ($a\ne0,\pm1$). There is at most one real solution exactly when the discriminant is at most $0$:
\[\Delta=a^2(a+1)^2-4a(a-1)(a+1)\cdot(a+1)=a(a+1)^2\bigl(a-4(a-1)\bigr)=a(a+1)^2(4-3a).\]
Since $(a+1)^2>0$, we need $a(4-3a)\le0$, i.e. $a<0$ or $a\ge\dfrac43$ (as $a\ne0$).

\textbf{Answer.} Combining the cases,
\[\boxed{a<-1,\quad\text{or}\quad-1<a\le0,\quad\text{or}\quad a=1,\quad\text{or}\quad a\ge\dfrac43}.\]
note: The post omits "= 0". The degenerate values a = -1 (every x is a solution), a = 0 and a = 1 are handled separately. Checked on a grid of rational a.

question: The decimal expansion of $\dfrac{1}{10!}$ is eventually periodic. How many digits after the decimal point come before the repeating part starts, and what is the length of the repeating block (the period)?
solution:
Factor $10!=2^8\cdot3^4\cdot5^2\cdot7=2^8\cdot5^2\cdot567$, where $567=3^4\cdot7$ is coprime to $10$.

The expansion of $x=\dfrac1{10!}$ consists of $k$ digits followed by a repeating block of length $p$ exactly when $10^k\left(10^p-1\right)x$ is an integer (shifting by $k$ digits and subtracting removes the repeating part). So we need
\[10!\ \Big|\ 10^k\left(10^p-1\right),\quad\text{i.e.}\quad2^8\cdot5^2\cdot567\ \Big|\ 2^k5^k\left(10^p-1\right).\]
Since $10^p-1$ is odd and not divisible by $5$, this requires $k\ge8$, and then $567\mid10^p-1$. So the repeating part starts after $8$ digits, and the period is the least $p$ with $567\mid10^p-1$, the order of $10$ modulo $567$. As $81$ and $7$ are coprime, this order is the least common multiple of the orders modulo $81$ and modulo $7$.
\begin{itemize}
\item Modulo $81$: $10^p-1=9\cdot\underbrace{11\cdots1}_{p}$, and $9$ divides the repunit $11\cdots1$ exactly when $9$ divides its digit sum $p$. So the order of $10$ modulo $81$ is $9$.
\item Modulo $7$: the powers $10^1,\dots,10^6$ are $3,2,6,4,5,1\pmod7$, so the order is $6$.
\end{itemize}
Hence the period is $\operatorname{lcm}(9,6)=18$:
\[\boxed{8\text{ digits before the repeating part, period }18}.\]
note: The post asks for a fast way to find the period of a repeating decimal, with 1/10! as its example; the record asks for the pre-period (8) and period (18) of 1/10!, checked by long division.

solution:
\textbf{(a)}
\[47\,300\,000=4.73\times10^7=47.3\times10^6,\qquad0.00052=5.2\times10^{-4}=520\times10^{-6}.\]

\textbf{(b)} Start from $a\times10^n$ with $1\le a<10$. Write $n=3q+r$ with $r\in\{0,1,2\}$. Then
\[a\times10^n=\left(a\times10^r\right)\times10^{3q},\]
and $1\le a\times10^r<10\cdot10^2=1000$, so this is the engineering form: move the decimal point $r$ places to the right and lower the exponent to the multiple of $3$ at or below $n$. For example $4.73\times10^7$ has $7=3\cdot2+1$, giving $47.3\times10^6$; and $5.2\times10^{-4}$ has $-4=3\cdot(-2)+2$, giving $520\times10^{-6}$.

The metric prefixes go up and down in steps of $10^3$, so a quantity in engineering notation can be read off directly with a prefix: $47.3\times10^6$ watts is $47.3$ megawatts, and $520\times10^{-6}$ m is $520$ micrometres. That is why engineering notation is used for measurements in science and engineering, while scientific notation (one digit before the decimal point) is preferred for comparing orders of magnitude.
note: The post asks for the difference between engineering and scientific notation; it is turned into a short exercise with conversions.

solution:
\textbf{(a)} Expand:
\[(2m-1)^2=4m^2-4m+1=4m(m-1)+1.\]
The product $m(m-1)$ of two consecutive integers is even, so $4m(m-1)$ is divisible by $8$ and $(2m-1)^2\equiv1\pmod8$. Since $8n^2\equiv0\pmod8$,
\[x=(2m-1)^2-8n^2\equiv\boxed{1}\pmod8.\]

\textbf{(b)} $m=n=1$ gives $x=1-8=-7$, while $m=2$, $n=1$ gives $x=9-8=1$. Both leave remainder $1$ on division by $8$, but they are different, so $x$ is not determined.
note: The post asks for "the value of x", which depends on m and n; the only determined information is that x is 1 mod 8 (every odd square is 1 mod 8). The record asks for that and for an example showing x is not determined.

question:
Simplify
\[\sqrt{97-56\sqrt3}+\sqrt{97+56\sqrt3}.\]
solution:
Look for $(p\pm q\sqrt3)^2=p^2+3q^2\pm2pq\sqrt3$ with $p^2+3q^2=97$ and $2pq=56$, i.e. $pq=28$. Trying $p=7$, $q=4$: $49+48=97$. So
\[97\pm56\sqrt3=\left(7\pm4\sqrt3\right)^2.\]
Both $7+4\sqrt3$ and $7-4\sqrt3$ are positive (since $4\sqrt3=\sqrt{48}<7$), so they are the principal square roots, and
\[\sqrt{97-56\sqrt3}+\sqrt{97+56\sqrt3}=\left(7-4\sqrt3\right)+\left(7+4\sqrt3\right)=\boxed{14}.\]
note: The post presents the two expressions as a calculator "magic trick"; the record asks for the exact values.

question:
Simplify
\[\sqrt{37+\sqrt{1200}}+\sqrt{61-\sqrt{2352}}.\]
solution:
First $\sqrt{1200}=\sqrt{400\cdot3}=20\sqrt3$ and $\sqrt{2352}=\sqrt{784\cdot3}=28\sqrt3$. Now
\[\left(5+2\sqrt3\right)^2=25+12+20\sqrt3=37+20\sqrt3,\qquad\left(7-2\sqrt3\right)^2=49+12-28\sqrt3=61-28\sqrt3.\]
Both $5+2\sqrt3$ and $7-2\sqrt3$ are positive ($2\sqrt3=\sqrt{12}<7$), so
\[\sqrt{37+\sqrt{1200}}+\sqrt{61-\sqrt{2352}}=\left(5+2\sqrt3\right)+\left(7-2\sqrt3\right)=\boxed{12}.\]

question:
Let
\[f(x)=\begin{cases}3x+6,&x<5,\\7x-20,&x\ge5.\end{cases}\]
Find $f(f(f(2)))$.

\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Prove the two-variable AM-GM inequality: for nonnegative real numbers $a$ and $b$,
\[\dfrac{a+b}{2}\ge\sqrt{ab},\]
with equality if and only if $a=b$.
\item[(b)] Find the minimum value of $x+\dfrac9x$ for $x>0$.
\item[(c)] If $x$ and $y$ are positive numbers with $x+y=10$, find the largest possible value of $xy$.
\end{enumerate}
solution:
\textbf{(a)} Since $a,b\ge0$, the numbers $\sqrt a$, $\sqrt b$ are real, and
\[\left(\sqrt a-\sqrt b\right)^2\ge0\iff a-2\sqrt{ab}+b\ge0\iff\dfrac{a+b}2\ge\sqrt{ab}.\]
Equality holds exactly when $\sqrt a=\sqrt b$, i.e. $a=b$. $\blacksquare$

In words: the arithmetic mean of two nonnegative numbers is at least their geometric mean. (More generally, $\dfrac{a_1+\cdots+a_n}{n}\ge\sqrt[n]{a_1\cdots a_n}$ for nonnegative $a_i$, with equality only when all are equal.) It is most useful when a sum is to be minimised and the product is constant, or a product maximised and the sum is constant.

\textbf{(b)} By (a) with $a=x$, $b=\dfrac9x$:
\[x+\dfrac9x\ge2\sqrt{x\cdot\dfrac9x}=6,\]
with equality when $x=\dfrac9x$, i.e. $x=3$. The minimum is $\boxed{6}$.

\textbf{(c)} By (a), $\sqrt{xy}\le\dfrac{x+y}{2}=5$, so $xy\le25$, with equality when $x=y=5$. The largest value is $\boxed{25}$.
note: The post asks for a summary of AM-GM; it is turned into an exercise: the proof of the two-variable case and two standard applications.

question:
The Fermat numbers are $F_k=2^{2^k}+1$ for $k=0,1,2,\dots$, so $F_0=3$, $F_1=5$, $F_2=17$, $F_3=257$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Prove that $F_0F_1\cdots F_{n-1}=F_n-2$ for every $n\ge1$.
\item[(b)] Deduce that any two different Fermat numbers are relatively prime.
\item[(c)] Deduce that there are infinitely many prime numbers.
\item[(d)] A student stated the identity in (a) as $F_1F_2\cdots F_n=F_{n+1}-2$. Show that this version is false.
\end{enumerate}
solution:
\textbf{(a)} Induction on $n$. For $n=1$: $F_0=3=5-2=F_1-2$. If $F_0\cdots F_{n-1}=F_n-2$, then
\[F_0\cdots F_{n-1}F_n=(F_n-2)F_n=\left(2^{2^n}-1\right)\left(2^{2^n}+1\right)=2^{2^{n+1}}-1=F_{n+1}-2.\ \blacksquare\]

\textbf{(b)} Let $m<n$ and let $d$ be a positive common divisor of $F_m$ and $F_n$. Since $F_m$ is one of the factors in (a), $d\mid F_0\cdots F_{n-1}=F_n-2$. Then $d$ divides $F_n-(F_n-2)=2$, so $d=1$ or $2$. All Fermat numbers are odd, so $d=1$. $\blacksquare$

\textbf{(c)} Each $F_k>1$ has a prime factor $p_k$. If $p_j=p_k$ for some $j\ne k$, this prime would divide both $F_j$ and $F_k$, contradicting (b). So $p_0,p_1,p_2,\dots$ are infinitely many different primes. $\blacksquare$

\textbf{(d)} For $n=1$ the statement says $F_1=F_2-2$, i.e. $5=15$, which is false. (The factor $F_0=3$ is missing: in fact $F_1\cdots F_n=\dfrac{F_{n+1}-2}{3}$.)
note: The post proves the infinitude of primes via Fermat numbers (an argument from Goldbach's 1730 letter to Euler), but states the identity with the product starting at F(1) (false: F_1 = 5 but F_2 - 2 = 15), ends its induction step with F(n+2) instead of F(n+2) - 2, and does not say why coprimality gives infinitely many primes. The record asks for a correct proof and for the counterexample. Checked for n up to 8.

question:
Nigel buys a car worth \$300,000 for only \$76,000. He then drives it until it is worth only $80\%$ of its original value. If he finds someone who will buy it from him for \$400,000, what percent of the car's original value will he have gained?

$\textbf{(A) }108\%\qquad\textbf{(B) }112\%\qquad\textbf{(C) }120\%\qquad\textbf{(D) }124\%\qquad\textbf{(E) }128\%$
solution:
Nigel paid \$76,000 and receives \$400,000, so he gains \$324,000. As a percentage of the car's original value of \$300,000, this is
\[\dfrac{324000}{300000}\cdot100\%=108\%.\]
The answer is $\boxed{\textbf{(A) }108\%}$. (The drop to $80\%$ of the original value does not change what Nigel pays or receives; it is extra information.)
note: "Gained" is read as the selling price minus the purchase price, as a percentage of the original value; the 80% depreciation is irrelevant to it.

question: For a nonnegative integer $n$, $n$ trees are to be planted in a row of $n+10$ plots, at most one tree per plot, so that no two trees are in adjacent plots. Each tree can be one of two types. Let $k(n)$ be the number of ways to plant the trees (choosing both the plots and the types). Find the sum of $k(n)$ over all nonnegative integers $n$ for which $k(n)>0$.
solution:
\textbf{Choosing the plots.} Number the plots $1,\dots,n+10$ and let the trees be in plots $p_1<p_2<\cdots<p_n$ with $p_{i+1}-p_i\ge2$. Put $q_i=p_i-(i-1)$. Then
\[1\le q_1<q_2<\cdots<q_n\le(n+10)-(n-1)=11,\]
and conversely every $n$-element subset $\{q_1<\cdots<q_n\}$ of $\{1,\dots,11\}$ gives a valid placement via $p_i=q_i+(i-1)$. So there are $\dbinom{11}{n}$ placements, which is $0$ for $n\ge12$.

\textbf{Types.} Each of the $n$ trees has $2$ types, so $k(n)=\dbinom{11}{n}2^n$ for $0\le n\le11$ and $k(n)=0$ for $n\ge12$.

\textbf{The sum.} By the binomial theorem,
\[\sum_{n=0}^{11}\dbinom{11}{n}2^n=(1+2)^{11}=3^{11}=\boxed{177147}.\]
note: Checked by brute force over all placements for n = 0 to 12.

question: Find all positive integers that are equal to the sum of the factorials of their digits (with $0!=1$).
solution:
Let $S(n)$ be the sum of the factorials of the digits of $n$.

\textbf{Bound.} If $n$ has $d$ digits, then $n\ge10^{d-1}$ and $S(n)\le d\cdot9!=362880d$. For $d=8$, $8\cdot362880=2903040<10^7$, and when $d$ increases by $1$ the bound $362880d$ grows by $362880$ while $10^{d-1}$ is multiplied by $10$. So $S(n)<n$ whenever $d\ge8$: a solution has at most $7$ digits, and $n\le7\cdot9!=2540160$.

\textbf{One and two digits.} $n=n!$ gives $n=1$ or $n=2$. For two digits, a digit $\ge5$ gives $S(n)\ge120>99$; so all digits are at most $4$ and $n=10a+b\le S(n)\le48$, i.e. $a\le4$. Then $a!+b!=10a+b$ means $b!=b+9$, $b+18$, $b+24$ or $b+16$ for $a=1,2,3,4$, and no $b\le4$ satisfies any of these.

\textbf{Three digits.} No digit is $7$ or more ($7!>999$). A digit $6$ would give $n=S(n)\ge720$, so the first digit would be at least $7$: impossible. If all digits are at most $4$, then $S(n)\le72<100$. So some digit is $5$, and $122\le S(n)\le360$, so the first digit $a$ is $1$, $2$ or $3$. If both other digits are $5$, then $S(n)=a!+240\in\{241,242,246\}$ while $n\in\{155,255,355\}$: no. Otherwise exactly one other digit is $5$ and the remaining digit $e$ is at most $4$, so $S(n)\le6+120+24=150$; then $a=1$ and $S(n)=121+e!\le145$, which rules out $n=15e\ge150$. So $n=1e5=105+10e$ with $105+10e=121+e!$, i.e. $e!=10e-16$, whose only solution with $e\le4$ is $e=4$: $n=145=1!+4!+5!$.

\textbf{Four to seven digits.} This is a finite check of the numbers from $1000$ to $2540160$ (it can be organised by the multiset of digits, since $S(n)$ depends only on the digits and not on their order); carried out by computer, it finds exactly one more solution:
\[40585=4!+0!+5!+8!+5!=24+1+120+40320+120.\]

So the numbers are $\boxed{1,\ 2,\ 145,\ 40585}$.
note: The "AMC infinity" story is dropped. The solution proves the bound and the cases with at most three digits by hand; the four- to seven-digit range (up to 7 x 9! = 2540160) is a finite search done by computer, which is stated in the solution. All numbers up to 2540160 were checked.

solution:
\textbf{(a)} The only integer $k$ with $1\le k\le1$ is $k=1$, and $\gcd(1,1)=1$. So $\varphi(1)=\boxed{1}$.

\textbf{(b)} There are no positive integers less than $1$, so that wording would give $0$ for $n=1$ (for $n\ge2$ the two definitions agree, since $\gcd(n,n)=n\ne1$). But $2$ and $1$ are relatively prime, so the multiplicative rule would give
\[\varphi(2)=\varphi(2\cdot1)=\varphi(2)\varphi(1)=\varphi(2)\cdot0=0,\]
while $\varphi(2)=1$ (only $k=1$ is coprime to $2$). So the rule requires $\varphi(1)=1$, which is why the definition uses $1\le k\le n$.

question:
Find all pairs of positive integers $(m,n)$ such that
\[2023^m=17^n+2006.\]
solution:
Factor the constants: $2023=7\cdot17^2$ and $2006=2\cdot17\cdot59$.

Since $m\ge1$, the left side is divisible by $17^2=289$. Now look at the right side modulo $289$.
\begin{itemize}
\item If $n\ge2$, then $289\mid17^n$, so $17^n+2006\equiv2006=6\cdot289+272\equiv272\pmod{289}$, which is not $0$. So there is no solution with $n\ge2$.
\item If $n=1$, the right side is $17+2006=2023$, so $2023^m=2023$ and $m=1$.
\end{itemize}
Hence the only solution is $\boxed{(m,n)=(1,1)}$.

(If $0$ is counted as a natural number, nothing new appears: $m=0$ gives $1=17^n+2006$, impossible, and $n=0$ gives $2023^m=2007$, which is not a power of $2023$.)
note: The post says "solve in N"; the record asks for positive integers and remarks that allowing 0 adds nothing. Checked by direct search over small m and n.

question: Geoff the frog starts at the origin of the coordinate plane. Each move is either one unit to the right ($R$) or one unit up ($U$). Every up move must be immediately followed by a right move, except that the last move of the sequence may be an up move. How many different sequences of moves take Geoff from the origin to the point $(9,5)$?
solution:
Every sequence ending at $(9,5)$ consists of $9$ moves $R$ and $5$ moves $U$, $14$ moves in all. We split by the last move.

\textbf{Last move $R$.} Then every $U$ is immediately followed by an $R$. Glue each $U$ to the $R$ after it, forming a block $UR$. The sequence becomes an arrangement of $5$ blocks $UR$ and $9-5=4$ single moves $R$, and conversely every such arrangement gives a valid sequence ending in $R$ (the last item is a block $UR$ or a single $R$). There are $\dbinom{9}{5}=126$ arrangements of $9$ items, $5$ of which are blocks.

\textbf{Last move $U$.} The first $13$ moves contain $9$ moves $R$ and $4$ moves $U$, and each of these $U$ must be followed by $R$ (a $U$ in position $13$ would be followed by the final $U$, which is not allowed). So the first $13$ moves form a sequence of the previous kind with $4$ blocks $UR$ and $5$ single $R$: there are $\dbinom{9}{4}=126$ of them.

The total is $126+126=\boxed{252}$.
note: Checked by listing all arrangements of 9 R and 5 U.
The post asks in general how to find the other endpoint from one endpoint and the midpoint; the record proves the formula and adds a numerical example.

solution:
\textbf{(a)} The output in second $k$ is uniform on $\{1,\dots,k\}$, so its expected value is $\dfrac{1+k}{2}$. By linearity of expectation,
\[E(S_n)=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\dfrac{k+1}{2}=\dfrac12\left(\dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}+n\right)=\boxed{\dfrac{n(n+3)}{4}}.\]

\textbf{(b)} We need $n(n+3)=1120$, i.e. $n^2+3n-1120=0$, which factors as $(n-32)(n+35)=0$. So $\boxed{n=32}$.

(Remark: this is not the same as the expected number of seconds until the sum first reaches $280$. That waiting time is a different random variable; computed exactly it is about $32.58$, not $32$.)
note: The post asks for the expected number of seconds until the sum is at least 280. Computed exactly by dynamic programming this is about 32.577, a rational number with a huge denominator and no reasonable closed form, so the record asks instead for the time at which the expected sum equals 280 (n = 32) and remarks on the difference. Checked by the exact DP and by the formula. Problem 6 of the post is aliased.

solution:
\textbf{(a)} \emph{Step 1 is invalid.} The partial sums of $1-1+1-1+\cdots$ are $1,0,1,0,\dots$, which do not approach any number, so the series has no sum. (The value $\dfrac12$ is the average of the partial sums, a different notion; treating it as a sum leads to contradictions, since grouping the terms as $(1-1)+(1-1)+\cdots$ would give $0$ and as $1-(1-1)-(1-1)-\cdots$ would give $1$.)

\emph{Step 2 is valid.} Indeed $\dfrac{1}{11}=0.\overline{09}$ and $\dfrac{10}{11}=0.\overline{90}$, and the alternating series converges absolutely:
\[\dfrac{9}{10}-\dfrac{9}{100}+\dfrac{9}{1000}-\cdots=\dfrac{\dfrac{9}{10}}{1+\dfrac{1}{10}}=\dfrac{9}{11},\]
which agrees with $x=1$.

\emph{Step 3 is invalid.} The inequality $\left(\sum a_i\right)\left(\sum b_i\right)\ge\left(\sum\sqrt{a_ib_i}\right)^2$ follows from Cauchy--Schwarz only when all $a_i$ and $b_i$ are \emph{nonnegative} (apply Cauchy--Schwarz to the vectors $(\sqrt{a_i})$ and $(\sqrt{b_i})$), and for infinite series it also needs the series to converge. Here the terms alternate in sign, and $\sum a_i$ does not converge at all. With signed terms the inequality is simply false: for $a=(1,-1)$ and $b=(1,-1)$,
\[\left(\sum a_i\right)\left(\sum b_i\right)=0\cdot0=0<4=\left(\sqrt1+\sqrt1\right)^2.\]
(The arithmetic in step 3 is correct, since $\sum_{i\ge1}\dfrac{3}{10^{\dfrac i2}}=\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{10}-1}$, but the inequality it starts from does not apply.)

\textbf{(b)} By definition $0.\overline{9}=\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\dfrac{9}{10^i}$, the limit of the partial sums
\[s_n=\dfrac{9}{10}+\dfrac{9}{100}+\cdots+\dfrac{9}{10^n}=1-\dfrac{1}{10^n}.\]
As $n\to\infty$, $\dfrac{1}{10^n}\to0$, so $s_n\to1$ and $\boxed{0.\overline{9}=1}$. $\blacksquare$
note: A joke "thesis" claiming 0.999... >= 4.705 is turned into a find-the-errors exercise: step 1 (1 - 1 + 1 - ... = 1/2) and step 3 (Cauchy-Schwarz with signed terms and a divergent series) are invalid; step 2 is correct. The numerical value 22/(sqrt10 - 1)^2 = 4.7055 was checked.
