solution:
\textbf{(a)} Suppose $ax\equiv1\pmod n$, so $ax-1=ny$ for some integer $y$. Any common divisor $d$ of $a$ and $n$ divides $ax-ny=1$, so $\gcd(a,n)=1$.

Conversely, suppose $\gcd(a,n)=1$. Look at the $n$ numbers $a\cdot0,\ a\cdot1,\ \dots,\ a\cdot(n-1)$. If two of them were congruent, $ai\equiv aj\pmod n$ with $0\le j<i\le n-1$, then $n\mid a(i-j)$. Since $a$ and $n$ have no common prime factor, every prime power dividing $n$ must divide $i-j$, so $n\mid i-j$, which is impossible because $0<i-j<n$. So the $n$ numbers have $n$ different remainders modulo $n$; that is, every remainder $0,1,\dots,n-1$ occurs exactly once. In particular $ax\equiv1\pmod n$ for some $x$. $\blacksquare$

\textbf{(b)} $\gcd(9,26)=1$, so $9$ is invertible modulo $26$; since $9\cdot3=27\equiv1\pmod{26}$, an inverse is $3$. But $\gcd(13,26)=13$, so $13$ is not invertible: indeed $13x$ is always $\equiv0$ or $\equiv13\pmod{26}$, never $\equiv1$.

So $\boxed{9\text{ is invertible (inverse }3\text{), }13\text{ is not}}$.
note: The post asks how to tell whether a number is invertible mod n; the record asks for the proof of the criterion gcd(a, n) = 1, with a worked example.

question: Find the tens digit of $123456789^{10111213141516171819}$. Explain why it is enough to work modulo $100$.
solution:
\textbf{Why modulo $100$.} Any positive integer $N$ can be written as $N=100q+r$ with $0\le r\le99$, where $r$ is the number formed by the last two digits of $N$. So the tens digit of $N$ is the tens digit of the remainder $r=N\bmod100$, and we only need $N$ modulo $100$.

\textbf{The computation.} Let $e=10111213141516171819$. Since $123456789\equiv89\equiv-11\pmod{100}$ and $e$ is odd,
\[123456789^{e}\equiv(-11)^e=-11^e\pmod{100}.\]
By the binomial theorem,
\[11^e=(1+10)^e=1+\dbinom e1\cdot10+\dbinom e2\cdot10^2+\cdots\equiv1+10e\pmod{100}.\]
As $e\equiv9\pmod{10}$, we have $10e\equiv90\pmod{100}$, so $11^e\equiv91$ and
\[123456789^{e}\equiv-91\equiv9\pmod{100}.\]
The number ends in the digits $09$, so its tens digit is $\boxed{0}$.
note: The post (from a number theory marathon) only asks why one works mod 100; the record asks for the tens digit as well. Checked with modular exponentiation.

solution:
Since $2\cdot7=14\equiv1\pmod{13}$, multiplying by $7$ undoes multiplying by $2$ modulo $13$.

\textbf{(a)} $x\equiv7\cdot5=35\equiv9\pmod{13}$. Check: $2\cdot9=18\equiv5$.

\textbf{(b)} $x\equiv7\cdot6=42\equiv3\pmod{13}$. Check: $2\cdot3=6$.

No integer satisfies both: that would need $5\equiv2x\equiv6\pmod{13}$, which is false. (Equivalently, $x\equiv9$ and $x\equiv3\pmod{13}$ are incompatible.)

So the solutions are $\boxed{x\equiv9\pmod{13}}$ for (a) and $\boxed{x\equiv3\pmod{13}}$ for (b), and there is no common solution.
note: The post lists the two congruences without saying whether they form a system; the record solves each one and also answers the system reading (no solution).

question:
Without a calculator, explain why
\[(5\cdot11)(3\cdot11)-15=15\left(11\cdot11-1\right),\]
and use this to evaluate $55\cdot33-15$.
solution:
Rearranging the factors (multiplication is commutative and associative),
\[(5\cdot11)(3\cdot11)=(5\cdot3)(11\cdot11)=15\cdot121.\]
So the expression is $15\cdot121-15\cdot1$, and taking out the common factor $15$ (the distributive law) gives
\[(5\cdot11)(3\cdot11)-15=15(121-1)=15\left(11\cdot11-1\right).\]
Hence
\[55\cdot33-15=15\cdot120=\boxed{1800}.\]
(One can also write $11\cdot11-1=(11-1)(11+1)=10\cdot12$.)

question:
For $x>0$, simplify
\[\sqrt{\dfrac{x}{1-\dfrac{x-1}{x}}}\,.\]
Explain why the answer is $x$ and not $\pm x$.
solution:
For $x\ne0$,
\[1-\dfrac{x-1}{x}=\dfrac{x-(x-1)}{x}=\dfrac1x,\qquad\text{so}\qquad\dfrac{x}{1-\dfrac{x-1}{x}}=\dfrac{x}{\dfrac1x}=x^2.\]
Hence the expression equals $\sqrt{x^2}$.

The symbol $\sqrt{\ \ }$ always means the \emph{nonnegative} square root, so $\sqrt{x^2}=|x|$ for every real $x$. (For example $\sqrt{(-3)^2}=\sqrt9=3$, not $-3$.) Since $x>0$, $|x|=x$, and the expression simplifies to $\boxed{x}$.

The sign $\pm$ appears when we \emph{solve} an equation such as $t^2=x^2$, which has the two solutions $t=\pm x$; but a single expression such as $\sqrt{x^2}$ has only one value. That is why the condition $x>0$ is given: it lets us replace $|x|$ by $x$.
note: The unbracketed "sqrt(x/1-(x-1/x))" is read, as the poster's own working shows, as the square root of x divided by 1 - (x - 1)/x. The exercise is from a textbook (AoPS Introduction to Algebra 20.1.3), not a competition.
The post asks a conceptual question about counting on a circle; the record turns it into a bracelet count with distinct beads plus the explanation.

question: A Pythagorean triple is a triple $(a,b,c)$ of positive integers with $a<b$ and $a^2+b^2=c^2$. Find all Pythagorean triples in which one of the three numbers is $2021$.
solution:
Note that $2021=43\cdot47$, a product of two primes, both $\equiv3\pmod4$.

\textbf{Case 1: $2021$ is a leg.} Let the other leg be $m$ and the hypotenuse $c$, so $(c-m)(c+m)=2021^2=43^2\cdot47^2$. The two factors are positive with $c-m<c+m$, and they are both odd since their product is odd. So $c-m=d$ is a divisor of $2021^2$ with $d<2021$, and $c+m=\dfrac{2021^2}{d}$. The divisors of $2021^2$ below $2021$ are $1$, $43$, $47$ and $43^2=1849$ (note $47^2=2209>2021$). They give
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{c|c|c|c}
$d=c-m$ & $c+m$ & $c$ & $m$\\
\hline
$1$ & $4084441$ & $2042221$ & $2042220$\\
$43$ & $94987$ & $47515$ & $47472$\\
$47$ & $86903$ & $43475$ & $43428$\\
$1849$ & $2209$ & $2029$ & $180$
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\textbf{Case 2: $2021$ is the hypotenuse.} We use a lemma: \emph{if $p$ is a prime with $p\equiv3\pmod4$ and $p\mid x^2+y^2$, then $p\mid x$ and $p\mid y$.} Indeed, if $p\nmid x$, let $x'$ be an inverse of $x$ modulo $p$ and $t=yx'$; then $t^2\equiv-1\pmod p$, so $p\nmid t$. Raising to the odd power $\dfrac{p-1}{2}$ gives $t^{p-1}\equiv(-1)^{\dfrac{p-1}{2}}=-1$, while Fermat's little theorem gives $t^{p-1}\equiv1$. Then $p\mid2$, which is false. So $p\mid x$, and then $p\mid y^2$, so $p\mid y$.

Now suppose $a^2+b^2=2021^2$ with $a,b>0$. As $43\mid a^2+b^2$, the lemma gives $43\mid a$ and $43\mid b$, and dividing by $43^2$, $\left(\dfrac a{43}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac b{43}\right)^2=47^2$. By the lemma with $p=47$, both $\dfrac a{43}$ and $\dfrac b{43}$ are multiples of $47$, so $\left(\dfrac{a}{2021}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{b}{2021}\right)^2=1$ with positive integers $\dfrac{a}{2021}$, $\dfrac{b}{2021}$. That is impossible, since the left side is at least $2$. So $2021$ is never the hypotenuse.

\textbf{Answer.} There are exactly four such triples:
\[\boxed{(180,2021,2029),\ (2021,43428,43475),\ (2021,47472,47515),\ (2021,2042220,2042221)}.\]
(For example, $180^2+2021^2=32400+4084441=4116841=2029^2$.)
note: The post only asks whether such a triple exists (yes); the record asks for all of them. Checked by brute force over all legs and all hypotenuse decompositions.

solution:
\textbf{(a)} For $n=3$, $2^3-7=1$ is not prime.

If $n\ge4$ is even, say $n=2k$, then $2^n=4^k\equiv1\pmod3$, so $2^n-7\equiv1-7=-6\equiv0\pmod3$. Since $2^n-7\ge9>3$, it is composite.

If $n\ge5$ and $n\equiv1\pmod4$, write $n=4k+1$; then $2^n=2\cdot16^k\equiv2\pmod5$, so $2^n-7\equiv-5\equiv0\pmod5$. Since $2^n-7\ge25>5$, it is composite.

The remaining $n\ge3$ are those with $n\equiv3\pmod4$, so a prime value needs $n\equiv3\pmod4$ (and $n\ge7$). $\blacksquare$

\textbf{(b)} By (a), only $n=7,11,15,19$ need checking:
\[2^7-7=121=11^2,\quad2^{11}-7=2041=13\cdot157,\quad2^{15}-7=32761=181^2,\quad2^{19}-7=524281=269\cdot1949.\]
All are composite, so $\boxed{2^n-7\text{ is composite for every }3\le n\le20}$, and the conjecture holds in this range.

(Remark: the conjecture is nevertheless false. A computer check shows that the smallest counterexample is $n=39$: $2^{39}-7=549755813881$ is prime.)
note: The conjecture is false, but its smallest counterexample (n = 39, 2^39 - 7 = 549755813881, prime) cannot be verified by hand; the record asks for the restriction n = 3 mod 4 and the check up to n = 20, and states the counterexample as a remark. Factorisations and the primality of 2^39 - 7 were checked with sympy.

question:
A student conjectures that the equation
\[z=\left(x^y+y-y^x\right)^{\dfrac1x}\]
has no solution in which $x$, $y$ and $z$ are all integers greater than $1$. Show that the conjecture is false.
solution:
Try $x=2$ and $y=4$, for which the powers $x^y=2^4=16$ and $y^x=4^2=16$ cancel:
\[x^y+y-y^x=16+4-16=4,\qquad z=4^{\dfrac12}=2.\]
So $(x,y,z)=\boxed{(2,4,2)}$ is a solution with all three numbers greater than $1$, and the conjecture is false.

(A computer search over $2\le x,y<40$ finds no other solution. Note that $x=y$ never works: then $z=y^{\dfrac1y}$, which lies strictly between $1$ and $2$ for $y\ge2$.)
note: "Other than 1" is read as all of x, y, z greater than 1. The search was checked with exact integer roots.

solution:
\textbf{(a)}
\[f(x)=\dfrac{1\cdot2\cdot3\cdots x}{2\cdot3\cdot4\cdots(x+1)}=\boxed{\dfrac{1}{x+1}},\]
since every factor $2,3,\dots,x$ appears once on top and once at the bottom.

\textbf{(b)} In every finite product the cancellation leaves two factors: the first numerator $1$ and the \emph{last} denominator $x+1$. The student cancelled all the denominators, but an infinite product has no last factor; the leftover denominator does not disappear, it only moves further out and grows. The value of an infinite product is defined as the limit of its partial products, and
\[\lim_{x\to\infty}f(x)=\lim_{x\to\infty}\dfrac{1}{x+1}=\boxed{0}.\]
This agrees with the observation that $f(x)$ keeps getting smaller. (The same faulty cancellation applied to $\dfrac21\cdot\dfrac32\cdot\dfrac43\cdots$ would also give $1$, although its partial products are $x+1$, which grow without bound.)
note: The poster asks whether their logic is wrong; the record asks for f(x) and for the error, with the limit as the value of the infinite product.

question:
A polynomial $f$ satisfies
\[f\left(2x+\dfrac1x\right)=x^2+\dfrac{1}{4x^2}+1\]
for every nonzero real number $x$. Find $f(x)$.
solution:
The right side is a perfect square:
\[\left(x+\dfrac{1}{2x}\right)^2=x^2+2\cdot x\cdot\dfrac{1}{2x}+\dfrac{1}{4x^2}=x^2+1+\dfrac{1}{4x^2},\qquad\text{and}\qquad x+\dfrac{1}{2x}=\dfrac12\left(2x+\dfrac1x\right).\]
So, writing $t=2x+\dfrac1x$, the condition says $f(t)=\dfrac{t^2}{4}$ for every number $t$ of this form.

Every $t\ge2\sqrt2$ is of this form: $2x+\dfrac1x=t$ means $2x^2-tx+1=0$, whose discriminant $t^2-8$ is nonnegative, and whose roots have positive product $\dfrac12$ and positive sum $\dfrac t2$, so they are positive real numbers. (By AM-GM, $2x+\dfrac1x\ge2\sqrt2$ for $x>0$, so these are exactly the values for $x>0$.)

Hence the polynomial $f(t)-\dfrac{t^2}{4}$ has infinitely many roots, so it is the zero polynomial, and
\[\boxed{f(x)=\dfrac{x^2}{4}}.\]
(Without the assumption that $f$ is a polynomial, the condition would fix $f(t)$ only for $|t|\ge2\sqrt2$, the values taken by $2x+\dfrac1x$.)
note: The unbracketed "1/4x^2" is read as 1/(4x^2). The record states that f is a polynomial (the title says "Polynomials"); otherwise f is determined only for |x| >= 2 sqrt 2. Checked symbolically.

question: Find two different positive integers that are relatively prime, whose decimal representations both contain the block of digits $1926$ (as consecutive digits), and whose sum is as small as possible.
solution:
The numbers containing the block $1926$, in increasing order, begin
\[1926,\ 11926,\ 19260,\ 19261,\ 19262,\ \dots,\ 19269,\ 21926,\ \dots\]
($1926$ is the only such number with four digits, and a five-digit one is $d1926$ or $1926d$ for a digit $d$).

A pair that does not contain $1926$ has both numbers at least $11926$, the smaller one, and $19260$, so its sum is at least $11926+19260=31186$.

A pair containing $1926=2\cdot3^2\cdot107$ must have an odd partner. The smallest odd number in the list after $1926$ is $19261$, and
\[\gcd(1926,19261)=\gcd(1926,\ 19261-10\cdot1926)=\gcd(1926,1)=1.\]
Its sum $1926+19261=21187$ is less than $31186$, and no pair containing $1926$ and a smaller odd partner exists. So the answer is
\[\boxed{1926\text{ and }19261}.\]
(This pair also has the smallest possible larger member.)
note: "The smallest two relatively prime numbers" is made precise as the pair with the smallest sum; the same pair also minimises the larger number. Checked by brute force.

question:
Let $S_n=1+2+\cdots+n$ for positive integers $n$. Find the maximum value of
\[f(n)=\dfrac{S_n}{(n+32)\,S_{n+1}}\]
over all positive integers $n$.
solution:
Since $S_n=\dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}$ and $S_{n+1}=\dfrac{(n+1)(n+2)}{2}$,
\[f(n)=\dfrac{n(n+1)}{(n+32)(n+1)(n+2)}=\dfrac{n}{n^2+34n+64}=\dfrac{1}{n+\dfrac{64}{n}+34}.\]
By the AM-GM inequality, $n+\dfrac{64}{n}\ge2\sqrt{64}=16$, with equality exactly when $n=\dfrac{64}{n}$, i.e. $n=8$. Hence
\[f(n)\le\dfrac{1}{16+34}=\dfrac{1}{50},\]
with equality at $n=8$: indeed $f(8)=\dfrac{S_8}{40\,S_9}=\dfrac{36}{40\cdot45}=\dfrac{1}{50}$. The maximum value is $\boxed{\dfrac{1}{50}}$.
note: The broken LaTeX of f(n) in the post (a fraction with a missing closing brace) is repaired as S_n / ((32 + n) S_{n+1}). Checked over n <= 200 with exact fractions.

question: Prove that the equation $a^2=b^2+278$ has no solutions in integers $a$ and $b$.
solution:
Suppose integers $a,b$ satisfy the equation. Then
\[(a-b)(a+b)=a^2-b^2=278=2\cdot139.\]
The two factors $a-b$ and $a+b$ differ by $2b$, so they have the same parity.
\begin{itemize}
\item If both are odd, their product is odd, but $278$ is even.
\item If both are even, their product is divisible by $4$, but $278=4\cdot69+2$ is not.
\end{itemize}
Either way we reach a contradiction, so there are no integer solutions. $\blacksquare$

(Equivalently: every square is $\equiv0$ or $1\pmod4$, so $a^2-b^2$ is $\equiv0$, $1$ or $3\pmod 4$, never $\equiv2$. The same argument shows that no number $\equiv2\pmod4$ is a difference of two squares.)
note: The post writes "a^2 = b^21 + 278" as an example of an equation with no solutions; this is read as a typo for a^2 = b^2 + 278, the standard example, and the post's general question (how to prove there are none) is answered by the proof.

question:
Let $a,b,c\ge0$ with $a+b+c=1$. Prove that
\[\sqrt{a+\dfrac{(b-c)^2}{4}}+\sqrt b+\sqrt c\le\sqrt3.\]
solution:
Write $b=x^2$ and $c=y^2$ with $x,y\ge0$, and let $s=x+y$ and $d=x-y$. Then
\[x^2+y^2=\dfrac{s^2+d^2}{2},\qquad b-c=x^2-y^2=sd,\qquad a=1-b-c=1-\dfrac{s^2+d^2}{2}.\]
Since $a\ge0$, we have $x^2+y^2\le1$, so $s^2=(x+y)^2\le2\left(x^2+y^2\right)\le2$. In particular $s\le\sqrt2<\sqrt3$.

The inequality to prove is $\sqrt{a+\dfrac{(b-c)^2}{4}}\le\sqrt3-s$. Both sides are nonnegative, so it is equivalent to
\[1-\dfrac{s^2+d^2}{2}+\dfrac{s^2d^2}{4}\le3-2\sqrt3\,s+s^2.\]
Moving everything to the right side, we must show that
\[2-2\sqrt3\,s+\dfrac32s^2+\dfrac{d^2}{2}-\dfrac{s^2d^2}{4}\ge0.\]
But this expression equals
\[\dfrac32\left(s-\dfrac{2}{\sqrt3}\right)^2+\dfrac{d^2}{4}\left(2-s^2\right),\]
as expanding $\dfrac32\left(s^2-\dfrac{4}{\sqrt3}s+\dfrac43\right)=\dfrac32s^2-2\sqrt3\,s+2$ shows. Both terms are nonnegative because $s^2\le2$. This proves the inequality. $\blacksquare$

\textbf{Equality} needs $s=\dfrac{2}{\sqrt3}$ and $d^2\left(2-s^2\right)=0$; since $s^2=\dfrac43\ne2$, $d=0$. So $x=y=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}$, i.e. equality holds exactly for $a=b=c=\dfrac13$.
note: The LaTeX of the post is repaired. The key identity was checked symbolically and the inequality numerically on random points of the simplex.

question: If $3$ miles equal $1$ league and $1$ league equals $24$ furlongs, how many furlongs are equal to $1$ mile?

question: If $k!=\left(2^7\right)\left(3^2\right)(5)(7)$, what is the value of $k$?
solution:
The prime $7$ divides $k!$, so $k\ge7$; the prime $11$ does not, so $k\le10$. The power of $3$ in $k!$ is $3^2$ for $6\le k\le8$ and $3^4$ for $k=9,10$, so $k\le8$. Finally $7!=2^4\cdot3^2\cdot5\cdot7$ has too few factors of $2$, while
\[8!=40320=2^7\cdot3^2\cdot5\cdot7.\]
So $k=\boxed{8}$.

question: If $d$ is $10\%$ greater than $c$, $c$ is $25\%$ less than $b$, and $a$ is $50\%$ greater than $b$, by what percent is $d$ less than $a$?
solution:
Express everything in terms of $b$:
\[c=0.75b,\qquad d=1.1c=0.825b,\qquad a=1.5b.\]
Then $\dfrac da=\dfrac{0.825}{1.5}=0.55$, so $d$ is $55\%$ of $a$, which is $\boxed{45\%}$ less than $a$.

question: The sum of nine nonnegative numbers is $200$. If $M$ and $A$ are the median and the arithmetic mean of the nine numbers, respectively, what is the greatest possible value of $M-A$? Express your answer as a common fraction.
solution:
The mean is fixed: $A=\dfrac{200}{9}$. So we must make the median $M$ as large as possible.

List the numbers in increasing order, $x_1\le x_2\le\cdots\le x_9$; the median is $M=x_5$. The five numbers $x_5,x_6,\dots,x_9$ are each at least $M$, and the other four are nonnegative, so
\[200=x_1+\cdots+x_9\ge5M,\qquad M\le40.\]
Equality is possible: $0,0,0,0,40,40,40,40,40$ has sum $200$ and median $40$. Hence the greatest value is
\[M-A=40-\dfrac{200}{9}=\boxed{\dfrac{160}{9}}.\]

question: The lines $x+y=a$, $3x+2y=a+15$ and $4x+5y=a+19$, when graphed in the $xy$-plane, all pass through the same point. What is the value of $a$? Express your answer as a common fraction.
solution:
Solve the first two equations for $x$ and $y$ in terms of $a$. From the first, $y=a-x$; substituting into the second, $3x+2a-2x=a+15$, so $x=15-a$ and $y=a-(15-a)=2a-15$.

This point must also lie on the third line:
\[4(15-a)+5(2a-15)=a+19\iff60-4a+10a-75=a+19\iff5a=34.\]
So $a=\boxed{\dfrac{34}{5}}$. (Check: the common point is $\left(\dfrac{41}{5},-\dfrac75\right)$, and $4\cdot\dfrac{41}{5}-5\cdot\dfrac75=\dfrac{129}{5}=\dfrac{34}{5}+19$.)

question: Rico showed his friends a card quickly before hiding it. Dee said the card was the $8$ of spades. Todd said it was the $7$ of hearts. Nia said it was the $6$ of spades. Each of Dee, Todd and Nia was correct about either the number or the suit of the card, but not both. What number was on the card?
solution:
\textbf{If the card is a spade,} Dee and Nia are right about the suit, so both are wrong about the number: it is neither $8$ nor $6$. Todd is wrong about the suit, so he must be right about the number: $7$. The card is the $7$ of spades, and all three statements fit.

\textbf{If the card is not a spade,} Dee and Nia are both wrong about the suit, so both must be right about the number. But then the number would be both $8$ and $6$, which is impossible.

So the card is the $7$ of spades, and the number is $\boxed{7}$.

question: Every student at Bo Jackson High School plays football, baseball, or both football and baseball. Half of the football players also play baseball, and twice as many students play baseball as play football. If $200$ students play both sports, how many students attend Bo Jackson High School?
solution:
Let $F$ and $B$ be the numbers of football and baseball players. Half of the football players play both sports, so $\dfrac F2=200$ and $F=400$. Then $B=2F=800$. Every student plays at least one of the sports, so by inclusion-exclusion the number of students is
\[F+B-200=400+800-200=\boxed{1000}.\]

question: The six-digit number $2A2{,}7B5$ is divisible by $99$, where $A$ and $B$ are digits. What is the value of $10A+B$?
solution:
Since $100\equiv1\pmod{99}$, a number is congruent modulo $99$ to the sum of its two-digit blocks taken from the right. The blocks of $\overline{2A27B5}$ are $\overline{2A}=20+A$, $27$ and $\overline{B5}=10B+5$, so
\[\overline{2A27B5}\equiv(20+A)+27+(10B+5)=52+A+10B\pmod{99}.\]
With digits $A,B$, the number $A+10B$ is between $0$ and $99$, so $52+A+10B$ lies between $52$ and $151$; the only multiple of $99$ in this range is $99$. Hence $A+10B=47$, so $B=4$ and $A=7$.

The number is $272{,}745=99\cdot2755$, and $10A+B=\boxed{74}$.

question: What is the arithmetic mean of all two-digit numbers whose digits add up to $9$?
solution:
The two-digit numbers with digit sum $9$ are
\[18,\ 27,\ 36,\ 45,\ 54,\ 63,\ 72,\ 81,\ 90,\]
an arithmetic sequence of $9$ terms with common difference $9$. The mean of an arithmetic sequence is the average of its first and last terms: $\dfrac{18+90}{2}=\boxed{54}$.

question: Explain why $2^{20}=1024^2$, and use this to find the value of $2^{20}$.
Prove that there is no Pythagorean triple $(a,b,c)$, that is, positive integers with $a^2+b^2=c^2$, in which $a$, $b$ and $c$ are all prime numbers.
solution:
Suppose $a$, $b$, $c$ are primes with $a^2+b^2=c^2$.

If $a$ and $b$ were both odd, then $a^2+b^2$ would be even, so $c^2$ and hence $c$ would be even, i.e. $c=2$. But $a^2+b^2\ge3^2+3^2=18>4=c^2$, a contradiction.

So one of $a$, $b$ is the even prime $2$; say $a=2$. Then
\[4=c^2-b^2=(c-b)(c+b).\]
Since $c>b\ge2$, we have $c-b\ge1$ and $c+b\ge5$, so the product is at least $5$, a contradiction. $\blacksquare$
note: The post states the conjecture; the record asks for its proof.

question: The last nonzero digit of a positive integer is its rightmost digit after all trailing zeros have been removed. Find, by hand, the last nonzero digit of $256!$.
solution:
\textbf{Trailing zeros.} The exponent of $5$ in $256!$ is
\[\left\lfloor\dfrac{256}{5}\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor\dfrac{256}{25}\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor\dfrac{256}{125}\right\rfloor=51+10+2=63,\]
and the exponent of $2$ is $128+64+32+16+8+4+2+1=255$. So $256!$ ends in exactly $63$ zeros, and we need the last digit of $M=\dfrac{256!}{10^{63}}$. Since $M$ still contains the factor $2^{192}$, it is even, so it is enough to find $M\bmod5$.

\textbf{Removing the factors $5$.} For $n\ge0$ let $n!_5$ be $n!$ with all factors $5$ removed, i.e. $\dfrac{n!}{5^v}$ where $5^v$ is the largest power of $5$ dividing $n!$. Write $n=5q+r$ with $0\le r\le4$. The numbers $1,\dots,n$ not divisible by $5$ fall into $q$ complete blocks $5j+1,\dots,5j+4$, each with product $\equiv1\cdot2\cdot3\cdot4=24\equiv-1\pmod5$, and a final block with product $\equiv r!$. The multiples of $5$ are $5\cdot1,5\cdot2,\dots,5\cdot q$, and removing their factors $5$ leaves $q!_5$. Hence
\[n!_5\equiv(-1)^q\,r!\,q!_5\pmod5.\]
With $256=5\cdot51+1$, $51=5\cdot10+1$, $10=5\cdot2$:
\[2!_5=2,\qquad10!_5\equiv(-1)^2\cdot0!\cdot2=2,\qquad51!_5\equiv(-1)^{10}\cdot1!\cdot2=2,\qquad256!_5\equiv(-1)^{51}\cdot1!\cdot2=-2\equiv3\pmod5.\]

\textbf{Finishing.} Since $256!=5^{63}\cdot256!_5=10^{63}M$, we have $256!_5=2^{63}M$. As $2^4\equiv1\pmod5$, $2^{63}\equiv2^3=8\equiv3$, so
\[3M\equiv3\pmod5,\qquad M\equiv1\pmod5.\]
The last digit of $M$ is even and $\equiv1\pmod5$, so it is $\boxed{6}$.
note: The post (from a number theory marathon, answer 6) asks for a full solution by hand. Checked by computing 256! exactly.

solution:
\textbf{(a)} The ratio $\dfrac ab$ is constant only while $c$ is held fixed; when $c$ changes, the ``constant'' changes too, so $d$ is really a function $d(c)$ of $c$. Likewise $e=e(b)$ depends on $b$. So $k=d(c)+e(b)$ is not a constant, and the equation $kbc=a(b+c)$, although true at each point, says nothing useful. For example, if $a=2bc$, then $d=2c$, $e=2b$ and $d+e=2(b+c)$, which varies. (Adding the two equations is also pointless: it throws away information.)

\textbf{(b)} Write $a=f(b,c)$. For each fixed $c$, $a$ is proportional to $b$, so $\dfrac{f(b,c)}{b}$ does not depend on $b$; call it $g(c)$. Thus
\[f(b,c)=g(c)\,b\qquad\text{for all }b,c>0.\]
For each fixed $b$, $a$ is proportional to $c$, so $\dfrac{f(b,c)}{c}=\dfrac{g(c)}{c}\,b$ does not depend on $c$. Taking $b=1$, $\dfrac{g(c)}{c}$ is a constant $k$, so $g(c)=kc$ and
\[a=f(b,c)=kbc.\qquad\blacksquare\]
For example, doubling $b$ and tripling $c$ multiplies $a$ by $6$.
note: The post asks why its proof fails and for a correct proof; the record asks for both and states precisely what "directly proportional to b and c" means (each with the other held fixed).

question: Define $f_1(x)=x^2$ and, for $n\ge1$, $f_{n+1}(x)=f_n\left(f_n(x)\right)$; so each new function is the previous one composed with itself. Find the remainder when $f_{327}(327)$ is divided by $7$.
solution:
\textbf{A closed form.} We show that $f_n(x)=x^{E_n}$ with $E_n=2^{2^{n-1}}$. For $n=1$, $f_1(x)=x^2$ and $E_1=2^{2^0}=2$. If $f_n(x)=x^{E_n}$, then
\[f_{n+1}(x)=f_n\left(x^{E_n}\right)=\left(x^{E_n}\right)^{E_n}=x^{E_n^2},\]
so $E_{n+1}=E_n^2$, and $E_n^2=2^{2\cdot2^{n-1}}=2^{2^n}$, as claimed.

\textbf{The remainder.} So $f_{327}(327)=327^{E}$ with $E=2^{2^{326}}$. Since $327=7\cdot46+5$, we need $5^E\bmod7$. By Fermat's little theorem $5^6\equiv1\pmod7$, so we need $E\bmod6$. The number $E$ is even, and since $2\equiv-1\pmod3$ and the exponent $2^{326}$ is even, $E\equiv(-1)^{2^{326}}=1\pmod3$. The even numbers that are $\equiv1\pmod3$ are $\equiv4\pmod6$, so $E\equiv4\pmod6$ and
\[5^E\equiv5^4=625=7\cdot89+2\equiv2\pmod7.\]
The remainder is $\boxed{2}$.
note: The functions awesomeming1, awesomeming2, ... are renamed f_1, f_2, .... Checked by computing with modular exponentiation (and the closed form for small n).

solution:
\textbf{(a)} If $p$ is a polynomial of degree $k\ge1$, then $p(n+1)-p(n)$ is a polynomial of degree $k-1$; so the $9$th differences of the values of a polynomial of degree at most $9$ are constant. Build the difference table of the ten given terms; the single $9$th difference is $790$. Keeping it constant and adding back up each column gives the new entries in bold:
\[\begin{array}{c|ccccccccccc}
\text{terms}&8&3&4&9&3&9&8&3&4&3&\mathbf{1090}\\
\Delta&-5&1&5&-6&6&-1&-5&1&-1&\mathbf{1087}&\\
\Delta^2&6&4&-11&12&-7&-4&6&-2&\mathbf{1088}&&\\
\Delta^3&-2&-15&23&-19&3&10&-8&\mathbf{1090}&&&\\
\Delta^4&-13&38&-42&22&7&-18&\mathbf{1098}&&&&\\
\Delta^5&51&-80&64&-15&-25&\mathbf{1116}&&&&&\\
\Delta^6&-131&144&-79&-10&\mathbf{1141}&&&&&&\\
\Delta^7&275&-223&69&\mathbf{1151}&&&&&&&\\
\Delta^8&-498&292&\mathbf{1082}&&&&&&&&\\
\Delta^9&790&\mathbf{790}&&&&&&&&&
\end{array}\]
(For example $292+790=1082$, then $69+1082=1151$, and so on up to $3+1087=1090$.) There is exactly one polynomial of degree at most $9$ taking the ten given values (Lagrange interpolation), and the table computes its value at $n=11$. So the eleventh term is $\boxed{1090}$.

(A single slip spoils such a table: computing the third $7$th difference as $-79-(-10)=-69$ instead of $-10-(-79)=69$ gives the wrong $9$th difference $652$ and the wrong next term $676$.)

\textbf{(b)} \emph{True:} for any $N$ given terms there is exactly one polynomial of degree at most $N-1$ through them, and the method always produces its next value; so it always gives \emph{a} next term that follows \emph{a} rule. \emph{Wrong:} finitely many terms never determine a sequence. For any number $x$, some polynomial of degree at most $N$ passes through the $N$ given values and takes the value $x$ next, so every $x$ is the ``next term'' of some rule, and the method cannot know which rule was intended. For instance, for $2,4,8,16$ the method gives $30$ (the differences are $2,4,8$, then $2,4$, then $2$), while the doubling rule gives $32$.
note: The post claims that the method of differences is "never wrong" and works this example to the next term 676. Its table has a sign error: the third 7th difference is -10 - (-79) = 69, not -69, so the 9th difference is 790 (not 652) and the next term is 1090 (not 676). The corrected table was checked by computing the interpolating polynomial exactly; part (b) explains in what sense the claim holds.

question: Solve $3x+10=4x-5$.
solution: Subtracting $3x$ from both sides gives $10=x-5$, and adding $5$ gives $x=\boxed{15}$. (Check: $3\cdot15+10=55=4\cdot15-5$.)

question: Five people, Sally, Bob, Methuselah, Mary and Susan, are to be seated in six seats arranged in two rows of three seats each; one seat stays empty. Two people are \emph{adjacent} if they sit next to each other in the same row. Sally may not sit adjacent to Bob, Bob may not sit adjacent to Methuselah, and Mary may not sit adjacent to Susan. In how many ways can they be seated?
solution:
Without restrictions there are $6\cdot5\cdot4\cdot3\cdot2=720$ seatings. Each row has $2$ pairs of adjacent seats, so there are $4$ adjacent pairs of seats in all. Let $X$, $Y$, $Z$ be the sets of seatings in which Sally-Bob, Bob-Methuselah and Mary-Susan, respectively, are adjacent. We count the bad seatings by inclusion-exclusion.

\textbf{One pair.} Choose an adjacent pair of seats ($4$ ways), the order of the two people in it ($2$), and seats for the other three people among the remaining $4$ seats ($4\cdot3\cdot2=24$): $|X|=|Y|=|Z|=4\cdot2\cdot24=192$.

\textbf{$X\cap Y$:} Bob sits in the middle of a row with Sally and Methuselah on either side: $2$ rows, $2$ orders, and $3\cdot2=6$ ways to seat Mary and Susan in the other three seats: $24$.

\textbf{$X\cap Z$:} the two adjacent pairs share no person, and two adjacent pairs of seats in the same row overlap, so they are in different rows: $4$ choices of seats for Sally-Bob, then $2$ for Mary-Susan in the other row, $2\cdot2$ orders, and $2$ seats for Methuselah: $4\cdot2\cdot4\cdot2=64$. Likewise $|Y\cap Z|=64$.

\textbf{$X\cap Y\cap Z$:} one row is Sally-Bob-Methuselah in some order with Bob in the middle ($2$ rows, $2$ orders) and Mary-Susan is an adjacent pair in the other row ($2$ positions, $2$ orders): $2\cdot2\cdot2\cdot2=16$.

So the number of bad seatings is $3\cdot192-(24+64+64)+16=440$, and the number of allowed seatings is
\[720-440=\boxed{280}.\]
note: Problem P2 of the post. "Adjacent" is not defined there; it is read as sitting next to each other in the same row, and seatings are counted with the empty seat allowed anywhere. (If people one behind the other also counted as adjacent, the answer would be 120.) Checked by brute force over all 720 seatings.

question: Find every real solution of $x^2+3x=5^x$, to the nearest thousandth.
solution:
Let $g(x)=5^x-x^2-3x$; we need the zeros of $g$.

\textbf{No solutions with $-3\le x\le0$.} There $x^2+3x=x(x+3)\le0<5^x$, so $g(x)>0$.

\textbf{No solutions with $x>0$.} For $x>0$, $g(x)>0$ is equivalent to $x\ln5>\ln\left(x(x+3)\right)$, that is, $\varphi(x)>0$ where
\[\varphi(x)=x\ln5-\ln x-\ln(x+3).\]
Since $\varphi''(x)=\dfrac{1}{x^2}+\dfrac{1}{(x+3)^2}>0$, $\varphi$ is convex on $(0,\infty)$, so it lies above its tangent line at $x=\dfrac34$:
\[\varphi\left(\dfrac34\right)=\dfrac34\ln5-\ln\dfrac{45}{16}\approx0.1730,\qquad\varphi'\left(\dfrac34\right)=\ln5-\dfrac43-\dfrac{4}{15}=\ln5-\dfrac85\approx0.0094>0.\]
Hence for every $x>0$, $\varphi(x)\ge\varphi\left(\dfrac34\right)+\varphi'\left(\dfrac34\right)\left(x-\dfrac34\right)>0.1730-0.0094\cdot\dfrac34>0$.

\textbf{Exactly one solution with $x<-3$.} On $(-\infty,-3]$, $5^x$ is increasing and $-x^2-3x=\dfrac94-\left(x+\dfrac32\right)^2$ is increasing too (as $x<-\dfrac32$), so $g$ is strictly increasing there. Since $g(-4)=\dfrac{1}{625}-4<0$ and $g(-3)=\dfrac{1}{125}>0$, there is exactly one zero $r$, with $-4<r<-3$.

\textbf{Locating it.} Near $x=-3$, $x^2+3x=x(x+3)$ is small. We find
\[g(-3.0025)=5^{-3.0025}-3.0025\cdot0.0025\approx0.0079679-0.0075063>0,\]
\[g(-3.0035)=5^{-3.0035}-3.0035\cdot0.0035\approx0.0079551-0.0105123<0,\]
so $-3.0035<r<-3.0025$ (in fact $r\approx-3.00265$). The equation has the single real solution $\boxed{x\approx-3.003}$.
note: Problem P3 of the post ("approximate x to the thousandths place"); the record asks for every real solution and proves there is only one. Checked numerically (bisection) and the bound on phi on a fine grid.

question: What is the last digit of the greatest common factor of $1900$ and $9001$?
solution:
Use the Euclidean algorithm:
\[9001=4\cdot1900+1401,\quad1900=1\cdot1401+499,\quad1401=2\cdot499+403,\]
\[499=1\cdot403+96,\quad403=4\cdot96+19,\quad96=5\cdot19+1.\]
So $\gcd(1900,9001)=\gcd(19,1)=1$, and its last digit is $\boxed{1}$.
note: Problem P5 of the post.

question:
Mandvil has one standard quarter and one special quarter with heads on both sides. He selects one of the two coins at random and, without looking at it, flips it three times. If he gets heads all three times, what is the probability that he selected the special quarter? Express your answer as a common fraction.

A student answers $\dfrac12\cdot1+\dfrac12\cdot\dfrac18=\dfrac{9}{16}$. What did the student compute, and why is it not the answer?
solution:
Let $S$ be the event that he picks the special quarter and $H$ the event of three heads. Then
\[P(S\text{ and }H)=\dfrac12\cdot1=\dfrac12,\qquad P(H)=\dfrac12\cdot1+\dfrac12\cdot\dfrac18=\dfrac{9}{16}.\]
The student computed $P(H)$, the probability of getting three heads. But we are told that three heads occurred, and we want the conditional probability
\[P(S\mid H)=\dfrac{P(S\text{ and }H)}{P(H)}=\dfrac{\dfrac12}{\dfrac{9}{16}}=\boxed{\dfrac89}.\]
Intuitively: in $16$ equally likely repetitions, about $8$ use the special coin (all give three heads) and $8$ the standard coin (about $1$ gives three heads). Of the $9$ runs with three heads, $8$ used the special coin.
note: The poster asks why their answer 9/16 is wrong; the record asks for the conditional probability and for the explanation.

question: Find all positive integers $n$ for which $\dfrac{(n+1)^2}{n+7}$ is an integer, and find the corresponding values of this fraction.
solution:
Write $n+1=(n+7)-6$. Then
\[(n+1)^2=(n+7)^2-12(n+7)+36,\qquad\text{so}\qquad\dfrac{(n+1)^2}{n+7}=n-5+\dfrac{36}{n+7}.\]
This is an integer exactly when $n+7$ divides $36$. Since $n\ge1$, $n+7\ge8$, and the divisors of $36$ that are at least $8$ are $9$, $12$, $18$ and $36$. So
\[n=2,\ 5,\ 11,\ 29,\qquad\text{with}\qquad\dfrac{9}{9}=1,\quad\dfrac{36}{12}=3,\quad\dfrac{144}{18}=8,\quad\dfrac{900}{36}=25.\]
The answer is $\boxed{n=2,5,11,29\text{, giving the values }1,3,8,25}$. (If $0$ is counted as a natural number, nothing changes, since $\dfrac17$ is not an integer.)
note: The unbracketed "(n+1)^2/n+7" is read as (n + 1)^2 / (n + 7). Checked by brute force.

question:
How many ordered quintuples $(a,b,c,d,e)$, in which each of $a,b,c,d,e$ is $-1$, $0$ or $1$, satisfy
\[a+b^2+c^3+d^4+e^5=2\,?\]
solution:
For $t\in\{-1,0,1\}$ we have $t^3=t^5=t$, while $t^2=t^4$ is $0$ if $t=0$ and $1$ if $t=\pm1$. So the equation reads
\[(a+c+e)+\left(b^2+d^4\right)=2.\]
Let $s=a+c+e$ and $u=b^2+d^4\in\{0,1,2\}$.
\begin{itemize}
\item The number of pairs $(b,d)$ with $u=0$, $1$, $2$ is $1$ (both $0$), $4$ (one of them $\pm1$, the other $0$) and $4$ (both $\pm1$).
\item The number of triples $(a,c,e)$ with $s=2$ is $3$ (two $1$s and a $0$); with $s=1$ it is $3+3=6$ (one $1$ and two $0$s, or two $1$s and a $-1$); with $s=0$ it is $1+6=7$ (all $0$, or a $1$, a $-1$ and a $0$ in any order).
\end{itemize}
We need $s+u=2$, so the total is
\[\underbrace{1\cdot3}_{u=0,\ s=2}+\underbrace{4\cdot6}_{u=1,\ s=1}+\underbrace{4\cdot7}_{u=2,\ s=0}=3+24+28=\boxed{55}.\]
note: The post asks what this MATHCOUNTS Chapter Sprint #30 problem is asking; the year is not given. "Coordinates of value -1, 0 or 1" is read as each entry being -1, 0 or 1. Checked by brute force over all 243 quintuples.

question: Seven students, including Alex, have perfect scores on a contest. Each of the other six, independently, has a $20\%$ chance of having their score cancelled; Alex's score is certainly valid. In the next competition, every competitor without a valid perfect score finishes below every student with a valid perfect score, and Alex is equally likely to finish in each of the positions $1,2,\dots,k$, where $k$ is the number of students with valid perfect scores (including Alex). Alex qualifies if he finishes in the top $4$. To the nearest percent, what is the probability that Alex qualifies?
solution:
Let $X$ be the number of the other six students whose scores are valid. Each is valid with probability $\dfrac45$, independently, so
\[P(X=j)=\dbinom6j\left(\dfrac45\right)^j\left(\dfrac15\right)^{6-j}=\dfrac{\dbinom6j4^j}{15625}.\]
Given $X=j$, there are $j+1$ valid perfect scores and Alex's position is uniform among $1,\dots,j+1$; he qualifies with probability $1$ if $j\le3$ and $\dfrac{4}{j+1}$ if $j\ge4$. The probabilities for $j=4,5,6$ are
\[P(X=4)=\dfrac{3840}{15625},\qquad P(X=5)=\dfrac{6144}{15625},\qquad P(X=6)=\dfrac{4096}{15625},\]
so $P(X\le3)=\dfrac{15625-14080}{15625}=\dfrac{1545}{15625}$. Hence
\[P(\text{qualify})=\dfrac{1}{15625}\left(1545+\dfrac45\cdot3840+\dfrac46\cdot6144+\dfrac47\cdot4096\right)=\dfrac{1}{15625}\left(8713+\dfrac{16384}{7}\right)=\dfrac{77375}{109375}=\dfrac{619}{875}.\]
Since $\dfrac{619}{875}\approx0.7074$, the probability is about $\boxed{71\%}$.
note: Part A of the post. The story (other perfect scorers who "cheated" on an online AMC 8, a MATHCOUNTS state qualification) is retold neutrally as cancelled scores; the probability model is unchanged, and the exact answer 619/875 matches the poster's hidden answer. Part B (whether the model is realistic) is not a mathematical question and is not included. Checked with exact fractions.

question: You are making a blueprint of your bedroom using a scale factor of $\dfrac18$. The actual width of the room is $12$ feet and the actual length is $10$ feet. What are the width and the length of the room on the blueprint?
solution:
Every length on the blueprint is $\dfrac18$ of the actual length:
\[\text{width: }\dfrac{12}{8}=1.5\text{ feet}=18\text{ inches},\qquad\text{length: }\dfrac{10}{8}=1.25\text{ feet}=15\text{ inches}.\]
So the blueprint shows the room as $\boxed{1.5\text{ ft}\ (18\text{ in})\text{ wide and }1.25\text{ ft}\ (15\text{ in})\text{ long}}$.

question: In the $xy$-plane, the point $(p,r)$ lies on the line with equation $y=x+b$, where $b$ is a constant. The point with coordinates $(2p,5r)$ lies on the line with equation $y=2x+b$. If $p\ne0$, what is the value of $\dfrac rp$?
solution:
The two conditions are
\[r=p+b\qquad\text{and}\qquad5r=2\cdot2p+b=4p+b.\]
Subtracting the first equation from the second eliminates $b$: $4r=3p$. Since $p\ne0$,
\[\dfrac rp=\boxed{\dfrac34}.\]
(For example, $p=4$, $r=3$, $b=-1$ works: $3=4-1$ and $5\cdot3=15=2\cdot8-1$.)
note: Problem 1 of the post (an SAT-style question; no competition source).

question: What is the greatest whole number that divides the sum of any six consecutive whole numbers? Does the answer change if ``whole numbers'' (that is, $0,1,2,\dots$) is replaced by ``integers''?
solution:
Six consecutive numbers starting at $n$ have sum
\[n+(n+1)+\cdots+(n+5)=6n+15=3(2n+5),\]
which is always divisible by $3$. On the other hand, the sums for $n=0$ and $n=1$ are $15$ and $21$, and $\gcd(15,21)=3$, so no number larger than $3$ divides every such sum. The answer is $\boxed{3}$.

Allowing all integers does not change it: $3$ still divides $3(2n+5)$ for every integer $n$, and the examples $15$ and $21$ (which use whole numbers only) still rule out anything larger. For instance $-2+(-1)+0+1+2+3=3$.
note: The poster doubts the answer 3 because the problem says whole numbers while the explanation used negative integers; the record shows that the answer is 3 either way.
The post asks why "translate right, then reflect in the y-axis" does not give f(-x + 1); the record asks for the correct description, the explanation of the error and the general case f(ax + b).

question: An integer $x$ is chosen uniformly at random from $\{1,2,\dots,3000\}$. Given that $x$ is divisible by $3$, what is the probability that $x$ is divisible by $15$? Explain why the answer is the same for $\{1,2,\dots,N\}$ whenever $N$ is a multiple of $15$.
solution:
There are $\dfrac{3000}{3}=1000$ multiples of $3$ and $\dfrac{3000}{15}=200$ multiples of $15$ in the set, and every multiple of $15$ is a multiple of $3$. So
\[P(15\mid x\ \mid\ 3\mid x)=\dfrac{200}{1000}=\boxed{\dfrac15}.\]
In general, the multiples of $3$ up to $N$ are $3m$ for $m=1,\dots,\dfrac N3$, and $3m$ is divisible by $15$ exactly when $5\mid m$. When $15\mid N$, exactly one fifth of the numbers $1,\dots,\dfrac N3$ are multiples of $5$, so the probability is again $\dfrac15$. (There is no uniform random choice from \emph{all} integers; a statement such as ``a random integer divisible by $3$ is divisible by $15$ with probability $\dfrac15$'' means exactly this kind of limit.)
note: "An integer x" with no range does not define a probability; the record chooses x from {1, ..., 3000} and explains why 1/5 is the natural answer, confirming the poster's guess.

question: A drawer holds $4$ blue socks, $8$ black socks and $2$ white socks. Socks are taken out without looking. What is the least number of socks that must be taken out to be sure of getting two socks of the same colour?
solution:
Three socks are not enough: one blue, one black and one white sock could come out, with no two of the same colour.

Four socks are always enough: there are only $3$ colours, so by the pigeonhole principle two of any $4$ socks have the same colour.

So the answer is $\boxed{4}$. (The numbers $4$, $8$ and $2$ do not matter, as long as each colour has at least one sock.)
note: "The least number of socks that I have to pick up so there are two socks with a matching color" is read as the number that guarantees a matching pair.

solution:
\textbf{A key lemma.} For a yes-or-no question $Q$, let $E(Q)$ be the question ``If I asked you $Q$, would you answer Meow?'' If Truecat or Liecat is asked $E(Q)$, the answer is Meow exactly when $Q$ is true.

\emph{Proof.} Check the four cases.
\begin{itemize}
\item Truecat, Meow $=$ yes: Truecat would answer $Q$ with Meow exactly when $Q$ is true, so $E(Q)$ is true exactly when $Q$ is true, and the truthful answer is Meow ($=$ yes) exactly then.
\item Truecat, Meow $=$ no: Truecat would answer $Q$ with Meow exactly when $Q$ is false; so $E(Q)$ is false exactly when $Q$ is true, and the truthful answer ``no'' is Meow exactly then.
\item Liecat, Meow $=$ yes: Liecat would answer $Q$ with Meow ($=$ yes) exactly when $Q$ is false; so $E(Q)$ is false exactly when $Q$ is true, and the lying answer ``yes'' $=$ Meow comes exactly then.
\item Liecat, Meow $=$ no: Liecat would answer $Q$ with ``no'' $=$ Meow exactly when $Q$ is true; so $E(Q)$ is true exactly when $Q$ is true, and the lying answer ``no'' $=$ Meow comes exactly then.
\end{itemize}
In every case the answer is Meow exactly when $Q$ is true. $\blacksquare$ (The question $E(Q)$ is about facts and the cat's own behaviour, so it causes no paradox.)

\textbf{(a) Three questions.} Call the cats $A$, $B$, $C$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Ask $A$: $E(\text{``Is }B\text{ Randomcat?''})$. If the answer is Meow, then either $A$ is Randomcat, or $A$ is not and (by the lemma) $B$ is Randomcat; in both cases $C$ is \emph{not} Randomcat. If the answer is Nya, then either $A$ is Randomcat, or $A$ is not and $B$ is not Randomcat; in both cases $B$ is not Randomcat. Either way we know a cat $X\ne A$ that is not Randomcat.
\item Ask $X$: $E(\text{``Are you Truecat?''})$. By the lemma, Meow means $X$ is Truecat and Nya means $X$ is Liecat.
\item Ask $X$: $E(\text{``Is }A\text{ Randomcat?''})$. By the lemma this tells us whether $A$ is Randomcat. The other cat besides $X$ and $A$ then gets the remaining name.
\end{enumerate}
After three questions every cat is identified.

\textbf{(b) Two questions are not enough.} There are $3!=6$ possible ways to assign the names. With two questions there are at most $4$ possible answer sequences (Meow-Meow, Meow-Nya, Nya-Meow, Nya-Nya), even if the second question depends on the first answer. The final conclusion depends only on the answers, so a two-question strategy can only ever announce at most $4$ different assignments. Some assignment is then never announced, and if it is the true one, the strategy fails, whatever the cats answer.

So the least number of questions that always suffices is $\boxed{3}$.
note: A variation of the "hardest logic puzzle ever" (True, False and Random gods with unknown words for yes and no). The cat Ajkeofkrmtjgdoxcat is renamed Randomcat; "Randomcat randomly chooses what to say" is kept, and the rule about paradoxes is kept (such questions may not be asked, so they give no information). The post asks whether it is possible and for the least number; the answer 3 is proved with a lower bound. The strategy was checked by simulation over all 6 assignments, both meanings of the words and all random answers.

question: If $2^x\cdot9^y$ equals the four-digit number $\overline{2x9y}$, where $x$ is its hundreds digit and $y$ its units digit, what is the product $xy$?
solution:
The number $N=\overline{2x9y}=2090+100x+y$ lies between $2090$ and $2999$, and $N=2^x\cdot9^y$.
\begin{itemize}
\item $y=0$: $N=2^x$, but $2^{11}=2048<2090$ and $2^{12}=4096>2999$. Impossible.
\item $y=1$: $2^x=\dfrac N9$ is between $233$ and $333$, so $2^x=256$, $x=8$ and $N=2304\ne2891$. Impossible.
\item $y=2$: $2^x=\dfrac{N}{81}$ is between $26$ and $37$, so $2^x=32$, $x=5$ and $N=2592=\overline{2592}$, which matches $x=5$, $y=2$.
\item $y=3$: $2^x=\dfrac{N}{729}$ is between $2.9$ and $4.2$, so $2^x=4$, $x=2$ and $N=2916\ne2293$. Impossible.
\item $y\ge4$: $9^y\ge6561>2999$. Impossible.
\end{itemize}
So $x=5$, $y=2$ (indeed $2^5\cdot9^2=32\cdot81=2592$), and $xy=\boxed{10}$.
note: The post's title gives the source (2000 MATHCOUNTS State Sprint Round #11). Checked by brute force over all digits x, y.

question: How many integers are there from $45$ to $317$ inclusive?
solution: Subtracting $44$ from each of the integers $45,46,\dots,317$ turns the list into $1,2,\dots,273$, which has $273$ members. So there are $317-45+1=\boxed{273}$ integers. (The difference $317-45=272$ counts the steps from one integer to the next; the list has one more integer than steps.)
note: The poster got 274 and the answer key 273; the key is right.

question: A spiral is made by starting with a semicircle of radius $1$ unit and then endlessly attaching semicircles, each with half the radius of the previous one, alternately on opposite sides. What is the length of the whole spiral? Express your answer in terms of $\pi$.
note: The post's title gives the source (2015 MATHCOUNTS School Sprint #29). Its figure is missing but, as the poster says, not needed; the solution draws the spiral.

solution:
\textbf{(a)} Arrange $p$ stars and $2$ bars in a row. Let $x$, $y$, $z$ be the numbers of stars before the first bar, between the bars, and after the second bar. This is a one-to-one correspondence between the rows and the solutions in \emph{nonnegative} integers (bars may be adjacent or at the ends, giving zeros). Choosing the positions of the $2$ bars among $p+2$ places gives $\boxed{\dbinom{p+2}{2}}$ solutions.

\textbf{(b)} For positive integers put $x=x'+1$, $y=y'+1$, $z=z'+1$; then $x'+y'+z'=p-3$ in nonnegative integers, which has $\dbinom{p-1}{2}$ solutions by (a). Equivalently, line up the $p$ stars and put the $2$ bars into $2$ different gaps among the $p-1$ gaps between stars. So there are $\boxed{\dbinom{p-1}{2}}$ positive solutions (which is $0$ for $p<3$).

\textbf{(c)} The basic picture, with the bars allowed anywhere, counts the nonnegative solutions; the positive solutions correspond to bars in different inner gaps, or to the substitution above. For $p=10$: $\dbinom{12}{2}=66$ nonnegative solutions and $\dbinom92=36$ positive ones.
note: The post asks whether stars and bars counts nonnegative or positive solutions; the record asks for both counts and the explanation. Checked by brute force for p = 10.

question: Starting with an empty box, the elf and the reindeer add candy canes to it: $5$ purple candy canes at the end of every week, $4$ green candy canes at the end of every five days, and $8$ red candy canes at the end of every two weeks. How many green and purple candy canes (together) are on the box after one year of $365$ days?
solution:
Only complete periods count. In $365$ days there are $\left\lfloor\dfrac{365}{7}\right\rfloor=52$ complete weeks, giving $52\cdot5=260$ purple candy canes, and exactly $\dfrac{365}{5}=73$ five-day periods, giving $73\cdot4=292$ green candy canes. Together there are
\[260+292=\boxed{552}\]
green and purple candy canes. (The red ones are not asked for; there would be $\left\lfloor\dfrac{365}{14}\right\rfloor\cdot8=208$ of them.)
note: Question Three of the post. "Decimal candy canes aren't counted" is read as counting only complete periods, with canes added at the end of each period.

question:
In triangle $ABC$, the bisector of angle $A$ meets side $BC$ at $D$. Let $AB=c$, $AC=b$, $BD=m$, $DC=n$ and $AD=d$. Prove the angle bisector length formula
\[d^2=bc-mn.\]
note: The post asks what the "angle bisector formula" d^2 + mn = bc is; the record asks for its proof and gives two. Checked numerically on random triangles.

question: Prove that the equation $n^2+n^3=n^6$ has no solution in positive integers $n$.
solution:
Suppose a positive integer $n$ satisfies the equation. Dividing by $n^2>0$ gives
\[1+n=n^4.\]
For $n=1$ this says $2=1$, which is false. For $n\ge2$, $n^4=n^3\cdot n\ge8n>n+1$, so it is false as well. Hence there is no solution. $\blacksquare$

(Another way: $n\mid n^4-n=1$, so $n=1$, which fails. Among all integers, the only solution is $n=0$.)
note: The post states the conjecture; the record asks for its proof.

solution:
Writing $n$ with additions and subtractions of copies of $x$ and $y$ means exactly writing $n=ax+by$ with integers $a$ and $b$: here $a$ is the number of copies of $x$ that are added minus the number that are subtracted, and similarly for $b$. (For instance $15=3\cdot12-3\cdot7$, and $0=x-x$.)

\textbf{(a)} Take $x=3$ and $y=9$; here $x$ is odd. Every number $3a+9b$ is a multiple of $3$, so for example $n=1$ cannot be written. The conjecture is false.

\textbf{(b)} Let $d=\gcd(x,y)$.

\emph{If $d>1$:} every number $ax+by$ is a multiple of $d$, so $n=1$ cannot be written.

\emph{If $d=1$:} consider the $x$ numbers $y,2y,3y,\dots,xy$. No two of them leave the same remainder on division by $x$: if $iy$ and $jy$ did, with $1\le j<i\le x$, then $x$ would divide $(i-j)y$; since $\gcd(x,y)=1$, $x$ would divide $i-j$, which is impossible because $0<i-j<x$. So these $x$ numbers leave all $x$ remainders $0,1,\dots,x-1$, and in particular some $ky$ leaves remainder $1$:
\[ky=mx+1\quad\text{for some integer }m,\qquad\text{so}\qquad 1=ky-mx.\]
Multiplying by $n$ gives $n=(nk)y-(nm)x$ for every integer $n$.

Hence every integer can be written exactly when $\gcd(x,y)=1$. $\blacksquare$

(The condition ``at least one of $x$, $y$ is odd'' only rules out a common factor $2$; the correct condition is that $x$ and $y$ have no common factor at all.)
note: The post states the conjecture with only an example (15 = 3*12 - 3*7, which is correct). The conjecture is false (x = 3, y = 9); the record asks for a counterexample and for a proof of the correct condition gcd(x, y) = 1.

question:
For an integer $n\ge2$, let $c(n)$ be the number of ordered sums of integers greater than $1$ that add up to $n$ (a single number counts as a sum). For example, for $n=6$ the sums are
\[6,\quad 4+2,\quad 2+4,\quad 3+3,\quad 2+2+2,\]
so $c(6)=5$. Let $F_1=F_2=1$ and $F_{k+1}=F_k+F_{k-1}$ be the Fibonacci numbers.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Prove that $c(n)=F_{n-1}$ for every $n\ge2$.
\item[(b)] By counting the sums with exactly $k$ terms, prove that
\[\sum_{k=1}^{\left\lfloor \dfrac n2\right\rfloor}\dbinom{n-k-1}{k-1}=F_{n-1}\qquad\text{for every } n\ge2.\]
\end{enumerate}
solution:
\textbf{(a)} We have $c(2)=1$ (just $2$) and $c(3)=1$ (just $3$). Let $n\ge4$ and split the sums for $n$ by their last term.
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{Last term $2$.} Deleting it leaves a sum for $n-2$ (with $n-2\ge2$), and every sum for $n-2$ arises exactly once (append $+2$). There are $c(n-2)$ of these.
\item \emph{Last term at least $3$.} Decreasing the last term by $1$ leaves a sum for $n-1$ whose terms are still greater than $1$. Conversely, increasing the last term of any sum for $n-1$ by $1$ gives a sum for $n$ whose last term is at least $3$. So there are $c(n-1)$ of these.
\end{itemize}
Hence $c(n)=c(n-1)+c(n-2)$ for $n\ge4$. The sequence $F_{n-1}$ has the same starting values ($F_1=F_2=1$) and the same recurrence, so by induction $c(n)=F_{n-1}$ for all $n\ge2$. For example $c(4)=2$, $c(5)=3$, $c(6)=5$.

\textbf{(b)} Count the sums $a_1+a_2+\cdots+a_k=n$ with every $a_i\ge2$. Put $b_i=a_i-1\ge1$; then $b_1+\cdots+b_k=n-k$, and this is a bijection with the ordered sums of $k$ positive integers equal to $n-k$. Writing $n-k$ as a row of $n-k$ ones, such a sum is chosen by picking $k-1$ of the $n-k-1$ gaps between the ones, so there are $\dbinom{n-k-1}{k-1}$ of them (stars and bars). A sum with $k$ terms needs $2k\le n$, so $k$ runs from $1$ to $\left\lfloor\dfrac n2\right\rfloor$. Adding over $k$ counts every sum once, so by (a)
\[\sum_{k=1}^{\left\lfloor \dfrac n2\right\rfloor}\dbinom{n-k-1}{k-1}=c(n)=F_{n-1}.\qquad\blacksquare\]
(For $n=6$: $\dbinom40+\dbinom31+\dbinom22=1+3+1=5=F_5$.)
note: The scraped example list for n = 6 repeats four of the sums; the list is given once (5 sums). The post finds the binomial sum but only guesses from three cases that it equals F(n-1) ("This must equal F_{n-1}"); the record proves c(n) = F(n-1) by a recurrence and deduces the identity. Checked by brute force for n <= 25.

The post asks how to find the equation of a parabola from its x- and y-intercepts "with this example", but the example is missing. The record asks for the general method and adds a worked example with chosen numbers.

question:
Give a counting argument (not an algebraic calculation) showing that
\[1+2+3+\cdots+n=\dbinom{n+1}{2}\]
for every positive integer $n$.
solution:
Count the $2$-element subsets $\{a,b\}$ of $\{1,2,\dots,n+1\}$ in two ways.

\emph{Directly:} there are $\dbinom{n+1}{2}$ of them.

\emph{By the larger element:} write the subset with $a<b$. If the larger element is $b=j+1$ (where $1\le j\le n$), the smaller element can be any of $1,2,\dots,j$, which gives $j$ subsets. Every subset is counted once, for its own larger element, so the number of subsets is
\[1+2+\cdots+n.\]
The two counts are equal, which proves the identity. $\blacksquare$

(For example, with $n=3$ the subsets of $\{1,2,3,4\}$ are $\{1,2\}$; $\{1,3\},\{2,3\}$; $\{1,4\},\{2,4\},\{3,4\}$, that is $1+2+3=6=\dbinom42$.)
note: Conceptual post asking when combinations should be used; it mentions that n + (n-1) + ... + 1 is counted by a combination. The record asks for that counting argument.

question: Cube $ABCDEFGH$ has faces $ABCD$, $ABEF$ and $ADGF$, and $AB=6$. Point $P$ is chosen so that $PB<PG$. If the volume of tetrahedron $PACE$ is $64$, what is the volume of tetrahedron $FPHD$?
note: Checked with coordinates for random points P on both candidate planes (volumes 64 and 100, or 64 and 28 on the excluded side).

question:
Amy and Mary play a game of $n$ rounds, where $n$ is fixed in advance. In each round they take turns flipping a fair coin, and whoever flips heads first loses that round. Amy flips first in round $1$; in each later round, the loser of the previous round flips first. The winner of the last round wins the game.

Prove that the probability that Amy wins the game is
\[\dfrac12-\dfrac{1}{2\cdot3^n}.\]
solution:
\textbf{Lemma.} In a single round, the player who flips first wins with probability $\dfrac13$.

\emph{Proof.} The first player wins exactly when the first heads appears on an even-numbered flip: on flip $2$ (tails, heads), on flip $4$ (three tails, then heads), and so on. Hence
\[P(\text{first player wins})=\dfrac14+\dfrac1{16}+\dfrac1{64}+\cdots=\dfrac{\dfrac14}{1-\dfrac14}=\dfrac13.\]
(A heads certainly appears eventually, so the round ends with probability $1$.)

\textbf{Recurrence.} Let $p_n$ be the probability that Amy wins round $n$, which is the probability that she wins the $n$-round game. By the lemma, $p_1=\dfrac13$. If Amy wins round $n$, then Mary flips first in round $n+1$ and Amy wins it with probability $\dfrac23$; if Amy loses round $n$, she flips first and wins round $n+1$ with probability $\dfrac13$. So
\[p_{n+1}=\dfrac23p_n+\dfrac13(1-p_n)=\dfrac13p_n+\dfrac13.\]

\textbf{Induction.} The formula holds for $n=1$: $\dfrac12-\dfrac16=\dfrac13$. If $p_n=\dfrac12-\dfrac{1}{2\cdot3^n}$, then
\[p_{n+1}=\dfrac13\left(\dfrac12-\dfrac1{2\cdot3^n}\right)+\dfrac13=\dfrac12-\dfrac1{2\cdot3^{n+1}}.\]
Hence $p_n=\dfrac12-\dfrac{1}{2\cdot3^n}$ for every $n\ge1$. $\blacksquare$

(So Amy's disadvantage from flipping first in round $1$ shrinks by a factor of $3$ each round, and $p_n\to\dfrac12$.)
note: The post gives this proof; it is correct. The record states the rules precisely and writes p_n as the probability that Amy wins round n (the post says "wins n rounds"). Checked with exact fractions and by simulation.

question:
The numbers $a,b,c,d,e$ are chosen from $\{0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8\}$ (repetition allowed). How many different values can
\[81a+27b+9c+3d+e\]
take?
solution:
The value is at least $0$ and at most $8(81+27+9+3+1)=968$. We show that every integer from $0$ to $968$ occurs, so there are $\boxed{969}$ values.

For $k\ge1$ let $T_k$ be the set of values of $3^{k-1}x_{k-1}+\cdots+3x_1+x_0$ with all $x_i\in\{0,1,\dots,8\}$, and let $M_k=8\left(3^{k-1}+\cdots+3+1\right)=4\left(3^k-1\right)$ be its largest element. We prove by induction that $T_k$ consists of all integers from $0$ to $M_k$.

For $k=1$, $T_1=\{0,1,\dots,8\}$ and $M_1=8$. Suppose the claim holds for $k$. Every element of $T_{k+1}$ has the form $3t+x$ with $t\in T_k$ and $x\in\{0,\dots,8\}$. Take an integer $m$ with $0\le m\le M_{k+1}=3M_k+8$.
\begin{itemize}
\item If $\left\lfloor\dfrac m3\right\rfloor\le M_k$, take $t=\left\lfloor\dfrac m3\right\rfloor$ and $x=m-3t\in\{0,1,2\}$.
\item Otherwise $m\ge3M_k+3$; take $t=M_k$ and $x=m-3M_k$, which lies between $3$ and $8$.
\end{itemize}
In both cases $m\in T_{k+1}$, which completes the induction.

The expression in the problem gives the set $T_5$, which is $\{0,1,\dots,968\}$: $969$ values.

(The number of choices of $(a,b,c,d,e)$ is $9^5=59049$, but many of them give the same value; for example $a=0,b=3$ and $a=1,b=0$ both give $81$.)
note: The post asks "How many possibilities?"; this is read as the number of different values of the expression (the number of 5-tuples, 9^5 = 59049, would be immediate). Checked by brute force.

question:
Find all real numbers $x$ such that
\[x+\dfrac8x+\dfrac{8}{x+\dfrac8x}=9.\]
solution:
We need $x\ne0$. Let $z=x+\dfrac8x$. For real $x\ne0$ we have $z\ne0$, because $x+\dfrac8x=\dfrac{x^2+8}{x}$ and $x^2+8>0$. The equation becomes
\[z+\dfrac8z=9\iff z^2-9z+8=0\iff(z-1)(z-8)=0,\]
so $z=1$ or $z=8$. Both values must be checked:
\begin{itemize}
\item $x+\dfrac8x=1\iff x^2-x+8=0$, whose discriminant is $1-32<0$: no real solutions.
\item $x+\dfrac8x=8\iff x^2-8x+8=0\iff x=4\pm2\sqrt2$.
\end{itemize}
So the real solutions are $\boxed{x=4+2\sqrt2\ \text{and}\ x=4-2\sqrt2}$.

(Clearing denominators directly, by multiplying by $x\left(x^2+8\right)$, gives the quartic
\[x^4-9x^3+24x^2-72x+64=0,\qquad\text{which factors as}\qquad\left(x^2-x+8\right)\left(x^2-8x+8\right)=0,\]
matching the two cases above. Over the complex numbers there are also the two roots $\dfrac{1\pm i\sqrt{31}}{2}$ of $x^2-x+8$.)
note: The post asks which of z = 1 and z = 8 to use: both must be checked, and only z = 8 gives real x. The post's expanded quartic x^4 - 9x^3 + 24x^2 - 8x = 0 is wrong; the correct one is x^4 - 9x^3 + 24x^2 - 72x + 64 = 0. The record asks for the real solutions. Checked symbolically.

solution:
\textbf{(a)} Let $S=1+3+\cdots+(2n-1)$. Write the sum forwards and backwards:
\begin{align*}
S&=1+3+\cdots+(2n-3)+(2n-1),\\
S&=(2n-1)+(2n-3)+\cdots+3+1.
\end{align*}
Adding term by term, each of the $n$ columns sums to $2n$, so $2S=n\cdot2n$ and $S=\boxed{n^2}$. $\blacksquare$

\textbf{(b)} Each even number is one more than the corresponding odd number: $2k=(2k-1)+1$. So
\[2+4+\cdots+2n=\bigl(1+3+\cdots+(2n-1)\bigr)+n=\boxed{n^2+n=n(n+1)}.\]
(Equivalently $2+4+\cdots+2n=2(1+2+\cdots+n)=2\cdot\dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}$.) For example $2+4+6+8=20=4\cdot5$.
note: The post asks why the first n odd numbers sum to n^2 and whether there is a similar rule for even numbers; both are asked for.

question:
Compute the sum of the digits of
\[2021\times222111222111111222111222.\]
solution:
Let $N=222111222111111222111222$ and let $n_j$ be its digit in the $10^j$ place ($n_j=0$ when $j<0$ or $j>23$). Every digit of $N$ is $1$ or $2$, and their sum is $4\cdot6+4\cdot3=36$. Since $2021\,N=2\cdot10^3N+2\cdot10N+N$, long multiplication gives in the $10^j$ column the total
\[c_j=2n_{j-3}+2n_{j-1}+n_j.\]

\textbf{No carries.} Always $c_j\le2\cdot2+2\cdot2+2=10$, with equality only if $n_{j-3}=n_{j-1}=n_j=2$. Now $N$ is made of blocks of three equal digits,
\[222\ 111\ 222\ 111\ 111\ 222\ 111\ 222,\]
and no two $222$ blocks are next to each other. If $n_{j-1}=n_j=2$, these two digits are therefore in the same $222$ block, so $j$ is the middle or the top digit of that block, and the place $j-3$ lies in the next lower block, which is a $111$ block (or lies beyond the units digit). So $n_{j-3}\le1$ and $c_j\le8$. Hence every column total is at most $9$: there are no carries, and the digits of the product are exactly the numbers $c_j$.

\textbf{The digit sum.} Therefore the digit sum of the product is
\[\sum_j c_j=(2+2+1)\sum_j n_j=5\cdot36=\boxed{180}.\]
(Indeed $2021\times N=448886779886555779886779662$.)
note: The "solve in less than ten seconds" framing and the edit about another post are dropped. Checked with exact integers.

question: What is the remainder when the sum $1^2+2^2+3^2+\cdots+2016^2$ is divided by $17$?
solution:
\textbf{Periodicity.} The remainder of $k^2$ on division by $17$ depends only on the remainder of $k$. Any $17$ consecutive integers leave each remainder $0,1,\dots,16$ once, and
\[0^2+1^2+\cdots+16^2=\dfrac{16\cdot17\cdot33}{6}=1496=17\cdot88\equiv0\pmod{17}.\]
Since $2016=17\cdot118+10$, the numbers $1,\dots,2006$ form $118$ complete blocks of $17$ consecutive integers, and the remaining numbers $2007,\dots,2016$ are congruent to $1,2,\dots,10$. Hence
\[\sum_{k=1}^{2016}k^2\equiv1^2+2^2+\cdots+10^2=385=17\cdot22+11\equiv\boxed{11}\pmod{17}.\]

\textbf{Check with the formula.} The sum is $\dfrac{2016\cdot2017\cdot4033}{6}=336\cdot2017\cdot4033$, and $336\equiv13$, $2017\equiv11$, $4033\equiv4\pmod{17}$, so the sum is $\equiv13\cdot11\cdot4=572=17\cdot33+11\equiv11$.
note: Checked by direct computation.

question: Factor $b^4-25b^2+144$ completely over the integers.
solution:
Treat it as a quadratic in $u=b^2$: $u^2-25u+144$. We need two numbers with product $144$ and sum $25$, namely $9$ and $16$:
\[b^4-25b^2+144=\left(b^2-9\right)\left(b^2-16\right).\]
Each factor is a difference of squares, so
\[b^4-25b^2+144=\boxed{(b-3)(b+3)(b-4)(b+4)}.\]
(Check: $(b^2-9)(b^2-16)=b^4-16b^2-9b^2+144$.)

question:
Simplify
\[2+\sqrt2+\dfrac{1}{2+\sqrt2}+\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2-2}.\]
solution:
Rationalise the two denominators:
\[\dfrac{1}{2+\sqrt2}=\dfrac{2-\sqrt2}{(2+\sqrt2)(2-\sqrt2)}=\dfrac{2-\sqrt2}{2},\qquad\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2-2}=\dfrac{\sqrt2+2}{(\sqrt2-2)(\sqrt2+2)}=-\dfrac{2+\sqrt2}{2}.\]
Their sum is $\dfrac{2-\sqrt2-2-\sqrt2}{2}=-\sqrt2$. Therefore the expression equals
\[2+\sqrt2-\sqrt2=\boxed{2}.\]

question: In how many ways can $5$ distinguishable balls be put into $3$ indistinguishable boxes, if boxes may be left empty? Also explain how the answer can be obtained by first counting with distinguishable boxes and then correcting for the overcount.
note: The post asks whether stars and bars plus a correction can be used. The record explains the correct correction (from 3^5 labelled distributions; stars and bars counts identical balls). Checked by brute force.

question:
Real numbers $a,b,c,d$ satisfy
\[ad=2+c,\qquad bc=2+a,\qquad ab=a+c,\qquad ac=d+b.\]
Find all possible values of $a+b$.
solution:
\textbf{Reduce to two unknowns.} The third and fourth equations say $c=a(b-1)$ and $d=ac-b=a^2(b-1)-b$. Substituting into the second equation:
\[ab(b-1)=2+a\iff a\left(b^2-b-1\right)=2.\tag{i}\]
In particular $a\ne0$. Substituting into the first equation:
\[a^3(b-1)-ab=2+a(b-1)\iff a^3(b-1)-a(2b-1)-2=0.\]
Replacing $2$ by $a\left(b^2-b-1\right)$ from (i) and dividing by $a\ne0$:
\[a^2(b-1)-(2b-1)-\left(b^2-b-1\right)=0\iff a^2(b-1)=b^2+b-2=(b-1)(b+2).\]
So the system is equivalent to (i) together with $(b-1)\left(a^2-b-2\right)=0$, with $c$ and $d$ given by the formulas above.

\textbf{Case $b=1$.} Then (i) gives $-a=2$, so $a=-2$, $c=0$, $d=-1$, and $a+b=-1$.

\textbf{Case $b=a^2-2$.} Substituting into (i):
\[a\left(\left(a^2-2\right)^2-\left(a^2-2\right)-1\right)=2\iff a^5-5a^3+5a-2=0\iff(a-2)\left(a^2+a-1\right)^2=0.\]
(Check: $\left(a^2+a-1\right)^2=a^4+2a^3-a^2-2a+1$, and $(a-2)\left(a^4+2a^3-a^2-2a+1\right)=a^5-5a^3+5a-2$.)
\begin{itemize}
\item $a=2$ gives $b=2$, $c=2$, $d=2$, and $a+b=4$.
\item $a^2+a-1=0$, i.e. $a=\dfrac{-1\pm\sqrt5}{2}$, gives $b=a^2-2=(1-a)-2=-1-a$, so $a+b=-1$.
\end{itemize}
Every step is reversible, so there are exactly four solutions $(a,b,c,d)$:
\begin{gather*}
(-2,1,0,-1),\qquad(2,2,2,2),\\
\left(\dfrac{-1+\sqrt5}{2},\dfrac{-1-\sqrt5}{2},\dfrac{-1-\sqrt5}{2},\dfrac{-1+\sqrt5}{2}\right),\qquad\left(\dfrac{-1-\sqrt5}{2},\dfrac{-1+\sqrt5}{2},\dfrac{-1+\sqrt5}{2},\dfrac{-1-\sqrt5}{2}\right).
\end{gather*}
Hence $a+b$ is $\boxed{4\ \text{or}\ -1}$; the value $4$ comes from the only positive solution $a=b=c=d=2$.
note: The post asks for "the value" of a + b, but it is not unique: the system has four real solutions, one with a + b = 4 (a = b = c = d = 2) and three with a + b = -1. The record asks for all possible values. Checked with a Groebner basis (sympy) and by substituting the four solutions.

question: Evaluate $\sqrt{3^7+3^7+3^7}$.
solution:
The three equal terms add up to $3\cdot3^7=3^8$. So
\[\sqrt{3^7+3^7+3^7}=\sqrt{3^8}=3^4=\boxed{81}.\]

question: What is the greatest possible number of intersection points of $8$ distinct lines in a plane?
solution:
Two distinct lines meet in at most one point, and there are $\dbinom82=28$ pairs of lines, so there are at most $28$ intersection points.

This is attained when no two lines are parallel and no three pass through a common point. For example, take the lines $\ell_k:\ y=kx+k^2$ for $k=1,2,\dots,8$. They have different slopes, so any two of them meet: $\ell_j$ and $\ell_k$ ($j\ne k$) meet where $(j-k)x=k^2-j^2$, i.e. at
\[x=-(j+k),\qquad y=-jk.\]
If a third line $\ell_m$ passed through this point, then $-jk=-m(j+k)+m^2$, i.e. $(m-j)(m-k)=0$, so $m=j$ or $m=k$. Hence the $28$ intersection points are all different, and the answer is $\boxed{28}$.
note: Problem P1 of the post ("How many possible intersections can be made with 8 lines"), read as the greatest possible number of intersection points.

question: Let $x=\sqrt{6\sqrt{6\sqrt{6\sqrt{6\cdots}}}}$, the value of the infinitely nested radical. Find $x-324$.
solution:
Make the nested radical precise: let $a_1=\sqrt6$ and $a_{n+1}=\sqrt{6a_n}$, so that $a_n$ has $n$ square roots, and $x=\lim a_n$. By induction,
\[a_n=6^{\dfrac12+\dfrac14+\cdots+\dfrac1{2^n}}=6^{1-\dfrac{1}{2^n}},\]
since $a_1=6^{\dfrac12}$ and $\sqrt{6\cdot6^{1-\dfrac1{2^n}}}=6^{\dfrac12\left(2-\dfrac1{2^n}\right)}=6^{1-\dfrac{1}{2^{n+1}}}$. As $n\to\infty$ the exponent tends to $1$, so $x=6$.

(Equivalently, once we know that the limit exists and is positive, $x=\sqrt{6x}$ gives $x^2=6x$ and $x=6$.)

Hence $x-324=\boxed{-318}$.
note: Problem P5 of the post reads "Simplify: sqrt(6 sqrt(6 sqrt 6))... - 324", with the dots after the radical; it is read as the infinite nested radical (value 6) minus 324.

question: Simplify $\sqrt{53-8\sqrt{15}}$.
solution:
Look for positive numbers $a>b$ with $\left(\sqrt a-\sqrt b\right)^2=53-8\sqrt{15}$, that is
\[a+b-2\sqrt{ab}=53-2\sqrt{240}.\]
It suffices to take $a+b=53$ and $ab=240$, so $a$ and $b$ are the roots of $t^2-53t+240=0$, namely $48$ and $5$. Since $\sqrt{48}>\sqrt5$,
\[\sqrt{53-8\sqrt{15}}=\sqrt{48}-\sqrt5=\boxed{4\sqrt3-\sqrt5}.\]
Check: $\left(4\sqrt3-\sqrt5\right)^2=48-8\sqrt{15}+5=53-8\sqrt{15}$, and $4\sqrt3-\sqrt5>0$.
note: Problem P6 of the post.

question: Write $\dfrac{3-4i}{5-6i}$ in the form $a+bi$ with real $a$ and $b$.
solution:
Multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate $5+6i$:
\[\dfrac{3-4i}{5-6i}=\dfrac{(3-4i)(5+6i)}{(5-6i)(5+6i)}=\dfrac{15+18i-20i-24i^2}{25+36}=\dfrac{39-2i}{61}=\boxed{\dfrac{39}{61}-\dfrac{2}{61}i}.\]
note: Problem P7 of the post.

question: How many zeros are at the end of $100!$?
solution: Each trailing zero comes from a factor $10=2\cdot5$, and $100!$ contains more factors $2$ than factors $5$, so the number of trailing zeros is the exponent of $5$ in $100!$. Among $1,\dots,100$ there are $\left\lfloor\dfrac{100}{5}\right\rfloor=20$ multiples of $5$, and $\left\lfloor\dfrac{100}{25}\right\rfloor=4$ of them are multiples of $25$ and contribute a second factor $5$; there are no multiples of $125$. So the exponent of $5$ is $20+4=24$, and $100!$ ends in $\boxed{24}$ zeros.
note: Problem P8 of the post.

question: A positive integer is \emph{abundant} if the sum of its proper divisors (all positive divisors except itself) is greater than the number, \emph{perfect} if this sum equals the number, and \emph{deficient} if it is smaller. Is $200$ abundant, perfect or deficient?
solution:
Since $200=2^3\cdot5^2$, the sum of all its positive divisors is
\[\left(1+2+4+8\right)\left(1+5+25\right)=15\cdot31=465.\]
The sum of its proper divisors is $465-200=265>200$, so $200$ is $\boxed{\text{abundant}}$.
note: Problem P9 of the post; the definitions are added.

question: Gong often misspells the word INCORRECT. In how many ways can the nine letters of INCORRECT be arranged in a row so that the result is \emph{not} the correct spelling INCORRECT?
solution:
The letters are I, N, C, O, R, R, E, C, T: nine letters, with C twice and R twice. The number of different arrangements is
\[\dfrac{9!}{2!\,2!}=\dfrac{362880}{4}=90720.\]
Exactly one of them is the correct spelling, so the number of misspellings is $90720-1=\boxed{90719}$.
note: Problem P10 of the post ("incorrectly spell the word INCORRECT using all of the letters").

question: The $80$th term of an arithmetic sequence is twice the $30$th term. If the first term of the sequence is $7$, what is the $40$th term?
solution:
Let the common difference be $d$, so the $n$th term is $7+(n-1)d$. The condition says
\[7+79d=2(7+29d)\iff 21d=7\iff d=\dfrac13.\]
So the $40$th term is $7+39\cdot\dfrac13=7+13=\boxed{20}$. (Check: the $30$th term is $7+\dfrac{29}{3}=\dfrac{50}{3}$ and the $80$th is $7+\dfrac{79}{3}=\dfrac{100}{3}$.)
note: Problem P12 of the post, marked "(From MATHCOUNTS)" without further details.

question: The geometric mean of two positive numbers $a$ and $b$ is $\sqrt{ab}$. The third term of an arithmetic sequence of positive numbers, in which the common difference is not $0$, is the geometric mean of the first and eleventh terms. What is the ratio of the second term to the first term of the sequence? Express your answer as a common fraction.
solution:
Let the first term be $a>0$ and the common difference $d\ne0$. The third term is $a+2d$ and the eleventh is $a+10d$, so
\[(a+2d)^2=a(a+10d)\iff a^2+4ad+4d^2=a^2+10ad\iff 4d^2=6ad\iff d=\dfrac32a\]
(dividing by $2d\ne0$). The ratio of the second term to the first is
\[\dfrac{a+d}{a}=\dfrac{a+\dfrac32a}{a}=\boxed{\dfrac52}.\]
(Check: the terms are $a,\dfrac52a,4a,\dots,16a,\dots$, all positive, and $4a=\sqrt{a\cdot16a}$.)
note: Problem P13 of the post, marked "(From MATHCOUNTS)" without further details.

question: Two fair dice, one red and one blue, are rolled together again and again. A roll is recorded as the ordered pair (red number, blue number), so there are $36$ possible outcomes. What is the expected number of rolls needed until every one of the $36$ outcomes has appeared at least once?
solution:
Split the waiting into stages. Once exactly $j$ different outcomes have appeared ($0\le j\le35$), each roll shows a new outcome with probability $\dfrac{36-j}{36}$, independently of earlier rolls. So the number of rolls until the next new outcome is geometric with mean $\dfrac{36}{36-j}$. By linearity of expectation, the expected total is
\[\sum_{j=0}^{35}\dfrac{36}{36-j}=36\left(1+\dfrac12+\dfrac13+\cdots+\dfrac1{36}\right)=\boxed{\dfrac{54801925434709}{364655436600}}\approx150.3.\]
note: The post asks for the expected number of rolls "to get all of the possible combinations for rolling" two dice. This is read as all 36 ordered outcomes (distinguishable dice). (If the 21 unordered outcomes were meant, with doubles half as likely as the others, inclusion-exclusion gives 54484723852241/573029971800, about 95.08.) Checked with exact fractions and by simulation.

question: Two fair six-sided dice are rolled. What is the probability that the sum of the two numbers plus the product of the two numbers is even?
solution:
Let the numbers be $a$ and $b$. Then
\[a+b+ab=(a+1)(b+1)-1,\]
which is even exactly when $(a+1)(b+1)$ is odd, that is, when $a+1$ and $b+1$ are both odd, i.e. when $a$ and $b$ are both even. Each die is even with probability $\dfrac12$, independently, so the probability is $\dfrac12\cdot\dfrac12=\boxed{\dfrac14}$.

(Directly: if both are even, all three of $a$, $b$, $ab$ are even; if exactly one is odd, $a+b$ is odd and $ab$ is even; if both are odd, $a+b$ is even and $ab$ is odd. Only the first case gives an even total.)

question: A game of dots and boxes is played on a board of $10\times10$ unit boxes, that is, on an $11\times11$ square array of dots. On each turn a player draws one unit segment joining two neighbouring dots. A player who draws the fourth side of a box completes it. What is the largest number of segments that can be drawn so that no box has three or four of its sides drawn (so that nobody can complete a box on the next turn)? Show how this number can be reached.
