question:
Five positive integers $n,p,r,b,q$ satisfy all of the following.
\begin{itemize}
\item Exactly one of the five numbers is prime.
\item $npb$ is a perfect square.
\item None of the numbers contains the digit $6$.
\item Exactly one of the numbers is divisible by $5$.
\item $n+p+r+b+q=95$.
\item No number is larger than $50$.
\item $b\equiv p\pmod 9$.
\item The last digit of $q$ is $3$.
\item All five numbers are odd.
\item $r-p=6$.
\end{itemize}
Find $n,p,r,b,q$.
solution:
The odd numbers up to $50$ ending in $3$ are $3,13,23,33,43$, so $q$ is one of these; all except $33$ are prime.

\textbf{Case $q=33$.} Then $n+2p+b=95-33-6=56$. Since $b\equiv p\pmod 9$, also $b\equiv p\pmod3$, so $n+3p\equiv56\equiv2\pmod 3$, i.e. $n\equiv2\pmod3$. With $n$ odd, $n\in\{5,11,17,23,29,35,41,47\}$; all of these are prime except $35$.
\begin{itemize}
\item If $n$ is prime, then $p$ and $b$ are not prime, and since $npb$ is a square, $n$ divides $p$ or $b$. For $n\ge29$ the only odd multiple of $n$ up to $50$ is $n$ itself, which is prime; $34$ and $46$ are even; so $n=5$ or $n=11$. If $n=11$, then $p$ or $b$ is $33$, and $2p+b=45$ gives $b=-21$ or $p=6$, impossible. If $n=5$, then $p$ or $b$ is also a multiple of $5$, so two numbers are divisible by $5$, impossible.
\item If $n=35$, it is the only multiple of $5$, but $npb$ square requires $5\mid pb$, impossible.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Case $q\in\{3,13,23,43\}$.} Then $q$ is the only prime, so $n,p,r,b$ are odd non-primes up to $50$ without the digit $6$:
\[1,9,15,21,25,27,33,35,39,45,49.\]
Both $p$ and $r=p+6$ are in this list only for $(p,r)=(9,15),(15,21),(21,27),(27,33),(33,39),(39,45)$. For each, $b$ is in the list with $b\equiv p\pmod 9$, and $n=95-p-r-b-q$:
\begin{itemize}
\item $(9,15)$, $b\in\{9,27,45\}$. For $b=9$: $n=62-q\in\{59,49,39,19\}$; $59$ and $19$ are prime, $39\cdot9\cdot9$ is not a square, and $n=49$, $q=13$ works: $49\cdot9\cdot9=63^2$. For $b=27$: $n=44-q\in\{41,31,21,1\}$; $41,31$ are prime, and $21\cdot9\cdot27=3^6\cdot7$ and $1\cdot9\cdot27=3^5$ are not squares. For $b=45$: $n=26-q\in\{23,13,3\}$, all prime.
\item $(15,21)$, $b\in\{15,33\}$. For $b=15$: two multiples of $5$ ($p$ and $b$). For $b=33$: $n=26-q\in\{23,13,3\}$, prime.
\item $(21,27)$, $b\in\{21,39\}$: $n=26-q$ (prime) or $n=8-q=5$ (prime).
\item $(27,33)$, $b\in\{9,27,45\}$: $n=26-q$ (prime), $n=8-q=5$ (prime), or $n<0$.
\item $(33,39)$, $b\in\{15,33\}$: $n=8-q=5$ (prime) or $n<0$.
\item $(39,45)$: $n=11-b-q<0$.
\end{itemize}
The only solution is $\boxed{n=49,\ p=9,\ r=15,\ b=9,\ q=13}$. Check: sum $95$, only $13$ is prime, only $15$ is divisible by $5$, $npb=3969=63^2$, $9\equiv9\pmod 9$, $15-9=6$.
note: The post's numbers are the counts of Chopin mazurkas, Prokofiev piano sonatas, Shostakovich and Mahler symphonies and Rachmaninoff Op. 32 preludes, but asks not to use that information. "One of the numbers is divisible by five" is read as exactly one: otherwise n = 1, p = 15, r = 21, b = 15, q = 43 is a second solution. Checked by brute force over all 5-tuples.

question: Nine different sketchbooks are put on a shelf in a row, except that three of them are identical. The three identical ones must be next to each other. Two particular sketchbooks $X$ and $Y$ must have one or two sketchbooks between them (so they are not next to each other). Another particular sketchbook $Z$ must be at one of the two ends of the row. How many arrangements are possible?
solution:
By symmetry, count the arrangements with $Z$ at the left end and double. The other eight books occupy places $2$ to $9$: the block $I$ of three identical books, $X$, $Y$ and three other different books $D,E,F$. Treat the block as one unit, so we arrange the $6$ units $I,X,Y,D,E,F$ in a row.

If $I$ were between $X$ and $Y$, there would be at least $3$ books between them. So between $X$ and $Y$ there are $1$ or $2$ of the single books $D,E,F$, and nothing else.
\begin{itemize}
\item One book between: choose it ($3$ ways) and the order of $X,Y$ ($2$ ways); the group of $3$ units and the other $3$ units ($I$ and two single books) are arranged in $4!=24$ ways: $3\cdot2\cdot24=144$.
\item Two books between: choose them in order ($3\cdot2=6$ ways) and the order of $X,Y$ ($2$ ways); the group of $4$ units with $I$ and the last single book: $3!=6$ ways: $6\cdot2\cdot6=72$.
\end{itemize}
So there are $144+72=216$ arrangements with $Z$ on the left, and $2\cdot216=\boxed{432}$ in all.
note: Q1 of the post. The record makes explicit that the six non-identical books are all different and that "at most two in between, yet not together" means one or two books between X and Y. Checked by listing all arrangements.

question: A wishing well hears a wish with probability $\dfrac16$. If it hears the wish, it takes it into consideration with probability $29\%$; a wish that is not considered is not granted. A wish is good or bad with probability $50\%$ each. A good wish that is considered is always granted; a bad wish that is considered is granted (for a noble reason) with probability $11\%$. What is the probability that a wish is granted?
solution:
A wish is granted only if it is heard and considered, which happens with probability $\dfrac16\cdot\dfrac{29}{100}$. Then it is granted with probability
\[\dfrac12\cdot1+\dfrac12\cdot\dfrac{11}{100}=\dfrac{111}{200}.\]
So the probability is
\[\dfrac16\cdot\dfrac{29}{100}\cdot\dfrac{111}{200}=\dfrac{3219}{120000}=\boxed{\dfrac{1073}{40000}}\approx2.68\%.\]
note: Q2 of the post. The record makes explicit that a wish that is not heard or not considered is not granted, and that a considered good wish is always granted. Checked with exact fractions.

solution:
\textbf{(a)} We count the ways to write $8$ as a sum of parts from $\{1,2,4,5\}$, ignoring order. With a $5$: the rest is $3=2+1=1+1+1$ ($2$ ways). Without a $5$, with two $4$'s: $1$ way; with one $4$: the rest is $4$ written with $1$'s and $2$'s: $2+2$, $2+1+1$, $1+1+1+1$ ($3$ ways); with no $4$: $8$ written with $1$'s and $2$'s, with $0$ to $4$ twos ($5$ ways). Total $2+1+3+5=\boxed{11}$.

\textbf{(b)} Let $a_k$ be the number of sequences with sum $k$. The first piece is $1,2,4$ or $5$, so
\[a_k=a_{k-1}+a_{k-2}+a_{k-4}+a_{k-5},\qquad a_0=1,\ a_k=0\text{ for }k<0.\]
Then $a_1=1$, $a_2=2$, $a_3=3$, $a_4=6$, $a_5=11$, $a_6=20$, $a_7=36$, and
\[a_8=a_7+a_6+a_4+a_3=36+20+6+3=\boxed{65}.\]
note: Q3 of the post ("how many ways can she put down the pieces" with labels 4, 5, 1, 2 adding up to 8). Both readings (order ignored, order counted) are asked. Checked by enumeration.

question: Five horses finish a race with no ties: Lightning, Crown, Texas, Selene and Comanche. The two horses whose names have five letters did not finish in places next to each other. Comanche finished third. The horse with the longest name finished second or fourth. Crown finished directly before or directly after Comanche. Selene finished ahead of Texas. What was the finishing order?
solution:
The name lengths are Lightning $9$, Comanche $8$, Selene $6$, Crown $5$ and Texas $5$. Comanche is third, and Crown is next to Comanche, so Crown is second or fourth; Lightning (longest name) is also second or fourth. So Lightning and Crown take places $2$ and $4$, and Selene and Texas take places $1$ and $5$; since Selene is ahead of Texas, Selene is first and Texas fifth. The five-letter names Crown and Texas are not adjacent, so Crown is not fourth: Crown is second and Lightning fourth. The order is
\[\boxed{\text{Selene, Crown, Comanche, Lightning, Texas}}.\]
note: Q4 of the post. Checked by listing all 120 orders (exactly one satisfies the clues).

question: Find the value of $\sqrt{30\cdot31\cdot32\cdot33+1}$, and explain the method.
solution:
Pair the outer and inner factors: $30\cdot33=990$ and $31\cdot32=992=990+2$. With $m=990$,
\[30\cdot31\cdot32\cdot33+1=m(m+2)+1=m^2+2m+1=(m+1)^2.\]
So the value is $m+1=\boxed{991}$. In general $n(n+1)(n+2)(n+3)+1=\left(n^2+3n+1\right)^2$.
note: Near-miss: aops-topic-3133653-q01 (the same idea with 20, 21, 22, 23). Checked exactly.

question: In the year $2020$ ($366$ days), $20$ events happened, each on a day chosen uniformly at random from the $366$ days, independently. What is the probability that at least two of the events happened on the same day? Give an exact expression and a decimal approximation.
solution:
By the complement, the probability that all $20$ days are different is
\[\dfrac{366\cdot365\cdot364\cdots347}{366^{20}}\approx0.5894,\]
since the first event can be on any day, the second must avoid one day, and so on. So the probability that some two events share a day is
\[\boxed{1-\dfrac{366\cdot365\cdots347}{366^{20}}\approx0.411}.\]
note: The post says the events are "spaced randomly through 2020"; the record makes the model explicit (independent, uniform over the 366 days of the leap year). Checked with exact fractions.

question:
In a puzzle, each integer is to be written using exactly five $2$'s and operations such as $+,-,\times,\div$, powers, square roots, factorials, logarithms, $\lfloor\ \rfloor$ (floor) and $\lceil\ \rceil$ (ceiling). Writing $22$ uses two $2$'s, $222$ uses three, and $.2=0.2$ uses one. A student claims the following. For each claim, find the value of the right-hand side and decide whether the claim is correct (right value and exactly five $2$'s).
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] $29=(2+2)!+2+2+\left\lfloor\sqrt2\right\rfloor$
\item[(b)] $55=\left(2+\dfrac{\left\lfloor\sqrt2\right\rfloor}{.2}\right)\cdot22$
\item[(c)] $105=\dfrac{22+\dfrac22}{.2}$
\item[(d)] $139=\left\lfloor\sqrt{\dfrac{(2\cdot2\cdot2)!}{2}}\right\rfloor-2$
\item[(e)] $152=22\left\lfloor\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\right\rfloor-2$
\item[(f)] $197=\left\lceil22\log_{\sqrt2}22\right\rceil$
\item[(g)] $215=222+\left\lfloor\dfrac{\sqrt2}{.2}\right\rfloor$
\end{enumerate}
Then correct (c) and (g) by changing one symbol in each.
solution:
Recall $\left\lfloor\sqrt2\right\rfloor=1$ since $1<\sqrt2<2$. Every right-hand side above uses exactly five $2$'s, so only the values matter.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] $24+2+2+1=29$: \textbf{correct}.
\item[(b)] $\dfrac{1}{.2}=5$, so the value is $(2+5)\cdot22=154$: \textbf{wrong}.
\item[(c)] $\dfrac{22+1}{.2}=\dfrac{23}{0.2}=115$: \textbf{wrong}.
\item[(d)] $(2\cdot2\cdot2)!=8!=40320$, half of it is $20160$, and $141^2=19881\le20160<20164=142^2$, so the floor of the square root is $141$ and the value is $141-2=139$: \textbf{correct}.
\item[(e)] $\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\approx0.707$ has floor $0$, so the value is $0-2=-2$: \textbf{wrong}.
\item[(f)] $\log_{\sqrt2}22=2\log_2 22$. Since $2^{4.459}\approx22$ (more precisely $\log_222\approx4.4594$), this is about $8.9189$, and $22\cdot8.9189\approx196.2$, whose ceiling is $197$: \textbf{correct}. (To be sure of the ceiling: $196<22\log_{\sqrt2}22<197$ means $2^{\dfrac{196}{44}}<22<2^{\dfrac{197}{44}}$, and indeed $2^{4.4545}\approx21.93$ and $2^{4.4773}\approx22.28$.)
\item[(g)] $\dfrac{\sqrt2}{.2}=5\sqrt2\approx7.07$ has floor $7$, so the value is $229$: \textbf{wrong}.
\end{enumerate}
So (a), (d) and (f) are correct, and (b), (c), (e), (g) are wrong.

Corrections: $105=\dfrac{22-\dfrac22}{.2}=\dfrac{21}{0.2}$, and $215=222-\left\lfloor\dfrac{\sqrt2}{.2}\right\rfloor=222-7$.
note: The post lists representations of 1 to 222 with five 2s and warns that some may be wrong; the record checks seven of them, four of which are wrong as posted (55, 105, 152 and 215; the 105 line repeats the expression for 115). Values checked numerically and with exact integer square roots.

question: Write each of the integers $1,2,\dots,10$ using exactly three $3$'s, together with $+,-,\times,\div$, parentheses, powers, square roots, factorials and the decimal point (so that, for example, $0.3$ or the repeating decimal $0.\overline{3}=\dfrac13$ may be written with a single $3$).
solution:
One possible list:
\[1=\left(\dfrac33\right)^3,\quad 2=\dfrac{3+3}{3},\quad 3=3+3-3,\quad 4=3+\dfrac33,\quad 5=\dfrac{3!}{3}+3,\]
\[6=3\cdot3-3,\quad 7=3!+\dfrac33,\quad 8=\left(\dfrac{3!}{3}\right)^3,\quad 9=3+3+3,\quad 10=3\cdot\left(3+0.\overline3\right).\]
Each uses exactly three $3$'s. The last one works because $3+0.\overline3=3+\dfrac13=\dfrac{10}{3}$. (Many other answers are possible.)
note: The post allows "any operations"; the record fixes a list of operations. A depth-limited computer search (sums, differences, products, quotients, powers, square roots, factorials of small integers and concatenation, without a decimal point) found no way to make 10, which is why the decimal point is included. Every expression was checked exactly.

solution:

\[\dfrac{22}{7}=\boxed{3.\overline{142857}}=3.142857142857\ldots\]

\textbf{(b)} $\dfrac{22}7-\pi=3.14285714\ldots-3.14159265\ldots=0.00126449\ldots\approx\boxed{0.00126}$. As a fraction of $\pi$ this is $\dfrac{0.0012645}{3.14159}\approx0.000402$, i.e. about $\boxed{0.0402\%}$. So $\dfrac{22}{7}$ is a good approximation of $\pi$ (correct to two decimal places), but it is not equal to $\pi$; a calculator shows $\dfrac{22}{7}$ as $3.14285714\ldots$ and $\pi$ as $3.14159265\ldots$.

solution:
Let the digits be $d_1,d_2,d_3,d_4$ and $S=d_1+d_2+d_3+d_4$. By (c) and (d), $S-3$ is divisible by $5$ and by $6$, hence by $30$: $S=3$ or $S=33$ (as $S\le36$).

\textbf{$S=33$ is impossible.} By (a), $d_2\le d_3-1$, and by (b), $d_3+d_4\le15$ (the largest options are $9+6$ and $6+9$). If $d_3=9$, then $d_4=6$, $d_2\le8$ and $S\le9+8+9+6=32$. If $d_3\le8$, then $d_2\le7$ and $d_3+d_4\le8+5$ or $\le6+9$, so $S\le9+7+15=31$. Either way $S<33$.

\textbf{$S=3$.} If $d_4=d_3+3$, then $d_3+d_4\ge1+4=5>3$ (as $d_3>d_2\ge0$). So $d_4=d_3-3$, hence $d_3\ge3$, and $d_3+d_4=2d_3-3\le3$ forces $d_3=3$, $d_4=0$, and then $d_1=d_2=0$.

The code is $\boxed{0030}$.

question:
Let $b$ and $d$ be positive integers with $\gcd(b,d)=1$, and let $b'$ be an inverse of $b$ modulo $d$, that is, an integer with $bb'\equiv1\pmod d$. For integers $a$ and $c$, let
\[n=bb'(c-a)+a.\]
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Prove that $n\equiv a\pmod b$ and $n\equiv c\pmod d$.
\item[(b)] Prove that the integers $m$ with $m\equiv a\pmod b$ and $m\equiv c\pmod d$ are exactly those with $m\equiv n\pmod{bd}$.
\item[(c)] Use the formula to solve $m\equiv2\pmod5$, $m\equiv3\pmod7$.
\end{enumerate}
solution:
\textbf{(a)} $n-a=b\cdot b'(c-a)$ is a multiple of $b$, so $n\equiv a\pmod b$. Modulo $d$, $bb'\equiv1$, so $n\equiv(c-a)+a=c\pmod d$.

\textbf{(b)} If $m\equiv n\pmod{bd}$, then $m\equiv n$ modulo $b$ and modulo $d$, so $m$ satisfies both congruences by (a). Conversely, if $m$ satisfies both, then $b\mid m-n$ and $d\mid m-n$; since $\gcd(b,d)=1$, $bd\mid m-n$.

\textbf{(c)} Here $a=2$, $b=5$, $c=3$, $d=7$. Since $5\cdot3=15\equiv1\pmod7$, take $b'=3$. Then $n=5\cdot3\cdot(3-2)+2=17$. Check: $17=3\cdot5+2=2\cdot7+3$. So $\boxed{m\equiv17\pmod{35}}$.

(The condition $\gcd(b,d)=1$ is needed for $b'$ to exist; for example $m\equiv0\pmod2$ and $m\equiv1\pmod4$ has no solution.)
note: The post claims the formula "b * b^{-1} (c - a) + a" for the system n = a (mod b), n = c (mod d) and asks for a proof. The record states the meaning of b^{-1} (an inverse of b modulo d) and the needed condition gcd(b, d) = 1, and adds the description of all solutions and an example. Checked by brute force for all small moduli.

question:
Prove the binomial theorem: for every positive integer $n$ and all numbers $x,y$,
\[(x+y)^n=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\dbinom nk x^{n-k}y^k.\]
solution:
Write $(x+y)^n=(x+y)(x+y)\cdots(x+y)$ with $n$ factors. Expanding the product by the distributive law, we choose one of the two terms $x$ or $y$ from each factor, multiply the choices, and add the results over all $2^n$ ways of choosing.

A choice in which $y$ is taken from exactly $k$ of the factors (and $x$ from the other $n-k$) gives the product $x^{n-k}y^k$. The number of such choices is the number of ways to pick the $k$ factors that contribute $y$, which is $\dbinom nk$. Collecting equal products,
\[(x+y)^n=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\dbinom nk x^{n-k}y^k.\qquad\blacksquare\]

(Alternatively, by induction on $n$: multiplying $\displaystyle\sum_k\dbinom{n}{k}x^{n-k}y^k$ by $x+y$ gives the coefficient $\dbinom nk+\dbinom n{k-1}=\dbinom{n+1}{k}$ for $x^{n+1-k}y^k$, by Pascal's rule.)
note: The post asks for the proof of the binomial theorem; the record asks to prove it. Checked symbolically for n up to 8.

question: Dream has $5$ ender pearls and $10$ health points. Every time he throws a pearl, he loses $1$, $2$ or $3$ health points, each with probability $\dfrac13$, independently. He dies when his health reaches $0$ or less. What is the probability that he dies before throwing his fifth pearl, that is, as a result of one of his first four throws?
solution:
He dies within the first four throws exactly when the total loss of the first four throws is at least $10$. Subtract $1$ from each loss: then we need four values in $\{0,1,2\}$ with sum at least $6$, out of $3^4=81$ equally likely outcomes.
\begin{itemize}
\item Sum $8$: $(2,2,2,2)$, $1$ outcome.
\item Sum $7$: three $2$'s and one $1$, $4$ outcomes.
\item Sum $6$: two $2$'s and two $1$'s, $\dbinom42=6$ outcomes; or three $2$'s and one $0$, $4$ outcomes.
\end{itemize}
That is $15$ outcomes, so the probability is $\dfrac{15}{81}=\boxed{\dfrac5{27}}$.
note: Problem 1 of the post. "A random number between 1 and 3" is taken as 1, 2 or 3 with equal probability, and "dies before he throws all 5 pearls" as dying from one of the first four throws. Checked by enumeration.

question: A player wins each game with probability $\dfrac34$, independently. He plays $10$ games. What is the probability that at some point he wins $3$ games in a row?
solution:
Let $q_n$ be the probability that $n$ games contain no $3$ consecutive wins. Such a sequence ends with a loss, or with a loss followed by one win, or with a loss followed by two wins (or it is just one or two wins at the start). Conditioning on the last loss gives, for $n\ge3$,
\[q_n=\dfrac14q_{n-1}+\dfrac34\cdot\dfrac14q_{n-2}+\left(\dfrac34\right)^2\dfrac14q_{n-3},\]
with $q_0=q_1=q_2=1$. Multiply by $4^n$ and let $Q_n=4^nq_n$ (the weighted count of good sequences, where a win has weight $3$ and a loss weight $1$):
\[Q_n=Q_{n-1}+3Q_{n-2}+9Q_{n-3},\qquad Q_0=1,\ Q_1=4,\ Q_2=16.\]
Then
\[Q_3=37,\ Q_4=121,\ Q_5=376,\ Q_6=1072,\ Q_7=3289,\ Q_8=9889,\ Q_9=29404,\ Q_{10}=88672.\]
(Check: $Q_3=64-27$, all weighted sequences minus $WWW$.) So $q_{10}=\dfrac{88672}{4^{10}}=\dfrac{2771}{32768}$, and the probability of $3$ wins in a row is
\[1-\dfrac{2771}{32768}=\boxed{\dfrac{29997}{32768}}\approx0.915.\]
note: Problem 2 of the post. Checked by summing over all 1024 win/loss sequences.

question: A year in the $21$st century ($2001$ to $2100$) is divisible by $10$ and by $67$. What is the year?
solution: Since $\gcd(10,67)=1$, the year is a multiple of $670$. The multiples of $670$ are $1340,2010,2680,\dots$, and only $\boxed{2010}$ lies between $2001$ and $2100$.

question: In each second, the number of clicks a player makes is one of $8,9,10,11,12$, with probability proportional to the number. What is the probability that he makes $12$ clicks in a given second?
solution: The probabilities are $\dfrac{k}{8+9+10+11+12}=\dfrac{k}{50}$ for $k=8,\dots,12$, so the probability of $12$ clicks is $\dfrac{12}{50}=\boxed{\dfrac{6}{25}}$.

\textbf{(a)} Everyone who uses both clients uses $L$, so the percentage using both is at most the percentage using $L$. But $60\%>30\%$, so the data are impossible.

\textbf{(b)} We need $0\le x\le30$ (the players using both are among the $30\%$ using $L$). By inclusion--exclusion the percentage using at least one client is $30+40-x=70-x$, so the percentage using neither is

question: A player's race time $T$ is uniformly distributed between $4$ minutes $30$ seconds and $5$ minutes. The average time $A$ of the whole field is independent of $T$ and uniformly distributed between $7$ minutes $30$ seconds and $14$ minutes. What is the probability that $T$ is less than half of $A$?
solution:
In seconds, $T$ is uniform on $[270,300]$ and $A$ is uniform on $[450,840]$, so $H=\dfrac A2$ is uniform on $[225,420]$. For a fixed $t$ in $[270,300]$,
\[P(H>t)=\dfrac{420-t}{420-225}=\dfrac{420-t}{195},\]
since $t$ lies inside $[225,420]$. This is a linear function of $t$, so its average over the uniform $T$ is its value at the midpoint $t=285$:
\[P(T<H)=\dfrac{420-285}{195}=\dfrac{135}{195}=\boxed{\dfrac{9}{13}}.\]
note: Problem 6 of the post (Ace Race times). Checked by exact integration with sympy.

question: A parkour course has $4$ jumps. On each attempt at a jump, the player succeeds with probability $90\%$, independently. If he fails, he respawns at the block he jumped from (instantly) and tries that jump again. A failed attempt takes $2$ seconds and a successful jump takes $1$ second. What is the expected time to complete the course?
solution:
For one jump, the number of failed attempts before the success, $F$, satisfies $P(F=k)=(0.1)^k\cdot0.9$. Its expected value is
\[E[F]=\sum_{k\ge0}k(0.1)^k(0.9)=\dfrac{0.1}{0.9}=\dfrac19.\]
(Equivalently: the expected number of attempts is $\dfrac{1}{0.9}=\dfrac{10}9$, one of which succeeds.) So one jump takes on average $1+2\cdot\dfrac19=\dfrac{11}9$ seconds, and by linearity of expectation the course takes
\[4\cdot\dfrac{11}{9}=\boxed{\dfrac{44}{9}\text{ seconds}}\approx4.89\text{ seconds}.\]
note: Problem 7 of the post. Checked with exact series and simulation-free algebra.

question: In a bow duel, Dream and Techno each start with $10$ hearts, and every arrow that hits takes away $4$ hearts. A player whose hearts reach $0$ or less dies. In each round both fire at the same time: Techno hits Dream with probability $\dfrac34$ and Dream hits Techno with probability $\dfrac12$, independently. The first to die loses; if both die in the same round, nobody wins. What is the probability that Dream wins?
solution:
Three hits kill ($2$ hits leave $2$ hearts, $3$ hits take $12$). Let $W(d,t)$ be the probability that Dream wins when Dream still needs $d$ hits on Techno and Techno still needs $t$ hits on Dream. In a round,
\begin{itemize}
\item both hit with probability $\dfrac12\cdot\dfrac34=\dfrac38$; only Dream hits: $\dfrac12\cdot\dfrac14=\dfrac18$; only Techno hits: $\dfrac12\cdot\dfrac34=\dfrac38$; nobody hits: $\dfrac18$.
\end{itemize}
Rounds where nobody hits change nothing, so we condition on something happening: both hit with probability $\dfrac37$, only Dream $\dfrac17$, only Techno $\dfrac37$. Hence
\[W(d,t)=\dfrac37W(d-1,t-1)+\dfrac17W(d-1,t)+\dfrac37W(d,t-1),\]
with $W(0,t)=1$ for $t\ge1$, $W(d,0)=0$ for all $d$ (Dream is dead, including a tie $W(0,0)=0$). Computing step by step:
\[W(1,1)=\dfrac17,\quad W(1,2)=\dfrac37+\dfrac17+\dfrac37\cdot\dfrac17=\dfrac{31}{49},\quad W(2,1)=\dfrac{1}{49},\]
\[W(1,3)=\dfrac37+\dfrac17+\dfrac37\cdot\dfrac{31}{49}=\dfrac{289}{343},\quad W(2,2)=\dfrac37\cdot\dfrac17+\dfrac17\cdot\dfrac{31}{49}+\dfrac37\cdot\dfrac1{49}=\dfrac{55}{343},\quad W(3,1)=\dfrac1{343},\]
\[W(2,3)=\dfrac37\cdot\dfrac{31}{49}+\dfrac17\cdot\dfrac{289}{343}+\dfrac37\cdot\dfrac{55}{343}=\dfrac{1105}{2401},\quad W(3,2)=\dfrac37\cdot\dfrac1{49}+\dfrac17\cdot\dfrac{55}{343}+\dfrac37\cdot\dfrac{1}{343}=\dfrac{79}{2401},\]
\[W(3,3)=\dfrac37\cdot\dfrac{55}{343}+\dfrac17\cdot\dfrac{1105}{2401}+\dfrac37\cdot\dfrac{79}{2401}=\dfrac{1155+1105+237}{16807}=\boxed{\dfrac{2497}{16807}}\approx0.149.\]
note: Problem 8 of the post. The record adds the Minecraft facts the problem relies on (10 hearts each, so 3 hits kill) and states what happens if both die together (no winner; probability 2619/16807). Checked by an exact recursion.

question: For positive integers $a$ and $b$, define $a\star b=a^4-b^4$. If $a\star b=5936$ and $a^2+b^2=106$, find $ab^2$.
solution:
Factor $a^4-b^4=(a^2+b^2)(a^2-b^2)$. Then $a^2-b^2=\dfrac{5936}{106}=56$. Adding and subtracting $a^2+b^2=106$ gives $a^2=81$ and $b^2=25$, so $a=9$, $b=5$, and
\[ab^2=9\cdot25=\boxed{225}.\]

note: The post asks how to find the equation of a line from its slope and a point; the record asks to derive the point-slope form and apply it. Near-miss: aops-topic-2465804-q01 (which starts from the point-slope form).

question:
Solve the system
\[\begin{aligned}4x+6y+3z&=-6\\2x+6y+3z&=6\\6x+4y+7z&=3\end{aligned}\]
solution:
Subtracting the second equation from the first gives $2x=-12$, so $x=-6$. The second equation becomes $6y+3z=18$, i.e. $2y+z=6$, and the third becomes $4y+7z=39$. Substituting $z=6-2y$:
\[4y+42-14y=39\ \Longrightarrow\ y=\dfrac{3}{10},\qquad z=6-\dfrac35=\dfrac{27}{5}.\]
So $\boxed{(x,y,z)=\left(-6,\dfrac3{10},\dfrac{27}5\right)}$. Check in the first equation: $-24+\dfrac{18}{10}+\dfrac{81}{5}=-24+1.8+16.2=-6$.
note: P1 of the post. Checked with sympy.

question:
Solve the system
\[\begin{aligned}7s+4t+2u&=-3\\7s+7t+2u&=7\\7s+4t+6u&=-2\end{aligned}\]
solution:
Subtracting the first equation from the second: $3t=10$, so $t=\dfrac{10}3$. Subtracting the first from the third: $4u=1$, so $u=\dfrac14$. Then
\[7s=-3-4\cdot\dfrac{10}{3}-2\cdot\dfrac14=-3-\dfrac{40}3-\dfrac12=-\dfrac{101}{6},\qquad s=-\dfrac{101}{42}.\]
So $\boxed{(s,t,u)=\left(-\dfrac{101}{42},\dfrac{10}{3},\dfrac14\right)}$.
note: P2 of the post. Checked with sympy.

question: A knight stands on the bottom-left square $a1$ of an $8\times8$ chessboard. Is it possible to move it to the top-right square $h8$ in exactly $2017$ moves? Prove your answer.
solution:
\textbf{No.} Colour the board in the usual chessboard pattern. A knight's move changes one coordinate by $1$ and the other by $2$, so it changes the sum of the coordinates by an odd number: every knight move goes from a square of one colour to a square of the other colour.

The squares $a1$ (coordinates $(1,1)$) and $h8$ (coordinates $(8,8)$) both have an even coordinate sum, so they have the same colour. After an odd number of moves, such as $2017$, the knight is on a square of the opposite colour to $a1$, so it cannot be on $h8$. $\blacksquare$
note: The poster knows the answer (impossible) and asks for a proof. Near-miss: aops-topic-3346757-q03 (counting knight paths from a1 to h8 in 25 moves).

question: A perk costs $20$ dollars. With probability $5\%$ it pays out a random whole number of dollars from $1$ to $400$, all equally likely; otherwise (probability $95\%$) it pays nothing. What is the expected profit from buying the perk?
solution:
When it pays out, the expected payment is the average of $1,2,\dots,400$, which is $\dfrac{1+400}{2}=200.5$ dollars. So the expected payment is $0.05\cdot200.5=10.025$ dollars, and the expected profit is
\[10.025-20=\boxed{-9.975\text{ dollars}},\]
a loss of about $9.98$ dollars on average.
note: "A one time payment of an amount of money between 1 and 400" is read as a uniformly random whole number of dollars (a uniform real amount in [1, 400] has the same mean). Checked with exact fractions.

question: Five nebulas are arranged in a row: a purple one, a blue one, a green one and two identical pink ones. The purple and blue nebulas may not be next to each other. Also, $8$ billion stars are shared among the nebulas so that each nebula gets a whole number of billions of stars, at least $1$ billion. In how many ways can the nebulas be arranged and the stars shared?
solution:
\textbf{Colours.} Without restriction there are $\dfrac{5!}{2!}=60$ colour sequences (the two pinks are identical). With purple and blue together, treat them as a block ($2$ orders) and arrange the block, green and two pinks: $2\cdot\dfrac{4!}{2!}=24$. So there are $60-24=36$ good colour sequences.

\textbf{Stars.} The places in the row get $x_1,\dots,x_5\ge1$ billion stars with $x_1+\cdots+x_5=8$. By stars and bars there are $\dbinom{7}{4}=35$ ways.

A configuration is a colour sequence together with a sequence of star counts for the five places, so the answer is $36\cdot35=\boxed{1260}$.
note: Q1 of the post. The post does not name the fifth nebula (here green) and does not say how stars are counted; the record takes whole numbers of billions. Checked by enumeration.

solution:
The name lengths are Io $2$, Thebe $5$, Metis $5$, Cyllene $7$, Ganymede $8$, Callisto $8$. Since Cyllene is ahead of Callisto, the winner (whose name starts with C) is Cyllene. Io has the shortest name, so Ganymede and Callisto (the longest names) both finished ahead of Io and not directly ahead of it. Thebe and Metis are next to each other with Thebe ahead, so Thebe is directly followed by Metis.

Who finished directly ahead of Io? Not Ganymede or Callisto; not Cyllene (Io would be second, ahead of the long names); not Thebe (Thebe is directly followed by Metis). So it was Metis, and Thebe, Metis, Io finished consecutively. Ganymede and Callisto are ahead of Io, hence ahead of this block, so the order is Cyllene, then Ganymede and Callisto in some order, then Thebe, Metis, Io. Both orders of Ganymede and Callisto satisfy every clue, so there are two possible finishing orders (from first to last):
\[\boxed{\text{Cyllene, Ganymede, Callisto, Thebe, Metis, Io}}\quad\text{or}\quad\boxed{\text{Cyllene, Callisto, Ganymede, Thebe, Metis, Io}}.\]
note: Q2 of the post. Ganymede and Callisto both have 8 letters, so "the moon with the most letters" applies to both, and the clues do not decide their order; the record asks for all possible orders (two). Checked by listing all 720 orders.

question: Apollo and Artemis each shoot once at each of $5$ targets, all shots independent. Apollo hits each of $3$ of the targets with probability $97\%$ and each of the other $2$ with probability $94\%$. Artemis hits each of $4$ of the targets with probability $99\%$ and the last one with probability $94\%$. What is the probability that Apollo hits exactly four targets and Artemis hits all five?
solution:
\textbf{Artemis hits all five:} $(0.99)^4(0.94)$.

\textbf{Apollo hits exactly four:} he misses exactly one target. Missing one of the $97\%$ targets: $3\cdot0.03\cdot(0.97)^2(0.94)^2$; missing one of the $94\%$ targets: $2\cdot0.06\cdot(0.97)^3(0.94)$. So
\[P(\text{Apollo }4)=3(0.03)(0.9409)(0.8836)+2(0.06)(0.912673)(0.94)\approx0.0748241+0.1029495=0.1777736.\]
By independence, the answer is
\[\left[3(0.03)(0.97)^2(0.94)^2+2(0.06)(0.97)^3(0.94)\right](0.99)^4(0.94)\approx0.17777\cdot0.90296\approx\boxed{0.1605}.\]
note: Q1 of the post. "Hits any four targets" is read as exactly four (missing exactly one). Checked with exact fractions.

The probability that she gives the belt is
\[\dfrac13\left(\dfrac12\cdot\dfrac45\right)+\dfrac13\cdot\dfrac1{16}+\dfrac13\cdot1=\dfrac13\left(\dfrac25+\dfrac1{16}+1\right)=\dfrac13\cdot\dfrac{32+5+80}{80}=\dfrac{117}{240}=\dfrac{39}{80}.\]
So the probability that she does not give it is $1-\dfrac{39}{80}=\boxed{\dfrac{41}{80}}$.
note: Q2 of the post, with the branches made explicit (in the first branch she gives the belt with probability 1/2 x 4/5). Checked with exact fractions.

question: Find the fourth term in the expansion of $(x+y)^{10}$ in decreasing powers of $x$.
solution:
The terms are $\dbinom{10}{k}x^{10-k}y^k$ for $k=0,1,\dots,10$, so the fourth term has $k=3$:
\[\dbinom{10}{3}x^7y^3=\boxed{120x^7y^3}.\]
note: P1 of the post.

question: Find the fifth term in the expansion of $(a+6b)^9$ in decreasing powers of $a$.
solution:
The fifth term has $k=4$:
\[\dbinom94a^5(6b)^4=126\cdot1296\,a^5b^4=\boxed{163296\,a^5b^4}.\]
note: P2 of the post. Checked with sympy.

question: Find the coefficient of $x^4$ in the expansion of $\left(x^2-3\right)^4$.
solution: The terms are $\dbinom4k\left(x^2\right)^{4-k}(-3)^k$. The power $x^4$ needs $4-k=2$, so $k=2$, and the coefficient is $\dbinom42(-3)^2=6\cdot9=\boxed{54}$.
note: P3 of the post.

question: Johnny masters a Prealgebra topic in $4.2$ minutes, a topic in Algebra, Counting, Number Theory or Geometry in $21$ minutes, and a topic in Intermediate Algebra or Precalculus in $69$ minutes. There are $100$ Prealgebra topics, $100$ topics in Algebra, Counting, Number Theory and Geometry combined, and $95$ topics in Intermediate Algebra and Precalculus combined. How long does it take him to master all the topics?
solution:
The total time is
\[100\cdot4.2+100\cdot21+95\cdot69=420+2100+6555=\boxed{9075\text{ minutes}},\]
which is $151.25$ hours.
note: Set 1 P1 of the post (the game "Alculoose"); "getting Grandmaster" is taken to mean mastering all topics.

question: Johnny starts with rating $0$ and gains $0.01$ rating for each problem he solves. Each problem takes him $1$ minute. How long does it take him to reach a rating of $69$?
solution: He needs $\dfrac{69}{0.01}=6900$ problems, which take $\boxed{6900\text{ minutes}}=115$ hours.
note: Set 1 P2 of the post; the starting rating 0 is made explicit.

question: Johnny starts with rating $0$ and gains $0.01$ rating for each problem he solves, at one problem per minute. Will he ever reach a rating of $100$? If so, how long does it take?
solution: Yes. His rating after $m$ minutes is $0.01m$, which grows without bound; it reaches $100$ after $\dfrac{100}{0.01}=\boxed{10000\text{ minutes}}$, that is, $166$ hours $40$ minutes (just under $7$ days).
note: Set 1 P3 of the post (a follow-up to P2), made self-contained.

question: If $a*b=a^3-2b^2$, what is $3*5$?
note: Set 2 P1 of the post.

question: Find the sum of the infinite geometric series $1+\dfrac23+\dfrac49+\dfrac8{27}+\cdots$.
solution:
The first term is $1$ and the common ratio is $\dfrac23$, with $\left|\dfrac23\right|<1$, so the sum is
\[\dfrac{1}{1-\dfrac23}=\boxed{3}.\]
note: Set 2 P2 of the post.

question:
Points $A$ and $B$ are the endpoints of an arc of a circle, and the arc has central angle $\theta$, where $0^\circ<\theta<360^\circ$. Let $N$ be the midpoint of the chord $AB$ and $M$ the midpoint of the arc.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Show that $M$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $AB$, on the same side of $AB$ as the arc, at distance
\[NM=\dfrac{AB}{2}\tan\dfrac{\theta}{4}\]
from $N$.
\item[(b)] For $A=(0,0)$, $B=(6,0)$ and an arc of $120^\circ$ above the line $AB$, find the coordinates of $M$.
\end{enumerate}
note: The post asks how to find the midpoint of an arc from its endpoints and its angle; the record asks for the general distance formula and a worked example. Checked numerically for many angles and in the example.

question: The price of petrol rises by $2$ cents per liter. Last week a man bought $20$ liters at the old price, and this week he bought $10$ liters at the new price. Altogether the petrol cost $9.20$ dollars. What was the old price of $1$ liter?
solution: Let the old price be $p$ dollars per liter. Then $20p+10(p+0.02)=9.20$, so $30p+0.2=9.2$, $30p=9$ and $p=0.30$. The old price was $\boxed{30\text{ cents}}$ per liter.
note: Problem 1 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com).

question: Teachers divided the students into groups of $3$. Each group wrote a report with $9$ pictures in it, and the students used $585$ pictures altogether. How many students were there?
solution: There were $\dfrac{585}{9}=65$ groups, so $65\cdot3=\boxed{195}$ students.
note: Problem 2 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com).

question: Vera is $4$ years old and her sister Vikki is $13$. How old will each sister be when Vikki is twice as old as Vera?
solution: In $t$ years, $13+t=2(4+t)$, so $t=5$. Then Vera will be $\boxed{9}$ and Vikki $\boxed{18}$.
note: Problem 3 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com).

question: A can do a piece of work in $14$ days, and A and B working together can do it in $10$ days. How long would B take working alone?
solution: Per day, A does $\dfrac1{14}$ of the work and together they do $\dfrac1{10}$, so B does $\dfrac1{10}-\dfrac1{14}=\dfrac{7-5}{70}=\dfrac1{35}$. B alone takes $\boxed{35\text{ days}}$.
note: Problem 4 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com).

question: $7$ workers can make $210$ pairs of cups in $6$ days. How many workers are needed to make $450$ pairs of cups in $10$ days, working at the same rate?
solution: One worker makes $\dfrac{210}{7\cdot6}=5$ pairs per day. In $10$ days one worker makes $50$ pairs, so $\dfrac{450}{50}=\boxed{9}$ workers are needed.
note: Problem 5 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com).

question: Ten years ago the ratio of the ages of Mohan and Suman was $3:5$. Eleven years from now it will be $11:16$. What is Mohan's present age?
solution:
Let their ages ten years ago be $3k$ and $5k$. Eleven years from now, $21$ years later, they are $3k+21$ and $5k+21$, so
\[16(3k+21)=11(5k+21)\ \Longrightarrow\ 48k+336=55k+231\ \Longrightarrow\ k=15.\]
Mohan is now $3\cdot15+10=\boxed{55}$ (and Suman $85$; check: in $11$ years $66:96=11:16$).
note: Problem 6 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com).

question: The ratio of girls to boys in a class is $9:7$, and there are $80$ students. How many girls are in the class?
solution: The class splits into $9+7=16$ equal parts of $5$ students, so there are $9\cdot5=\boxed{45}$ girls.
note: Problem 7 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com).

question: Solution X contains only ingredients a and b, in the ratio $2:3$. Solution Y contains only a and b, in the ratio $1:2$. Solution Z is made by mixing X and Y in the ratio $3:11$. How many ounces of ingredient a are in $2520$ ounces of Z?
solution:
In $2520$ ounces of Z there are $\dfrac{3}{14}\cdot2520=540$ ounces of X and $\dfrac{11}{14}\cdot2520=1980$ ounces of Y. X is $\dfrac25$ ingredient a and Y is $\dfrac13$ ingredient a, so the amount of a is
\[\dfrac25\cdot540+\dfrac13\cdot1980=216+660=\boxed{876}\text{ ounces}.\]
note: Problem 8 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com).

question: This week Bob filled up his truck's gas tank when it was half full. Five days later he filled it up again, when the tank was three fourths full. Altogether he bought $24$ gallons of gas. How many gallons does the tank hold?
solution: Each time he fills the tank completely. The first time he adds $\dfrac12$ of a tank and the second time $\dfrac14$ of a tank, $\dfrac34$ of a tank in all. So $\dfrac34T=24$ and $T=\boxed{32}$ gallons.
note: Problem 9 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com). The post says "half empty" and "about three fourths full"; the record states that Bob fills the tank completely each time, at exactly half full and three quarters full.

question: An airplane flying towards a radar station at $700$ mph is detected when it is $1000$ miles away. Half an hour later an interceptor plane flying at $800$ mph is sent from the station towards it. How long after it is sent does the interceptor meet the airplane?
solution: In the first half hour the airplane flies $350$ miles, so the distance is $650$ miles when the interceptor leaves. They approach each other at $700+800=1500$ mph, so they meet after $\dfrac{650}{1500}=\dfrac{13}{30}$ hour, that is, $\boxed{26\text{ minutes}}$.
note: Problem 10 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com). The post does not say in which direction the airplane flies; the record has it flying towards the station (head-on interception).

question: There are $40$ pigs and chickens in a farmyard, with $100$ legs in all. How many pigs and how many chickens are there?
solution: With $p$ pigs and $c$ chickens, $p+c=40$ and $4p+2c=100$. Subtracting twice the first equation, $2p=20$. So there are $\boxed{10\text{ pigs and }30\text{ chickens}}$.
note: Problem 11 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com).

question: The top of a box is a rectangle with perimeter $72$ inches, and the box is $8$ inches high. What dimensions give the largest volume?
note: Problem 12 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com).

question: You are raising money for a charity. Someone made a fixed donation of $500$ dollars, and each participant pledges at least $25$ dollars. What is the minimum amount raised if there are $224$ participants?
solution: The minimum is when every participant pledges exactly $25$ dollars: $500+25\cdot224=500+5600=\boxed{6100}$ dollars.
note: Problem 13 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com). "Each participant makes a pledge of 25 dollars" is read as a minimum pledge, which is what makes "minimum amount" meaningful.

solution:
\textbf{(a)} For positive $x$ and $y$, $x^2+y^2<x^2+2xy+y^2=(x+y)^2=16<28$. So the numbers cannot both be positive.

\textbf{(b)} From $(x+y)^2=x^2+y^2+2xy$ we get $16=28+2xy$, so $xy=-6$. The numbers are the roots of $t^2-4t-6=0$:
\[\boxed{2+\sqrt{10}\ \text{and}\ 2-\sqrt{10}}\ (\approx5.16\text{ and }-1.16).\]
note: Problem 14 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com). The post says "two positive numbers", which is impossible; the record asks to show this and to find the two (real) numbers.

question: Flying against the jet stream, a jet travels $1880$ miles in $4$ hours. Flying with the jet stream, it travels $5820$ miles in $6$ hours. What is the speed of the jet in still air, and what is the speed of the jet stream?
solution: Against the stream the speed is $\dfrac{1880}{4}=470$ mph, and with it $\dfrac{5820}{6}=970$ mph. So $j-w=470$ and $j+w=970$, giving a jet speed of $\boxed{720\text{ mph}}$ and a jet stream of $\boxed{250\text{ mph}}$.
note: Problem 15 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com).

question: Jenna has saved $110$ dollars and saves $20$ dollars more every week. Khalil has saved $80$ dollars and saves $25$ dollars more every week. After how many weeks will they have the same amount?
solution: After $x$ weeks, $110+20x=80+25x$, so $5x=30$ and $x=\boxed{6}$ weeks (both have $230$ dollars).
note: Problem 16 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com).

question: Three consecutive terms of a geometric sequence have sum $104$ and product $13824$. Find the terms.
solution: Write the terms as $\dfrac ar$, $a$, $ar$. Their product is $a^3=13824=24^3$, so $a=24$. Then $\dfrac{24}r+24+24r=104$, so $24r^2-80r+24=0$, i.e. $3r^2-10r+3=0$, with roots $r=3$ and $r=\dfrac13$. Either way the terms are $\boxed{8,\ 24,\ 72}$ (in one order or the other).
note: Problem 17 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com).

question: The sum of the first and last of four consecutive odd integers is $52$. What are the four integers?
solution: Let them be $n,n+2,n+4,n+6$. Then $2n+6=52$, so $n=23$: the integers are $\boxed{23,25,27,29}$.
note: Problem 18 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com).

question: A health club charges a one-time initiation fee and a monthly fee. John paid $100$ dollars for $2$ months of membership, and Peter paid $200$ dollars for $6$ months. How much will Sylvia pay for $1$ year?
solution: With fee $F$ and monthly fee $m$: $F+2m=100$ and $F+6m=200$, so $m=25$ and $F=50$. For $12$ months Sylvia pays $50+12\cdot25=\boxed{350}$ dollars.
note: Problem 19 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com).

question: The sum of two positive numbers is $4$ and the sum of their cubes is $28$. What is their product?
solution: Since $x^3+y^3=(x+y)^3-3xy(x+y)$, we get $28=64-12xy$, so $xy=\boxed{3}$. (The numbers are $1$ and $3$.)
note: Problem 20 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com).

question: A man's earnings are a linear function of the number of computer parts he sells. When he sells $16$ parts he earns $1700$ dollars, and when he sells $56$ parts he earns $4300$ dollars. What does he earn when he sells $30$ parts?
solution: The earnings increase by $\dfrac{4300-1700}{56-16}=\dfrac{2600}{40}=65$ dollars per part. So for $30$ parts he earns $1700+14\cdot65=1700+910=\boxed{2610}$ dollars.
note: Problem 21 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com). The record states that earnings are linear in the number of parts sold, which the post assumes.

question: A man has $15$ coins in his pocket, all dimes and quarters, worth $2.40$ dollars in all. How many of each does he have?
solution: With $d$ dimes and $q$ quarters, $d+q=15$ and $10d+25q=240$. Then $150+15q=240$, so $q=6$ and $d=9$: $\boxed{6\text{ quarters and }9\text{ dimes}}$.
note: Problem 22 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com).

question: The side lengths of a triangle are in the ratio $4:3:5$, and its perimeter is $18$ inches. Find the side lengths.
note: Problem 23 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com).

question: A growth fund, an income fund and a money market account return $10\%$, $7\%$ and $5\%$ per year respectively. You invest $3200$ dollars in total, with twice as much in the growth fund as in the money market. How should you invest to get a return of $250$ dollars in one year?
solution:
Let $M$ be the amount in the money market; then $2M$ is in the growth fund and $3200-3M$ in the income fund. The return is
\[0.1(2M)+0.07(3200-3M)+0.05M=224+0.04M=250,\]
so $M=650$. Invest
\[\boxed{1300\text{ dollars in the growth fund, }1250\text{ in the income fund, }650\text{ in the money market}}.\]
(Check: $130+87.5+32.5=250$.)
note: Problem 25 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com). The post adds "to maximize your return", which plays no role (the return is fixed at 250 dollars) and is dropped.

question: A shark's tail weighs $200$ pounds. Its head weighs as much as its tail plus half its body, and its body weighs as much as its head and tail together. What is the weight of the shark?
solution: With head $H$ and body $B$: $H=200+\dfrac B2$ and $B=H+200$. Substituting, $B=400+\dfrac B2$, so $B=800$ and $H=600$. The shark weighs $200+600+800=\boxed{1600}$ pounds.
note: Problem 26 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com).

solution:
\textbf{(a)} Let $t=\sqrt x\ge0$. Then $t^2-t-2=0$, so $(t-2)(t+1)=0$ and $t=2$ (as $t\ge0$). So $x=\boxed{4}$ (check: $2+2=4$).

\textbf{(b)} Squaring, $x+2=x^2$, so $(x-2)(x+1)=0$. Since $\sqrt{x+2}\ge0$ we need $x\ge0$, so $x=\boxed{2}$ ($x=-1$ is extraneous: $\sqrt1=1\ne-1$).
note: Problem 27 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com). The sentence is ambiguous; the record asks for both readings.

question: You have a coupon worth $6$ dollars off any item, and a store offers a $20\%$ discount. If the store lets you apply them in either order, which order saves more money, and by how much?
note: Problem 28 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com). The post asks "what do you need to do to save the most money"; the record makes the two orders explicit.

question: Your grades on three math exams are $80$, $93$ and $91$. What grade do you need on the fourth exam to have an average of at least $90$ on the four exams?
solution: You need $80+93+91+x\ge360$, i.e. $264+x\ge360$, so at least $\boxed{96}$.
note: Problem 29 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com).

question: A photograph is $5$ inches wide and $6$ inches long. Each side is enlarged by the same amount, and the new area is $182$ square inches. By how much was each side enlarged?
note: Problem 30 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com). The post calls the owner Peter and then "she"; the person is dropped.

question: It costs $1200$ dollars to start producing a book plus $9$ dollars per book, and each book sells for $15$ dollars. How many books must be sold to make a profit?
solution: Selling $n$ books gives a profit when $15n>1200+9n$, i.e. $6n>1200$, $n>200$. So at least $\boxed{201}$ books.
note: Problem 31 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com).

question: Store A sells CDs for $2$ dollars each after a one-time fee of $104$ dollars. Store B gives $12$ free CDs and charges $10$ dollars for each additional CD. For how many CDs do the two plans cost the same?
solution: For $n\ge12$ CDs, store A costs $104+2n$ and store B costs $10(n-12)$. Equal when $104+2n=10n-120$, so $8n=224$ and $n=\boxed{28}$ (both cost $160$ dollars). (For $n<12$, store B costs $0$ while A costs more than $104$.)
note: Problem 32 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com).

question: When $4$ is added to each of two numbers, their ratio becomes $5:6$. When $4$ is subtracted from each, their ratio becomes $1:2$. Find the two numbers.
solution: Let the numbers be $x$ and $y$. Then $6(x+4)=5(y+4)$ and $2(x-4)=y-4$. The second gives $y=2x-4$; substituting, $6x+24=10x$, so $x=6$ and $y=8$. The numbers are $\boxed{6\text{ and }8}$ (check: $10:12=5:6$ and $2:4=1:2$).
note: Problem 33 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com).

question: A store owner wants to sell $200$ pounds of a mixture of pistachios and walnuts for $5$ dollars per pound. Walnuts cost $4$ dollars per pound and pistachios $6$ dollars per pound. How many pounds of each should be mixed?
solution: With $w$ pounds of walnuts and $p$ of pistachios: $w+p=200$ and $4w+6p=5\cdot200=1000$. Then $800+2p=1000$, so $p=100$ and $w=100$: $\boxed{100\text{ pounds of each}}$.
note: Problem 34 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com).

question: A manufacturer makes $32$-ounce boxes of cereal and allows a difference of at most $0.06$ ounce from $32$ ounces. Write this as an absolute value inequality and find the range of acceptable weights.
solution: The weight $w$ must satisfy $|w-32|\le0.06$, that is, $-0.06\le w-32\le0.06$, so $\boxed{31.94\le w\le32.06}$ ounces.
note: Problem 35 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com).

question: A man weighing $600$ kg loses $3.12\%$ of his weight each month. What will he weigh after $20$ months?
solution:
Each month his weight is multiplied by $1-0.0312=0.9688$, so after $20$ months he weighs
\[600\cdot0.9688^{20}\approx600\cdot0.5305\approx\boxed{318.3\text{ kg}}.\]
note: Problem 36 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com). Checked numerically.

question: An object is thrown upward from a height of $60$ feet. After $1$ second it is $88$ feet high and after $2$ seconds $84$ feet high. Assuming its height is a quadratic function $h(t)=at^2+bt+60$ of the time, what was its initial (upward) speed?
solution: From $h(1)=88$ and $h(2)=84$: $a+b=28$ and $4a+2b=24$, i.e. $2a+b=12$. Subtracting, $a=-16$ and $b=44$. The initial speed is the coefficient $b$ (the rate of change of $h$ at $t=0$), so it was $\boxed{44\text{ feet per second}}$. (The value $a=-16$ matches the gravitational acceleration of $32$ feet per second per second.)
note: Problem 37 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com). The record states the quadratic model that the post assumes.

question: A transit (an angle-measuring instrument) is $200$ feet from the base of a building, and a man stands on top of the building. The angles of elevation from the transit to the top and to the bottom of the man (the man's head and feet) are $45^\circ$ and $44^\circ$. How tall is the man? (Ignore the height of the transit.)
note: Problem 38 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com). The record makes explicit that the angles go to the man's head and feet and that the transit is at ground level. Checked numerically.

question: Lemonade contains $6\%$ fruit juice and a strawberry drink contains $15\%$ fruit juice. How much of each should be mixed to get $4$ liters of a drink containing $10\%$ fruit juice?
solution: With $x$ liters of lemonade and $4-x$ of the strawberry drink: $0.06x+0.15(4-x)=0.10\cdot4$, so $0.6-0.09x=0.4$ and $x=\dfrac{20}9$. Mix $\boxed{\dfrac{20}{9}\approx2.22\text{ liters of lemonade and }\dfrac{16}{9}\approx1.78\text{ liters of strawberry drink}}$.
note: Problem 39 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com). The post says the lemonade is 6% "lemon juice"; it is treated as 6% fruit juice, as the question requires.

question: Ellen can wash her car in $60$ minutes, and her sister Sarah can do the same job in $45$ minutes. How long will it take if they wash the car together?
solution: Together they do $\dfrac1{60}+\dfrac1{45}=\dfrac{3+4}{180}=\dfrac7{180}$ of the job per minute, so they need $\boxed{\dfrac{180}7\approx25.7\text{ minutes}}$.
note: Problem 40 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com).

question: James invested half of his money in land, a tenth in stock and a twentieth in savings bonds. He put the remaining $21000$ dollars in a CD. How much money did he save or invest in total?
solution: The fractions add up to $\dfrac12+\dfrac1{10}+\dfrac1{20}=\dfrac{13}{20}$, so the CD holds $\dfrac7{20}$ of the money. The total is $21000\cdot\dfrac{20}7=\boxed{60000}$ dollars.
note: Problem 43 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com).

question: Motherboards cost $50$ dollars each to manufacture, and the development cost is $250000$ dollars. The first $20$ motherboards are samples and are not sold. How many salable motherboards must be made so that the average cost per salable motherboard is $6325$ dollars?
solution:
Making $n$ salable boards means making $n+20$ boards, at total cost $250000+50(n+20)=251000+50n$. We need
\[\dfrac{251000+50n}{n}=6325,\qquad251000=6275n,\qquad n=\boxed{40}.\]
note: Problem 44 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com). The total cost includes the 20 samples, and the average is over the salable boards. Checked exactly.

question: How many gallons of a $70\%$ orange juice drink must be mixed with $44$ gallons of a $20\%$ orange juice drink to obtain a $50\%$ orange juice drink?
solution: With $x$ gallons of the $70\%$ drink: $0.7x+0.2\cdot44=0.5(x+44)$, so $0.2x=22-8.8=13.2$ and $x=\boxed{66}$ gallons.
note: Problem 45 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com).

question: Peanuts cost $1.20$ dollars per pound, almonds $2.20$ dollars per pound and cashews $3.20$ dollars per pound. A shop wants $280$ pounds of a mixture costing $2.59$ dollars per pound, in which the weight of almonds and cashews together is three times the weight of peanuts. Find the weight of each kind of nut, rounded to the nearest pound.
solution:
Let the weights be $p$, $a$, $c$. Then $p+a+c=280$ and $a+c=3p$, so $4p=280$, $p=70$ and $a+c=210$. The cost condition is
\[1.2\cdot70+2.2a+3.2c=2.59\cdot280=725.2,\]
so $2.2a+3.2c=641.2$. With $a=210-c$: $462+c=641.2$, so $c=179.2$ and $a=30.8$. Rounded:
\[\boxed{70\text{ lb peanuts},\ 31\text{ lb almonds},\ 179\text{ lb cashews}}.\]
note: Problem 46 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com).

question: A basketball player has made $36$ of his last $48$ free throws. How many consecutive free throws must he make to raise his success rate to $80\%$?
solution: After $x$ more made shots, $\dfrac{36+x}{48+x}=0.8$, so $36+x=38.4+0.8x$, $0.2x=2.4$ and $x=\boxed{12}$ (then $48$ of $60$).
note: Problem 47 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com).

question: John washes cars $3$ times as fast as his son Erick. Working together, they wash $30$ cars in $6$ hours. How many hours would each of them take to wash the $30$ cars alone?
solution: Together they wash $5$ cars per hour. If Erick washes $e$ cars per hour, John washes $3e$, so $4e=5$: Erick washes $\dfrac54$ and John $\dfrac{15}4$ cars per hour. Alone, John needs $30\div\dfrac{15}{4}=8$ hours and Erick $30\div\dfrac54=24$ hours: $\boxed{\text{John }8\text{ hours, Erick }24\text{ hours}}$. (Check: $\dfrac{30}{8}+\dfrac{30}{24}=3.75+1.25=5$ cars per hour.)
note: Problem 48 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com).

question: At a college, $36\%$ of the students are under $20$ years old and $15\%$ are over $40$ years old. What is the probability that a randomly chosen student is under $20$ or over $40$?
solution: The two groups do not overlap, so the probability is $0.36+0.15=\boxed{0.51}$.
note: Problem 49 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com).

question: Twice a number plus the square root of the number equals twelve minus the square root of the number. Find the number.
solution: We need $2x+\sqrt x=12-\sqrt x$, i.e. $x+\sqrt x-6=0$. With $t=\sqrt x\ge0$: $t^2+t-6=(t+3)(t-2)=0$, so $t=2$ and $x=\boxed{4}$. (Check: $8+2=12-2$.)
note: Problem 50 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com). The post states the sentence without a question; the record asks for the number.

question: The light intensity $I$ of a bulb varies inversely as the square of the distance from the bulb. At $3$ meters, $I=1.5$ watts per square meter. What is the intensity at $2$ meters?
solution: $I=\dfrac{k}{d^2}$ with $k=1.5\cdot9=13.5$. At $d=2$, $I=\dfrac{13.5}{4}=\boxed{3.375\text{ watts per square meter}}$.
note: Problem 51 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com).

question: You open a book and notice that the product of the two page numbers on the facing pages is $650$. What are the page numbers?
solution: Facing pages are consecutive numbers $n$ and $n+1$, and $n(n+1)=650=25\cdot26$. Since $n(n+1)$ increases with $n$, the pages are $\boxed{25\text{ and }26}$.
note: Problem 54 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com).

question: Start with a number. Multiply it by $3$, add $7$, divide by $\dfrac12$, subtract $5$, and then divide by $12$. The result is $5$. What was the starting number?
solution: Work backwards: $5\cdot12=60$; $60+5=65$; dividing by $\dfrac12$ means doubling, so undo it by halving: $\dfrac{65}2$; subtract $7$: $\dfrac{51}2$; divide by $3$: $\boxed{\dfrac{17}{2}}$. (Check: $3\cdot8.5+7=32.5$, doubled $65$, minus $5$ is $60$, divided by $12$ is $5$.)
note: Problem 55 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com).

question: You have $156$ feet of fencing to enclose a rectangular garden that is $5$ times as long as it is wide. Find the dimensions of the garden.

question: The amount of water wasted by a dripping faucet varies directly with time. The faucet drips $2$ cups of water every $6$ minutes. How long does it take to drip $10.6465$ liters? (Use $1$ cup $=0.236589$ liter.)
solution: $10.6465$ liters is $\dfrac{10.6465}{0.236589}\approx45.000$ cups. At $2$ cups per $6$ minutes, i.e. $3$ minutes per cup, this takes $45\cdot3=\boxed{135\text{ minutes}}$.
note: Problem 57 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com). The post gives the volume in liters and the rate in cups without a conversion factor; the record states the US cup (0.236589 liter), for which the volume is 45 cups.

question: A washer costs $25\%$ more than a dryer. A clerk gives a $10\%$ discount on the dryer and a $20\%$ discount on the washer, and you pay $1900$ dollars for both. What was the price of the washer before the discount?
solution: Let the dryer cost $D$; the washer costs $1.25D$. You pay $0.9D+0.8\cdot1.25D=0.9D+D=1.9D=1900$, so $D=1000$ and the washer cost $\boxed{1250}$ dollars before the discount.
note: Problem 58 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com).

question: A tray of blueberry muffins takes $4$ cups of milk and $3$ cups of flour; a tray of pumpkin muffins takes $2$ cups of milk and $3$ cups of flour. A baker has $16$ cups of milk and $15$ cups of flour. The profit is $3$ dollars per tray of blueberry muffins and $2$ dollars per tray of pumpkin muffins. How many trays of each should be made to maximise the profit?
solution:
With $b$ blueberry and $p$ pumpkin trays ($b,p\ge0$):
\[4b+2p\le16\ (\text{i.e. }2b+p\le8),\qquad 3b+3p\le15\ (\text{i.e. }b+p\le5).\]
Adding the two inequalities, $3b+2p\le13$, so the profit is at most $13$ dollars. Equality needs $2b+p=8$ and $b+p=5$, i.e. $b=3$, $p=2$, which uses all the milk and flour. So make $\boxed{3\text{ trays of blueberry and }2\text{ of pumpkin}}$, for a profit of $13$ dollars.
note: Problem 59 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com). Checked by trying all whole-number tray counts (and the corners of the feasible region).

question: A company sells $1000-2p$ TVs per month when the price is $p$ dollars, where $p$ can be set anywhere from $200$ to $300$. What price maximises the monthly revenue, and what is the maximum revenue?
solution: The revenue is $R=p(1000-2p)=-2p^2+1000p=125000-2(p-250)^2$, which is largest at $p=250$, inside the allowed range. So set the price at $\boxed{250\text{ dollars}}$, for a revenue of $250\cdot500=\boxed{125000}$ dollars.
note: Problem 60 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com). The post writes "-2p + 1000 models the number of TVs sold"; the record states the model in words.

question: Your friend has $2.40$ dollars in equal numbers of quarters, dimes and nickels. How many of each coin does he have?
solution: One quarter, one dime and one nickel make $40$ cents, and $\dfrac{240}{40}=6$. He has $\boxed{6}$ of each.
note: Problem 61 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com).

question: A two-digit number has a tens digit that is $1$ less than twice its ones digit. When the tens digit is divided by the ones digit, the quotient is $1$ and the remainder is $4$. What is the number?
solution: Let the tens digit be $t$ and the ones digit $u$. Then $t=2u-1$ and $t=u+4$ with $4<u$. So $2u-1=u+4$, giving $u=5$ and $t=9$. The number is $\boxed{95}$ (check: $9=1\cdot5+4$).
note: Problem 62 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com).

question: A two-digit number is formed by choosing two different digits at random from $2,4,5,7$, in order. What is the probability that the number contains a $2$ or a $7$?
solution: There are $4\cdot3=12$ equally likely numbers. The ones with neither $2$ nor $7$ use only $4$ and $5$: $45$ and $54$. So the probability is $1-\dfrac2{12}=\boxed{\dfrac56}$.
note: Problem 63 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com).

question: In a survey of $30$ females and $20$ males, $6$ females and $2$ males use an electric toothbrush. What is the probability that a respondent does not use an electric toothbrush, given that the respondent is female?
solution: Of the $30$ females, $24$ do not use one, so the probability is $\dfrac{24}{30}=\boxed{\dfrac45}$.
note: Problem 64 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com).

question: An employer pays $15$ dollars per hour, plus an extra $5$ dollars per hour for every hour worked beyond $8$ hours, up to a maximum daily wage of $220$ dollars. Write the daily wage $W(h)$ for $h$ hours of work ($0\le h\le24$) as a piecewise function.
solution:
Up to $8$ hours the wage is $15h$. Beyond $8$ hours each hour pays $20$ dollars, so the wage is $120+20(h-8)=20h-40$, until it reaches $220$, at $h=13$. Hence
\[\boxed{W(h)=\begin{cases}15h,&0\le h\le8,\\ 20h-40,&8<h\le13,\\ 220,&13<h\le24.\end{cases}}\]
note: Problem 65 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com).

question: A number leaves remainder $5$ when divided by $7$. When it is divided by $3$, the remainder is $1$ and the quotient is $2$ less than $3$ times the previous quotient. What is the number?
solution: Write $N=7q+5$ and $N=3q'+1$ with $q'=3q-2$. Then $7q+5=9q-5$, so $q=5$ and $N=\boxed{40}$. (Check: $40=7\cdot5+5=3\cdot13+1$, and $13=3\cdot5-2$.)
note: Problem 66 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com).

question: A luggage maker requires that the length of a suitcase be $15$ inches greater than its depth, and that the length, width and depth add up to at most $50$ inches. All three dimensions are positive whole numbers of inches. What is the largest possible depth?
solution: With depth $d$, length $d+15$ and width $w\ge1$: $2d+15+w\le50$, so $2d\le35-w\le34$ and $d\le17$. Depth $17$ works (length $32$, width $1$). The largest depth is $\boxed{17}$ inches.
note: Problem 67 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com).

question: To make an open box, a man cuts equal squares of side $x$ inches from the corners of a sheet of metal $12$ inches wide and $16$ inches long, and folds up the sides. Find an expression for the volume of the box in terms of $x$, and the values of $x$ for which it makes sense.
note: Problem 68 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com).

question: Ten candidates are running in a student election. You may vote for one, two or three of them (at least one, and at most three, different candidates; the order does not matter). In how many ways can you vote?
note: Problem 69 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com). The post says the candidates run for president, vice-president and secretary and that you "may vote for as many as 3 candidates"; the record counts sets of 1 to 3 candidates (a blank ballot would add 1).

question: A medication has a half-life of $6$ hours. A doctor prescribes $100$ mg. How much is left after $78$ hours?
solution: $78$ hours is $13$ half-lives, so $100\cdot\left(\dfrac12\right)^{13}=\dfrac{100}{8192}=\boxed{\dfrac{25}{2048}\approx0.0122\text{ mg}}$ remains.
note: Problem 70 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com).

question: You roll a red die and a yellow die. Find the probability that both show a $2$, and the probability that they show the same number.
solution: There are $36$ equally likely outcomes. Both show $2$ in $1$ of them: $\boxed{\dfrac1{36}}$. They match in $6$ of them: $\boxed{\dfrac16}$.
note: Problem 71 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com).

question: One cinema is open $3$ days in a row and then closed $1$ day, repeatedly. Another is open $4$ days in a row and then closed $1$ day, repeatedly. Both are closed today, a Wednesday. When will they next both be closed on the same day?
solution: The first is closed every $4$ days and the second every $5$ days, so both are closed again after $\operatorname{lcm}(4,5)=20$ days. Since $20=2\cdot7+6$, that day is $6$ days of the week after Wednesday: a $\boxed{\text{Tuesday, }20\text{ days from today}}$.
note: Problem 72 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com).

question: An investor puts $5000$ dollars into an account paying $10\%$ per year and the rest into one paying $5\%$. The total yearly yield is one fifth of the amount invested at $10\%$. How much was invested at $5\%$?
solution: The total yield is $500+0.05x$, where $x$ is the amount at $5\%$, and it equals $\dfrac15\cdot5000=1000$. So $0.05x=500$ and $x=\boxed{10000}$ dollars.
note: Problem 73 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com).

question: $20000$ students took a test whose scores are normally distributed with mean $85$ and standard deviation $5$. Using the empirical $68$--$95$--$99.7$ rule, about how many students scored between $90$ and $95$?
solution: The scores $90$ and $95$ are $1$ and $2$ standard deviations above the mean. About $95\%$ of scores lie within $2$ standard deviations and $68\%$ within $1$, so by symmetry about $\dfrac{95\%-68\%}{2}=13.5\%$ lie between $1$ and $2$ standard deviations above the mean. That is about $0.135\cdot20000=\boxed{2700}$ students. (With the exact normal distribution, the fraction is about $13.59\%$, about $2718$ students.)
note: Problem 74 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com). The record asks for the empirical-rule estimate; the exact normal value is given as a remark. Checked numerically.

question: A satellite is in a circular orbit $2400$ km above the Earth's surface and takes $3$ hours to complete one orbit. Take the radius of the Earth to be $6400$ km. How far does the satellite travel in $1$ hour, and how far is it then (in a straight line) from where it started?
note: Problem 75 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com). The post asks "how far is the satellite after 1 hour" without the Earth's radius; the record supplies 6400 km and asks for both the distance travelled and the straight-line distance. Checked numerically.

question: In a group of $10$ people, what is the probability that at least two of them have the same birthday? (Assume $365$ equally likely birthdays, independent.)
solution:
The probability that all $10$ birthdays differ is $\dfrac{365\cdot364\cdots356}{365^{10}}\approx0.8831$, so the probability of a shared birthday is
\[\boxed{1-\dfrac{365\cdot364\cdots356}{365^{10}}\approx0.117}.\]
note: Problem 76 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com). Checked with exact fractions.

question: At a gala attended by $n$ people, everybody shakes hands with everyone else before the event, and again after it. How many handshakes take place?
solution: Each round has $\dbinom n2=\dfrac{n(n-1)}2$ handshakes, so there are $\boxed{n(n-1)}$ in all.
note: Problem 77 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com).

solution:
Let $r$ and $s$ be the hours at the restaurant and the store: $8r+10s\ge200$ and $r+s\le25$, with $r,s\ge0$.

\textbf{(a)} For example $(r,s)=(0,20)$ (earning $200$ in $20$ hours), $(5,16)$ ($40+160=200$ in $21$ hours) and $(25,0)$ ($200$ in $25$ hours).

\textbf{(b)} For a fixed $r$ (from $0$ to $25$), $s$ must satisfy $s\ge\dfrac{200-8r}{10}=20-\dfrac{4r}5$ and $s\le25-r$. The number of whole numbers $s$ in this range is
\[25-r-\left\lceil20-\dfrac{4r}{5}\right\rceil+1=6-r+\left\lfloor\dfrac{4r}5\right\rfloor=6-\left\lceil\dfrac r5\right\rceil.\]
This is $6$ for $r=0$, then $5,4,3,2,1$ for $r$ in $1$--$5$, $6$--$10$, $11$--$15$, $16$--$20$, $21$--$25$. The total is $6+5\cdot(5+4+3+2+1)=\boxed{81}$.
note: Problem 79 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com). The post asks only for three ways (an open question); the record adds the count of all whole-number possibilities to give a single answer. Checked by enumeration.

question: Company A earns $45$ dollars for $3$ hours of tutoring and $105$ dollars for $7$ hours. Company B earns $34$ dollars for $2$ hours and $102$ dollars for $6$ hours. Both earnings are proportional to the hours. If students sign up for the same number of hours at both companies, which company earns more?
solution: Company A charges $\dfrac{45}{3}=\dfrac{105}{7}=15$ dollars per hour, and company B charges $\dfrac{34}{2}=\dfrac{102}{6}=17$ dollars per hour. For the same positive number of hours, $\boxed{\text{company B}}$ earns more ($2$ dollars more per hour).

question: The average of three numbers is $47$. The largest is $5$ more than twice the smallest, and the range is $35$. Find the three numbers.
solution: Let the smallest be $s$; the largest is $2s+5$, and $(2s+5)-s=35$ gives $s=30$ and the largest $65$. The sum is $3\cdot47=141$, so the middle number is $141-95=46$. The numbers are $\boxed{30,46,65}$.

question: Peter drives to work at an average of $45$ miles per hour and back home at $60$ miles per hour. The total travel time is $2$ hours. How far is his house from work?
solution: With distance $d$: $\dfrac d{45}+\dfrac d{60}=2$, so $\dfrac{4d+3d}{180}=2$ and $d=\boxed{\dfrac{360}7\approx51.4\text{ miles}}$.

question: An advertising company keeps $20\%$ of all the revenue it generates for its affiliates and pays them the rest. If the affiliates were paid $15200$ dollars this month, how much revenue did the company generate?
solution: The affiliates get $80\%$, so the revenue is $\dfrac{15200}{0.8}=\boxed{19000}$ dollars.

\textbf{(a)} Since $2$ and $12$ are the roots, $R(x)=a(x-2)(x-12)$ for some $a\ne0$, and $R(20)=a\cdot18\cdot8=144a$, which depends on $a$. For instance $a=-1$ and $a=-2$ give different values.

question: A ball is dropped and bounces $4$ times, each time reaching three fourths of its previous height. After the fourth bounce it reaches $25$ cm. From what height was it dropped?
solution: After four bounces the height is $\left(\dfrac34\right)^4h=\dfrac{81}{256}h=25$, so $h=\dfrac{6400}{81}\approx\boxed{79.0\text{ cm}}$.
note: Problem 88 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com).

question: A rental company charges $40$ dollars per day plus $0.30$ dollars per mile. You rent a car for $4$ days and pay $325.50$ dollars, including a $5\%$ sales tax. How many miles did you drive?
solution: Before tax the bill was $\dfrac{325.50}{1.05}=310$ dollars, so $160+0.3m=310$ and $m=\boxed{500}$ miles.
note: Problem 89 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com).

question: Two students leave school at the same time and travel in opposite directions along the same road, one walking at $3$ mph and the other cycling at $8.5$ mph. After how long will they be $23$ miles apart?
solution: They separate at $3+8.5=11.5$ mph, so they are $23$ miles apart after $\dfrac{23}{11.5}=\boxed{2\text{ hours}}$.
note: Problem 90 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com).

question: Ethan, a boy, has as many male classmates as female classmates. His classmate Olivia, a girl, has three fourths as many female classmates as male classmates. How many students are in the class?
solution: Let there be $m$ boys and $f$ girls. Ethan's classmates are $m-1$ boys and $f$ girls, so $m-1=f$. Olivia's are $m$ boys and $f-1$ girls, so $f-1=\dfrac34m$. Then $m-2=\dfrac34m$, so $m=8$, $f=7$, and the class has $\boxed{15}$ students.
note: Problem 92 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com).

question: Noah wants to share some money equally among $10$ people. Instead, he keeps $20$ dollars for himself and shares the rest equally among $5$ people, and each of them gets the same amount as in the first plan. How much money is he sharing?
solution: With $A$ dollars, $\dfrac A{10}=\dfrac{A-20}5$, so $A=2A-40$ and $A=\boxed{40}$ dollars (each person gets $4$ dollars).
note: Problem 93 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com).

question: The square root of me plus the square root of me is me. Which numbers can I be?
solution: We need $2\sqrt x=x$ with $x\ge0$. Squaring, $4x=x^2$, so $x=0$ or $x=4$; both check ($0+0=0$ and $2+2=4$). I am $\boxed{0\text{ or }4}$.

question: A cash drawer contains $160$ bills, all $10$-dollar and $50$-dollar bills, with a total value of $1760$ dollars. How many of each are there?
solution: With $t$ tens and $f$ fifties: $t+f=160$ and $10t+50f=1760$. Then $1600+40f=1760$, so $f=4$ and $t=156$: $\boxed{156\text{ ten-dollar bills and }4\text{ fifty-dollar bills}}$.
note: Problem 95 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com).

question: Peanuts contain $7$ grams of protein per ounce and granola $3$ grams per ounce. A snack mix made of $1$ ounce of peanuts and some granola contains $28$ grams of protein. How many ounces of granola does it contain?
solution: $7+3g=28$, so $g=\boxed{7}$ ounces.

question: Jacob's hourly wage is $4$ times Noah's. Then Jacob gets a raise of $2$ dollars per hour, while Noah takes a new position paying $2$ dollars per hour less, and now Jacob earns $5$ times as much per hour as Noah. How much does each earn per hour now?
solution: If Noah earned $n$ dollars per hour, then $4n+2=5(n-2)$, so $n=12$. Now Jacob earns $4\cdot12+2=\boxed{50}$ dollars per hour and Noah $12-2=\boxed{10}$.

question: A catering business makes three kinds of cakes, each needing a decorator, a baker and a design consultant. Cake A takes $9$ decorator hours, $6$ baker hours and $1$ consultant hour; cake B takes $10$, $4$ and $2$ hours; cake C takes $12$, $4$ and $1$ hours. There are exactly $398$ decorator hours, $164$ baker hours and $58$ consultant hours available. How many cakes of each kind can be made if all the available hours are used?
solution:
With $a$, $b$, $c$ cakes:
\[9a+10b+12c=398,\qquad6a+4b+4c=164,\qquad a+2b+c=58.\]
From the third, $a=58-2b-c$. The second becomes $348-8b-2c=164$, so $c=92-4b$, and then $a=2b-34$. The first becomes $9(2b-34)+10b+12(92-4b)=798-20b=398$, so $b=20$, $c=12$, $a=6$. So make $\boxed{6\text{ of A},\ 20\text{ of B},\ 12\text{ of C}}$.
note: Problem 100 of the post (a list of 100 word problems credited to progitymath.com). The record states that all available hours are used, which the post's question implies.

question: This month a website gains on average $1$ new user per minute, and $1$ of every $10080$ new users is a troll. Before the pandemic it gained only $0.3$ new users per minute. Assuming that new trolls arrived at the same rate per minute as this month, what was the ratio of new users to new trolls before the pandemic?
solution: This month there is $1$ troll per $10080$ users, and $10080$ users arrive in $10080$ minutes, so trolls arrive at $1$ per $10080$ minutes (one per week). Before the pandemic, $10080$ minutes brought $0.3\cdot10080=3024$ new users and still $1$ troll. The ratio was $\boxed{3024:1}$.
