solution:
\textbf{(a)} By the change of base formula $\log_ab=\dfrac{\log b}{\log a}$,
\[\log_8 18=\dfrac{\log18}{\log8}=\dfrac{\log2+2\log3}{3\log2},\qquad\log_9 5=\dfrac{\log5}{\log9}=\dfrac{\log5}{2\log3},\]
since $18=2\cdot3^2$, $8=2^3$ and $9=3^2$. Dividing,
\[\dfrac{\log_8 18}{\log_9 5}=\dfrac{\log2+2\log3}{3\log2}\cdot\dfrac{2\log3}{\log5}=\dfrac{2\log3\,(\log2+2\log3)}{3\log2\,\log5}.\]

\textbf{(b)} With base $10$, $\log_{10}5=1-\log_{10}2\approx0.6990$. Then
\[\dfrac{2\cdot0.4771\cdot(0.3010+0.9542)}{3\cdot0.3010\cdot0.6990}=\dfrac{0.9542\cdot1.2552}{0.9030\cdot0.6990}\approx\dfrac{1.19771}{0.63120}\approx\boxed{1.898}.\]
(The exact value is $1.89761\ldots$. A calculator does essentially the same: it computes natural logarithms by fast-converging series or similar algorithms and divides.)
note: The post asks how to divide logarithms such as log_8 18 / log_9 5 without a calculator; the record asks to reduce it to log 2, log 3, log 5 and to estimate it from four-digit logarithms. Checked numerically.

question: A dishonest dealer uses faulty weights. When buying, he receives $x\%$ more goods than he pays for; when selling, he charges his customers for $x\%$ more goods than he actually gives them. He buys and sells at the same price per unit of weight. Show that his gain, as a percentage of his outlay, is $\left(2x+\dfrac{x^2}{100}\right)\%$.
solution:
Let the price be $c$ per unit of weight, and suppose he spends $C$. He pays for $\dfrac Cc$ units, but receives
\[\left(1+\dfrac{x}{100}\right)\dfrac Cc\]
units. When he sells, every unit he actually hands over is charged as $1+\dfrac{x}{100}$ units, so selling all his goods brings in
\[\left(1+\dfrac{x}{100}\right)\dfrac Cc\cdot\left(1+\dfrac{x}{100}\right)c=\left(1+\dfrac{x}{100}\right)^2C.\]
His gain is
\[\left(1+\dfrac{x}{100}\right)^2C-C=\left(\dfrac{2x}{100}+\dfrac{x^2}{10000}\right)C=\dfrac{1}{100}\left(2x+\dfrac{x^2}{100}\right)C,\]
that is, $\left(2x+\dfrac{x^2}{100}\right)\%$ of his outlay. $\blacksquare$ (For example, $x=10$ gives a gain of $21\%$, not $20\%$: the two frauds compound.)
note: The post gives the answer (2x + x^2/100)% and asks for an algebraic solution. The record states the model that gives this answer: x% more goods received when buying, and customers charged for x% more than they receive. (If instead he gave x% less when selling, the gain would be ((100+x)/(100-x) - 1) x 100%.) Checked symbolically.

question: Factor $64-p^6$ completely over the integers.
solution:
As a difference of squares, $64-p^6=8^2-\left(p^3\right)^2=\left(8-p^3\right)\left(8+p^3\right)$. Then by the difference and sum of cubes,
\[8-p^3=(2-p)\left(4+2p+p^2\right),\qquad8+p^3=(2+p)\left(4-2p+p^2\right).\]
So
\[64-p^6=\boxed{(2-p)(2+p)\left(p^2+2p+4\right)\left(p^2-2p+4\right)}.\]
The quadratic factors cannot be factored further, since their discriminants are $4-16<0$.
note: Checked with sympy.

question: The bisector of angle $A$ in triangle $ABC$ meets the circumcircle of the triangle again at $K\ne A$. Prove that $K$ is the midpoint of the arc $BC$ that does not contain $A$.
note: The post calls the point k; it is renamed K. Checked numerically on random triangles.

question: Solve $\dfrac13\left(x+\dfrac{11}{6}\right)=\dfrac32\left(x+\dfrac52\right)-1$.
solution:
Multiply both sides by $36$:
\[12\left(x+\dfrac{11}{6}\right)=54\left(x+\dfrac52\right)-36\iff12x+22=54x+135-36\iff12x+22=54x+99.\]
So $-42x=77$ and $x=-\dfrac{77}{42}=\boxed{-\dfrac{11}{6}}$. (Check: the left side is $\dfrac13\cdot0=0$, and the right side is $\dfrac32\cdot\dfrac46-1=1-1=0$.)
note: Despite the title ("complex calculus equation") this is a linear equation.

question: Factor $-2m^5+250m^2$ completely over the integers.
solution:
Take out the common factor $-2m^2$: $-2m^5+250m^2=-2m^2\left(m^3-125\right)$. By the difference of cubes, $m^3-125=m^3-5^3=(m-5)\left(m^2+5m+25\right)$. So
\[-2m^5+250m^2=\boxed{-2m^2(m-5)\left(m^2+5m+25\right)}.\]
The quadratic factor cannot be factored further, since its discriminant is $25-100<0$.
note: Checked with sympy.

question: A crafting table has a $3\times3$ grid of squares. To make magma cream, Steve places one slime ball and one blaze powder in two different squares of the grid. In how many ways can he place them?
solution: The slime ball can go in any of the $9$ squares, and then the blaze powder in any of the other $8$. Since the two items are different, the placements are all different, and there are $9\cdot8=\boxed{72}$ ways.
note: Problem 1 of the post. The post does not say how many of each item are used; the record uses one slime ball and one blaze powder (the actual recipe).

question: A forest is a rectangle of square blocks, $125$ blocks long and $91$ blocks wide. A fire starts in the centre block at time $0$. Every $3$ seconds the fire spreads by one block in all directions, including diagonally, so after $3$ seconds a $3\times3$ square of blocks is burning, after $6$ seconds a $5\times5$ square, and so on. After how many seconds does the fire first reach a block on the border of the forest?
solution: Across the width, the centre block has $\dfrac{91-1}{2}=45$ blocks on each side; along the length it has $\dfrac{125-1}{2}=62$ blocks on each side. After $k$ spreads, the fire covers the square of blocks within $k$ steps of the centre in each direction, so it reaches the border first in the width direction, when $k=45$. This happens after $45\cdot3=\boxed{135}$ seconds.
note: Problem 3 of the post; "touch the border" is read as reaching a block on the edge of the forest. Problems 2 (three identical magma creams in three slots) and 4 (a story) are not included.

question:
Let $a$ and $b$ be positive numbers different from $1$, and let $n\ne0$. Prove that
\[\log_{b^n}a=\dfrac{\log_ba}{n}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\log_ba=\dfrac{1}{\log_ab}.\]
solution:
Let $L=\log_ba$, so that $b^L=a$.

\textbf{First identity.} $\left(b^n\right)^{\dfrac Ln}=b^L=a$, so the exponent to which $b^n$ must be raised to give $a$ is $\dfrac Ln$. That is, $\log_{b^n}a=\dfrac{L}{n}=\dfrac{\log_ba}{n}$. (Here $b^n$ is positive and different from $1$, so it is a valid base.)

\textbf{Second identity.} Let $M=\log_ab$, so $a^M=b$. Then
\[a=b^L=\left(a^M\right)^L=a^{ML}.\]
Since $a>0$ and $a\ne1$, equal powers of $a$ have equal exponents, so $ML=1$. ($L\ne0$ because $a\ne1$.) Hence $\log_ba=L=\dfrac1M=\dfrac{1}{\log_ab}$. $\blacksquare$
note: The post asks how to prove the two identities without simply quoting the change of base formula; the record proves them from the definition. Near-miss: aops-topic-2656186-q01 (proof of the change of base formula).

question: A bucket is $15\%$ full of oil, and it contains $45$ mL of oil. How much oil can the bucket hold when full?
solution: If the bucket holds $V$ mL, then $0.15V=45$, so $V=\dfrac{45}{0.15}=\boxed{300}$ mL.
note: Problem P1 of the post; the posted answer 300 is correct.

question: $25\%$ of a song lasts $3$ minutes. How long is the whole song?
solution: $25\%$ is one quarter, so the whole song lasts $4\cdot3=\boxed{12}$ minutes.
note: Problem P2 of the post; the posted answer 12 is correct.

question: In triangle $ABC$, the line $XY$ through $C$ is parallel to $AB$, with $C$ between $X$ and $Y$. The lines $AX$ and $BY$ are the bisectors of the angles at $A$ and $B$; $AX$ meets $BC$ at $D$, and $BY$ meets $AC$ at $E$. Prove that if $YE=XD$, then $AC=BC$.
note: The post asks to prove AC = BC; the order of the points on the line (C between X and Y) is made explicit. The formulas for XD and YE and the conclusion are checked numerically on random triangles.
The post asks how to compute sums and differences of arguments of complex numbers; the record asks for the rule arg(zw) = arg z + arg w and two applications. Checked numerically.

question: Show that the equation $17+2x-7=4x+3-2x$ has no solution, not even among the complex numbers.
solution: Collect terms on each side: the left side is $10+2x$ and the right side is $2x+3$. If some number $x$, real or complex, satisfied $10+2x=2x+3$, then subtracting $2x$ from both sides (which is allowed for complex numbers too) would give $10=3$, which is false. So $\boxed{\text{there is no solution}}$, real or complex. Complex numbers create solutions for equations like $x^2=-1$; they cannot help when the variable cancels and leaves a false statement about numbers.
note: The post asks whether the equation, which has no real solution, has complex solutions; the record asks to show that it has none.

question:
Let $N$ be a positive multiple of $5$. One red ball and $N$ green balls are arranged in a line in random order. Let $P(N)$ be the probability that at least $\dfrac35$ of the green balls are on the same side of the red ball. Observe that $P(5)=1$ and that $P(N)$ approaches $\dfrac45$ as $N$ grows large. What is the sum of the digits of the least value of $N$ such that $P(N)<\dfrac{321}{400}$?

$\textbf{(A) }12\qquad\textbf{(B) }14\qquad\textbf{(C) }16\qquad\textbf{(D) }18\qquad\textbf{(E) }20$
solution:
Write $N=5k$. The red ball is equally likely to be in each of the $N+1$ positions, so the number $g$ of green balls to its left is equally likely to be each of $0,1,\dots,N$. At least $\dfrac35N=3k$ green balls are on one side exactly when $g\ge3k$ or $N-g\ge3k$, that is, $g\ge3k$ or $g\le2k$. These are $2k+1$ values ($0,\dots,2k$) plus $2k+1$ values ($3k,\dots,5k$), with no overlap, so
\[P(N)=\dfrac{4k+2}{5k+1}.\]
(Check: $k=1$ gives $\dfrac66=1$, and for large $k$ the value approaches $\dfrac45$.) Now
\[\dfrac{4k+2}{5k+1}<\dfrac{321}{400}\iff400(4k+2)<321(5k+1)\iff1600k+800<1605k+321\iff5k>479.\]
The least $N=5k$ is $480$, whose digit sum is $4+8+0=12$. The answer is $\boxed{\textbf{(A) }12}$.
note: 2016 AMC 10A Problem 17, as the post title says; the poster asks for a solution other than the official one. Checked with exact fractions for all multiples of 5 up to 1000.

question:
What is the units digit of $13^{2012}$?

$\textbf{(A) }1\qquad\textbf{(B) }3\qquad\textbf{(C) }5\qquad\textbf{(D) }7\qquad\textbf{(E) }9$

A published solution notes that the units digits of $3^1,3^2,3^3,3^4,\dots$ repeat in the cycle $3,9,7,1$; it then subtracts $1$ from $2012$, divides $2011$ by $4$ (remainder $3$), and concludes that the units digit is that of $3^{3+1}$. Explain why $1$ is subtracted, and give a shorter way to finish.
solution:
The units digit of a product depends only on the units digits of the factors, so $13^{2012}$ has the same units digit as $3^{2012}$.

The units digits of $3^1,3^2,3^3,3^4,3^5,\dots$ are
\[3,\ 9,\ 7,\ 1,\ 3,\ 9,\ 7,\ 1,\ \dots,\]
because each one is obtained from the previous one by multiplying by $3$ and keeping the units digit, and $1\cdot3=3$ starts the cycle again. The cycle starts at the exponent $1$, not $0$: the exponents $1,5,9,\dots$ give the 1st term $3$, the exponents $2,6,10,\dots$ the 2nd term $9$, and so on. In general the exponent $k$ gives the term in position $r+1$ of the cycle, where $r$ is the remainder of $k-1$ on division by $4$. That is why $1$ is subtracted: it counts the positions from $0$. For $k=2012$, $2011=4\cdot502+3$, so $r=3$ and we need the 4th term of the cycle, which is $1$ (the units digit of $3^4$).

\textbf{Shorter.} Since $3^4=81$ ends in $1$, every power of $81$ ends in $1$. As $2012=4\cdot503$,
\[3^{2012}=\left(3^4\right)^{503}=81^{503}\]
ends in $1$. Equivalently: when the exponent is a multiple of $4$, the units digit is the last term of the cycle.

The answer is $\boxed{\textbf{(A) }1}$.
note: 2012 AMC 8 Problem 12, as titled. The poster asks why the published solution subtracts 1 from 2012; the record asks for that explanation and a shorter finish.

question: If $9^a=1681$ and $\left(\sqrt3\right)^b=2$, find the value of $3^a\cdot3^b-3^{a+b+1}$.
solution:
Since $9^a=\left(3^a\right)^2$ and $3^a>0$, the equation $\left(3^a\right)^2=1681=41^2$ gives $3^a=41$. Squaring the second equation,
\[3^b=\left(\left(\sqrt3\right)^b\right)^2=2^2=4.\]
Hence $3^a\cdot3^b=41\cdot4=164$ and $3^{a+b+1}=3\cdot3^a\cdot3^b=492$, so
\[3^a\cdot3^b-3^{a+b+1}=164-492=\boxed{-328}.\]
note: Problem 1 of the post (the stargazer story is dropped). The post asks for (3^a)^b - 3^(a+b+1). As written, (3^a)^b = 41^b = 41^(log_3 4), about 108.4, so the value is about -383.6 with no simple form. The data are designed to give 3^a = 41 and 3^b = 4, and the second term 3^(a+b+1) = 3 * 3^a * 3^b is built from the product 3^a * 3^b; so (3^a)^b is read as a typo for (3^a)(3^b), and the record asks for 3^a * 3^b - 3^(a+b+1) = -328. Checked with exact arithmetic and numerically.

question: The apparent area of a distant object, as seen by an observer, is inversely proportional to the square of its distance from the observer. An alien spaceship flies straight toward an observer at a constant speed of $2000$ miles per hour. When it is $10000$ miles away, its apparent area is $1$ square millimetre. What is its apparent area $2$ hours and $30$ minutes later?
solution: In $2.5$ hours the ship travels $2000\cdot2.5=5000$ miles, so its distance becomes $10000-5000=5000$ miles, half the original distance. Since the apparent area is proportional to $\dfrac{1}{d^2}$, halving the distance multiplies the apparent area by $2^2=4$. The apparent area is $\boxed{4\text{ square millimetres}}$.
note: Problem 2 of the post. The story is condensed, and the inverse-square law for the apparent area, which the post leaves implicit, is stated.

question: There are $135$ alien spaceships. The number of aliens in each ship is random: each of the whole numbers $1,2,\dots,100$ is equally likely. What is the expected total number of aliens in all the ships?
solution:
The expected number of aliens in one ship is
\[\dfrac{1+2+\cdots+100}{100}=\dfrac{5050}{100}=50.5.\]
By linearity of expectation (which needs no independence), the expected total is the sum of the $135$ expected values:
\[135\cdot50.5=\boxed{6817.5}.\]
note: Problem 3 of the post; the story is trimmed. Problem 4 (a joke about throwing a potion at aliens) has no mathematical content.

question: Prove that the product of three consecutive positive integers is never a perfect square.
solution:
Suppose that $n(n+1)(n+2)=m^2$ for a positive integer $n$ and an integer $m$. Note that $n(n+2)=(n+1)^2-1$.

\textbf{The factors $n+1$ and $n(n+2)$ are coprime.} A common divisor $d$ of $n+1$ and $(n+1)^2-1$ divides $(n+1)^2$ and $(n+1)^2-1$, hence divides their difference $1$.

\textbf{Both are squares.} In the prime factorisation of $m^2$ every exponent is even. Each prime divides only one of the coprime factors $n+1$ and $n(n+2)$, so it appears in that factor with the same even exponent. Hence $n+1$ and $n(n+2)$ are both perfect squares.

\textbf{Contradiction.} But
\[n^2<n^2+2n<n^2+2n+1=(n+1)^2,\]
so $n(n+2)=n^2+2n$ lies strictly between the consecutive squares $n^2$ and $(n+1)^2$ and is not a square. Therefore $n(n+1)(n+2)$ is never a perfect square. $\blacksquare$

question:
Let $S(n)=1!+2!+3!+\cdots+n!$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] A student looking for a formula for $S(n)$ starts from the claim
\[1!+2!+3!+\cdots+n!=n\cdot1+(n-1)\cdot2+(n-2)\cdot3+\cdots+1\cdot n,\]
and after more work concludes that $S(n)=\dfrac{n(2n+1)(2n-1)}{3}$ for odd $n$. Show that the conclusion is wrong and that the starting claim is already false.
\item[(b)] Prove that there is no polynomial $P(x)$ with $P(n)=S(n)$ for every positive integer $n$.
\end{enumerate}
solution:
\textbf{(a)} For $n=3$: $S(3)=1+2+6=9$, but $\dfrac{3\cdot7\cdot5}{3}=35$. So the conclusion is wrong.

The starting claim fails already for $n=2$: $1!+2!=3$, while $2\cdot1+1\cdot2=4$; for $n=3$ it gives $3\cdot1+2\cdot2+1\cdot3=10\ne9$. In fact
\[\sum_{k=1}^{n}k(n+1-k)=(n+1)\cdot\dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}-\dfrac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}=\dfrac{n(n+1)(n+2)}{6},\]
a cubic in $n$, while $n!$ alone is far larger for large $n$. The claim treats the products $k!=1\cdot2\cdots k$ as if they were sums. (The final formula $\dfrac{n(2n+1)(2n-1)}{3}$ is the sum $1^2+3^2+\cdots+(2n-1)^2$ of the first $n$ odd squares, which has nothing to do with $S(n)$.)

\textbf{(b)} Suppose such a polynomial $P$ exists. Let $Q(x)=P(x)-P(x-1)$, also a polynomial. For every integer $n\ge2$,
\[Q(n)=S(n)-S(n-1)=n!.\]
Hence for every integer $n\ge2$,
\[Q(n+1)=(n+1)!=(n+1)\cdot n!=(n+1)\,Q(n).\]
So the polynomial $Q(x+1)-(x+1)Q(x)$ has infinitely many roots, and is therefore the zero polynomial: $Q(x+1)=(x+1)Q(x)$ for all $x$. Now $Q$ is not the zero polynomial, since $Q(2)=2$. If $Q$ has degree $d$, then $Q(x+1)$ has degree $d$ while $(x+1)Q(x)$ has degree $d+1$, a contradiction. Hence no such polynomial exists. $\blacksquare$
note: The post asks whether there is a formula for 1! + 2! + ... + n! and offers a derivation ending in n(2n+1)(2n-1)/3; its first step is false. The record asks to refute the derivation and to prove that no polynomial formula exists. Checked numerically for small n.

question: Square $ABCD$ has vertices $A(0,0)$, $B(4,0)$, $C(4,4)$ and $D(0,4)$. A point $P$ in the interior of square $ABCD$ is chosen and reflected over the line containing segment $CD$ to point $Q$. Point $Q$ is then reflected over the line containing segment $BC$ to point $R$. What are the coordinates of the midpoint of segment $PR$? Express your answer as an ordered pair.
note: Problem 9 of the post, from the 2012 MATHCOUNTS Chapter competition as the post says (the round is not stated). Checked with coordinates for random points P.

question: In one round of a television game show, three questions are asked. The second question is worth twice as much as the first. The third question is worth three times as much as the second. If the third question is worth $\$12{,}000$, what is the first question worth, in dollars?
solution: The second question is worth $\dfrac{12000}{3}=4000$ dollars, so the first is worth $\dfrac{4000}{2}=\boxed{2000}$ dollars.
note: Problem 11 of the post (2012 MATHCOUNTS Chapter).

question: In a stack of six cards, each card is labelled with a different integer from $0$ to $5$, inclusive. If two cards are selected at random without replacement, what is the probability that their sum will be $3$? Express your answer as a common fraction.
solution: There are $\dbinom62=15$ equally likely pairs of cards. The pairs with sum $3$ are $\{0,3\}$ and $\{1,2\}$. The probability is $\boxed{\dfrac{2}{15}}$.
note: Problem 20 of the post (2012 MATHCOUNTS Chapter).

question: Okta can stay in the sun for $16$ minutes before getting sunburned. If he uses a sunscreen with SPF $20$, he can stay in the sun $20$ times as long before getting sunburned, or $20\cdot16=320$ minutes. This morning, he spent $9$ minutes in the sun before putting on sunscreen. If he then applies SPF $20$ sunscreen, how many more minutes can he stay in the sun before getting burned?
solution:
Without sunscreen each minute uses up $\dfrac1{16}$ of the exposure that burns him; with SPF $20$ each minute uses only $\dfrac1{320}$ of it. After $9$ unprotected minutes, $\dfrac9{16}$ is used up and $\dfrac7{16}$ remains. With sunscreen this lasts
\[\dfrac{7}{16}\cdot320=\boxed{140}\text{ minutes}.\]
(Equivalently: the remaining $16-9=7$ unprotected minutes are stretched by a factor of $20$.)
note: Problem 21 of the post (2012 MATHCOUNTS Chapter). The solution makes the model explicit: each unprotected minute uses 1/16 of the burn exposure, each protected minute 1/320.

question: A bag contains red and yellow balls. There are ten of each colour, and the balls of each colour are numbered $1$ through $10$. If Arthur draws two balls at random, one after the other without replacement, what is the probability that he draws the yellow ball numbered $3$ followed by a red ball? Express your answer as a common fraction.
solution:
The first ball is the yellow $3$ with probability $\dfrac1{20}$. Given that, $19$ balls remain, $10$ of them red, so the second ball is red with probability $\dfrac{10}{19}$. The probability is
\[\dfrac{1}{20}\cdot\dfrac{10}{19}=\boxed{\dfrac{1}{38}}.\]
note: Problem 22 of the post (2012 MATHCOUNTS Chapter). Checked by enumerating the 380 ordered draws.

question: A car travelled a certain distance at $20$ miles per hour. The car then travelled twice the original distance at $40$ miles per hour. If the entire trip lasted four hours, what was the total number of miles driven?
solution:
Let the first distance be $d$ miles. The two parts take $\dfrac{d}{20}$ and $\dfrac{2d}{40}=\dfrac{d}{20}$ hours, so
\[\dfrac{d}{20}+\dfrac{d}{20}=\dfrac{d}{10}=4,\]
and $d=40$. The total distance is $d+2d=3\cdot40=\boxed{120}$ miles.
note: Problem 25 of the post (2012 MATHCOUNTS Chapter).

question:
Let $E$ be any point in the interior of parallelogram $ABCD$. Prove that
\[[AEB]+[CED]=\dfrac12[ABCD],\]
where $[\,\cdot\,]$ denotes area.

A student gives this proof: ``Let $AB=CD=x$, and let $h$ be the distance between the parallel lines $AB$ and $CD$, so that $[ABCD]=xh$. If $h_1$ and $h_2$ are the distances from $E$ to the lines $AB$ and $CD$, then $h_1+h_2=h$, so
\[[AEB]+[CED]=\dfrac12xh_1+\dfrac12xh_2=\dfrac12x(h_1+h_2)=\dfrac12xh=\dfrac12[ABCD].\text{''}\]
Is this proof correct? Justify the step $h_1+h_2=h$.
note: The post asks whether this short proof is valid compared with a longer textbook proof (the figure is a standard one). The record asks to judge the proof and justify h1 + h2 = h; the proof is correct.

question: Do there exist distinct primes $a$, $b$, $c$ such that $a+b+c$ is also prime and $abc$ is divisible by $a+b+c$? If so, find the least possible value of $abc$.
solution:
No such primes exist.

Suppose $p=a+b+c$ is prime and $p\mid abc$. A prime that divides a product divides one of the factors, so $p$ divides one of $a$, $b$, $c$, say $p\mid a$. Since $a$ is prime, its only divisors greater than $1$ are $a$ itself, so $p=a$. But $p=a+b+c>a$ because $b,c\ge2$. This is a contradiction, so there are $\boxed{\text{no such primes}}$, and the least value asked for does not exist. (The argument does not use that $a,b,c$ are distinct.)
note: As posted ("find the least possible value of abc", with a, b, c, a + b + c prime and a + b + c | abc) the problem has no answer: no such primes exist. The record asks whether they exist. "a != b != c" is read as pairwise distinct.

question: Compute $91+89+87+85+\cdots+5+3$.
solution:
The terms are the odd numbers from $3$ to $91$. There are $\dfrac{91-3}{2}+1=45$ of them, and the average of the first and last terms is $\dfrac{91+3}{2}=47$, so the sum is
\[45\cdot47=\boxed{2115}.\]
(Check: $1+3+\cdots+91$ is the sum of the first $46$ odd numbers, which is $46^2=2116$; removing the $1$ leaves $2115$.)

question: Prove that $3^{-\dfrac{3}{4}}>4^{-\dfrac{5}{6}}$.
solution:
Both sides are positive. Since $3^{-\dfrac34}=\dfrac{1}{3^{\dfrac34}}$ and $4^{-\dfrac56}=\dfrac{1}{4^{\dfrac56}}$, the inequality is equivalent to
\[3^{\dfrac34}<4^{\dfrac56}.\]
For positive numbers, $u<v$ holds exactly when $u^{12}<v^{12}$. Raising both sides to the $12$th power gives
\[\left(3^{\dfrac34}\right)^{12}=3^9=19683\qquad\text{and}\qquad\left(4^{\dfrac56}\right)^{12}=4^{10}=1048576.\]
Since $19683<1048576$, we get $3^{\dfrac34}<4^{\dfrac56}$, and therefore $3^{-\dfrac34}>4^{-\dfrac56}$. $\blacksquare$

question: In a pile of $25$ tiles, each tile has one of the letters A through E and one of the integers from $1$ through $5$. Each possible combination of a letter and a number appears on exactly one of the tiles. Jessica selects three tiles at random, without replacement, from the pile. What is the probability that each of the three tiles Jessica chooses has a letter or a number in common with at least one of the other chosen tiles? Express your answer as a common fraction.
solution:
Think of the tiles as the cells of a $5\times5$ grid, with the letter giving the row and the number giving the column. Two tiles are \emph{related} if they are in the same row or the same column. There are $\dbinom{25}{3}=2300$ equally likely choices of three tiles. We count the choices in which no tile is unrelated to both others. Among three tiles, this happens exactly when at least two of the three pairs are related.

\textbf{All three pairs related.} If $X,Y$ share a row and $X,Z$ share a column, then $Y$ and $Z$ differ in both row and column. So three pairwise related tiles lie in one row or in one column: $5\dbinom53+5\dbinom53=100$ choices.

\textbf{Exactly two pairs related.} Then one tile $X$ is related to both others and $Y,Z$ are unrelated. By the observation above, one of $Y,Z$ is in the row of $X$ and the other in its column. Choose $X$ ($25$ ways), another tile in its row ($4$ ways) and another in its column ($4$ ways): $25\cdot16=400$ choices, each counted once (the corner $X$ is determined by the set).

So $100+400=500$ choices work, and the probability is
\[\dfrac{500}{2300}=\boxed{\dfrac{5}{23}}.\]
note: Second of the two 2017 National MATHCOUNTS problems in the post (the problem number is not given). Checked by enumerating all 2300 choices.

question: Find all positive integers $n$ and $k$ such that $n!+8=2^k$.
solution:
Check small $n$: $1!+8=9$, $2!+8=10$, $3!+8=14$ are not powers of $2$, while
\[4!+8=32=2^5,\qquad 5!+8=128=2^7.\]
For $n\ge6$, $n!$ is divisible by $6!=720=16\cdot45$, so $n!+8\equiv8\pmod{16}$. A power of $2$ that leaves remainder $8$ on division by $16$ must be $8$ itself (powers $2^k$ with $k\ge4$ are divisible by $16$, and $1,2,4\not\equiv8$). But $n!+8>8$. So there are no solutions with $n\ge6$.

The solutions are $\boxed{(n,k)=(4,5)\text{ and }(5,7)}$.
note: Checked by direct computation for n <= 30.

question:
A company makes a Wi-Fi phone. The total cost of manufacturing $n$ phones is modelled by
\[C(n)=-0.002n^2+20n+30{,}000\]
dollars, and each phone is sold for $\$84.95$, so the revenue is $R(n)=84.95n$ dollars.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Find the function that gives the total profit from selling $n$ phones.
\item[(b)] How much profit is earned if $400$ phones are sold?
\item[(c)] How much profit is earned if $5000$ phones (the production limit) are sold?
\item[(d)] How many phones must be sold for the company to break even?
\end{enumerate}
note: In (d) the break-even point 455.5 is not a whole number; the record gives the least number of phones with nonnegative profit (456). Checked with exact decimals.

question: Solve for $x$: $4x-7(2-x)=3x+2$.
solution: Expanding, $4x-14+7x=3x+2$, so $11x-14=3x+2$. Then $8x=16$ and $x=\boxed{2}$. (Check: $8-7\cdot0=8$ and $6+2=8$.)
note: The title says "Polynomial"; the equation is linear.

The post asks to prove that a 15 x 15 table cannot be tiled by the figure "1111 with a 2 under the second 1" (the Y-pentomino; every 1 and 2 is a unit square). With rotations and reflections allowed, as usual, the claim is false; the tiling in the figure was found by an exact-cover search and is checked in chk.py (45 Y-pieces, all cells covered once). The same search finds no tiling of 5 x 15 or of 15 x 15 minus a 10 x 10 corner. If reflections were forbidden (rotations only), an exhaustive computer search finds no tiling of the 15 x 15 table (confirmed by a separate search in review), so the poster may have had that version in mind; that is a computer result without a known short proof, so it is not used and the record makes no claim about it.

solution:
\textbf{(a)} Let $x=\log_ab$ and $y=\log_bc$, so $a^x=b$ and $b^y=c$. Then $c=b^y=\left(a^x\right)^y=a^{xy}$, so $\log_ac=xy=\log_ab\cdot\log_bc$.

\textbf{(b)} Take $c=a$ in (a): $\log_ab\cdot\log_ba=\log_aa=1$, since $a^1=a$. As the product is $1$, $\log_ab\ne0$ and $\log_ba=\dfrac1{\log_ab}$.

\textbf{(c)} Let $y=\log_{\dfrac1a}b$, so $\left(\dfrac1a\right)^y=b$, that is, $a^{-y}=b$. Hence $-y=\log_ab$, so $y=-\log_ab$.

\textbf{(d)} Since $m\ne0$ and $a\ne1$, the base $a^m$ is positive and different from $1$. Let $y=\log_{a^m}a^n$, so $\left(a^m\right)^y=a^n$, that is, $a^{my}=a^n$. For $a>0$, $a\ne1$, the function $t\mapsto a^t$ is one-to-one, so $my=n$ and $y=\dfrac nm$.

\textbf{About $\log_a1=0$.} For every admissible base, $a^0=1$, so $\log_a1=0$. The right condition is the condition for $a$ to be a base at all: $a>0$ and $a\ne1$. The condition $a\ne0$ is not enough: for $a=1$ every power $1^y$ equals $1$, so $\log_11$ would not be a single number, and for a negative base such as $a=-2$ the powers $a^y$ are not defined for all real $y$.
note: The post asks how to memorise logarithm properties for the AMC 12 and AIME and lists several, including "log_a 1 = 0 where a != 0". The record turns the list into proofs from the definition and corrects that condition (a > 0, a != 1).

question: Milk costs $36$ rupees per litre, and water costs nothing. In what ratio must water be mixed with milk so that the mixture is worth $28$ rupees per litre? Solve algebraically.
solution:
Mix $w$ litres of water with $1$ litre of milk. The mixture has volume $1+w$ litres and costs $36$ rupees, so
\[\dfrac{36}{1+w}=28\quad\Longrightarrow\quad1+w=\dfrac{36}{28}=\dfrac97\quad\Longrightarrow\quad w=\dfrac27.\]
So water and milk are mixed in the ratio $\boxed{2:7}$. (Check: $9$ litres of mixture contain $7$ litres of milk worth $252$ rupees, and $\dfrac{252}{9}=28$.)
note: "Cost of the mixture" is read as the value per litre, with water free.

question: Which is greater, $2^{60}$ or $5^{24}$?
solution:
Both exponents are multiples of $12$:
\[2^{60}=\left(2^5\right)^{12}=32^{12},\qquad5^{24}=\left(5^2\right)^{12}=25^{12}.\]
Since $32>25$, we get $32^{12}>25^{12}$, so $\boxed{2^{60}}$ is greater.

question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\dfrac{k^2}{2^k}$.
solution:
Let
\[A=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\dfrac1{2^k}=1,\qquad B=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\dfrac{k}{2^k},\qquad C=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\dfrac{k^2}{2^k}.\]
These series converge: for $k\ge3$ the ratio of consecutive terms of $C$ is $\dfrac12\left(\dfrac{k+1}{k}\right)^2\le\dfrac12\cdot\dfrac{16}{9}=\dfrac89<1$, so the terms are eventually smaller than those of a geometric series, and the terms of $B$ are smaller than those of $C$.

Halving shifts the terms by one place: $\dfrac B2=\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\dfrac{k}{2^{k+1}}=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\dfrac{k-1}{2^{k}}$ (the new first term is $0$), so
\[B-\dfrac B2=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\dfrac{k-(k-1)}{2^k}=A=1,\qquad\text{hence }B=2.\]
In the same way $\dfrac C2=\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\dfrac{(k-1)^2}{2^k}$, so
\[C-\dfrac C2=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\dfrac{k^2-(k-1)^2}{2^k}=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\dfrac{2k-1}{2^k}=2B-A=3.\]
Therefore $C=\boxed{6}$.
note: Problem 1 of the post. Checked by partial sums.

question: Find $\dfrac{1}{2\cdot4}+\dfrac{1}{4\cdot6}+\dfrac{1}{6\cdot8}+\cdots$.
solution:
The $k$th term is
\[\dfrac{1}{2k(2k+2)}=\dfrac14\cdot\dfrac{1}{k(k+1)}=\dfrac14\left(\dfrac1k-\dfrac1{k+1}\right).\]
The sum of the first $n$ terms telescopes:
\[\dfrac14\left(1-\dfrac12+\dfrac12-\dfrac13+\cdots+\dfrac1n-\dfrac1{n+1}\right)=\dfrac14\left(1-\dfrac1{n+1}\right),\]
which tends to $\boxed{\dfrac14}$ as $n\to\infty$.
note: Problem 2 of the post ("*" written as a product).

question: A proper fraction is a fraction $\dfrac kd$ with integers $1\le k<d$. Find the sum of all proper fractions $\dfrac kd$ with denominator $d\le69$, where each pair $(k,d)$ is counted once (so, for example, $\dfrac12$ and $\dfrac24$ are both counted).
solution:
For a fixed denominator $d\ge2$, the numerators are $1,2,\dots,d-1$, so these fractions add up to
\[\dfrac{1+2+\cdots+(d-1)}{d}=\dfrac{(d-1)d}{2d}=\dfrac{d-1}{2}.\]
Summing over $d=2,3,\dots,69$:
\[\sum_{d=2}^{69}\dfrac{d-1}{2}=\dfrac12(1+2+\cdots+68)=\dfrac12\cdot\dfrac{68\cdot69}{2}=\boxed{1173}.\]
note: Problem 3 of the post. "All proper fractions with a denominator at most 69" is read as all pairs k < d <= 69, as the record states. If equal values were counted only once, the sum would be half the sum of Euler phi(d) for 2 <= d <= 69, that is 1469/2 (checked); that reading needs the totient function and is not used.

question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{10}\left(k^2+k+1\right)$, using $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{m}k^2=\dfrac{m(m+1)(2m+1)}{6}$.
note: Problem 4 of the post; the summand k^2 + k + 1 is bracketed.

question:
Let $0\le x\le\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ with $\sin x=\dfrac13$. Find
\[\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\dfrac{\sin(nx)}{3^n}.\]
solution:
Let $z=\dfrac{\cos x+i\sin x}{3}$. By De Moivre's theorem, $z^n=\dfrac{\cos(nx)+i\sin(nx)}{3^n}$, so the required sum is the imaginary part of $\displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}z^n$. Since $|z|=\dfrac13<1$, this geometric series converges to $\dfrac{1}{1-z}$.

Since $0\le x\le\dfrac\pi2$, $\cos x=\sqrt{1-\dfrac19}=\dfrac{2\sqrt2}{3}$, so $z=\dfrac{2\sqrt2}{9}+\dfrac{1}{9}i$ and $1-z=\dfrac{9-2\sqrt2}{9}-\dfrac19i$. Then
\[\dfrac{1}{1-z}=\dfrac{\overline{1-z}}{|1-z|^2},\qquad\operatorname{Im}\dfrac1{1-z}=\dfrac{\dfrac19}{|1-z|^2},\]
and
\[|1-z|^2=\dfrac{(9-2\sqrt2)^2+1}{81}=\dfrac{81-36\sqrt2+8+1}{81}=\dfrac{90-36\sqrt2}{81}=\dfrac{10-4\sqrt2}{9}.\]
Hence the sum is
\[\dfrac{\dfrac19}{\dfrac{10-4\sqrt2}{9}}=\dfrac{1}{10-4\sqrt2}=\dfrac{10+4\sqrt2}{100-32}=\boxed{\dfrac{5+2\sqrt2}{34}}\approx0.2302.\]
note: Problem 5 of the post ("sin x = 1/3"). Checked numerically by partial sums.

question:
Let $m$ and $n$ be fixed nonnegative integers. Evaluate
\[\sum_{k=0}^{n}\dbinom nk\dbinom mk\]
in closed form. (As usual, $\dbinom mk=0$ when $k>m$.)
solution:
Since $\dbinom mk=\dbinom m{m-k}$ (both are $0$ when $k>m$), the sum equals
\[\sum_{k=0}^{n}\dbinom nk\dbinom m{m-k}.\]
Count the ways to choose a committee of $m$ people from a group of $n$ men and $m$ women. Directly, there are $\dbinom{m+n}{m}$ ways. Counting by the number $k$ of men chosen, there are $\dbinom nk$ ways to choose the men and $\dbinom m{m-k}$ ways to choose the $m-k$ women, for $k=0,1,\dots,n$ (terms with $k>m$ are $0$). Hence
\[\sum_{k=0}^{n}\dbinom nk\dbinom mk=\boxed{\dbinom{m+n}{n}}.\]
note: Problem 6 of the post. Checked for all m, n <= 12.

question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{n}k\dbinom nk$ for a positive integer $n$.
solution:
The term $k\dbinom nk$ counts the ways to choose, from $n$ people, a committee of $k$ people together with a chair from the committee. Adding over $k$ counts all committees with a chair. Count them the other way: choose the chair first ($n$ ways), then choose any subset of the remaining $n-1$ people to join ($2^{n-1}$ ways). Hence
\[\sum_{k=1}^{n}k\dbinom nk=\boxed{n\cdot2^{n-1}}.\]
(Algebraically: $k\dbinom nk=n\dbinom{n-1}{k-1}$, and $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{n}\dbinom{n-1}{k-1}=2^{n-1}$.)
note: Problem 8 of the post. Checked for n <= 20.

question:
Let $Z=\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\dfrac{1}{n^3}=1+\dfrac18+\dfrac1{27}+\cdots$. Express
\[S=\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\dfrac{1}{mn(m+n)}\]
in terms of $Z$.
solution:
All terms are positive, so sums of these terms may be regrouped and reordered freely without changing their (possibly infinite) values. Write $H_k=1+\dfrac12+\cdots+\dfrac1k$ (with $H_0=0$) and let
\[T=\sum_{N=1}^{\infty}\dfrac{H_{N-1}}{N^2}=\dfrac{1}{4}+\dfrac{1+\dfrac12}{9}+\dfrac{1+\dfrac12+\dfrac13}{16}+\cdots.\]

\textbf{$T$ and $Z$ are finite.} For $n\ge2$, $\dfrac1{n^3}<\dfrac{1}{(n-1)n}=\dfrac1{n-1}-\dfrac1n$, so $Z<1+1=2$. For $j\ge1$, $\dfrac1j\le\dfrac1{\sqrt j}\le\dfrac{2}{\sqrt j+\sqrt{j-1}}=2\left(\sqrt j-\sqrt{j-1}\right)$, so $H_k\le2\sqrt k$. For $N\ge2$,
\[\dfrac1{\sqrt{N-1}}-\dfrac1{\sqrt N}=\dfrac{\sqrt N-\sqrt{N-1}}{\sqrt N\sqrt{N-1}}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt N\sqrt{N-1}\left(\sqrt N+\sqrt{N-1}\right)}\ge\dfrac{1}{2N\sqrt N},\]
so $\dfrac{H_{N-1}}{N^2}\le\dfrac{2\sqrt N}{N^2}=\dfrac{2}{N\sqrt N}\le4\left(\dfrac1{\sqrt{N-1}}-\dfrac1{\sqrt N}\right)$, and the sum telescopes: $T\le4$.

\textbf{First grouping: fix $n$.} By partial fractions, $\dfrac{1}{m(m+n)}=\dfrac1n\left(\dfrac1m-\dfrac1{m+n}\right)$. For fixed $n$, the sum over $m=1,\dots,M$ telescopes:
\[\sum_{m=1}^{M}\left(\dfrac1m-\dfrac1{m+n}\right)=H_n-\left(\dfrac1{M+1}+\cdots+\dfrac1{M+n}\right),\]
and the bracket is at most $\dfrac{n}{M+1}$, which tends to $0$ as $M\to\infty$. Hence $\displaystyle\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}\dfrac{1}{mn(m+n)}=\dfrac{H_n}{n^2}$, and since $H_n=H_{n-1}+\dfrac1n$,
\[S=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\dfrac{H_n}{n^2}=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\dfrac{H_{n-1}}{n^2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\dfrac1{n^3}=T+Z.\]

\textbf{Second grouping: fix $m+n$.} Since $\dfrac1m+\dfrac1n=\dfrac{m+n}{mn}$,
\[\dfrac{1}{mn(m+n)}=\dfrac{1}{(m+n)^2}\left(\dfrac1m+\dfrac1n\right)=\dfrac{1}{m(m+n)^2}+\dfrac{1}{n(m+n)^2}.\]
Swapping the names $m$ and $n$ shows that the two parts have the same sum over all pairs, so $S=2\displaystyle\sum_{m,n\ge1}\dfrac{1}{m(m+n)^2}$. Group the pairs by $N=m+n\ge2$: for fixed $N$, $m$ runs over $1,2,\dots,N-1$, giving $\dfrac{H_{N-1}}{N^2}$. Hence
\[S=2\sum_{N=2}^{\infty}\dfrac{H_{N-1}}{N^2}=2T.\]

\textbf{Conclusion.} From $S=T+Z$ and $S=2T$ with $T$ and $Z$ finite, $T=Z$ and
\[S=\boxed{2Z=2\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\dfrac1{n^3}}\approx2.4041.\]
(The number $Z\approx1.2021$ is $\zeta(3)$, Apery's constant; no simpler closed form for it is known.)
note: Problem 9 of the post ("evaluate", marked very hard). The value 2 zeta(3) has no elementary closed form, so the record asks to express the sum in terms of Z = sum 1/n^3 and proves S = 2Z by two regroupings, with elementary convergence bounds. Added in review (the draft dropped this problem). Checked numerically (partial sums and the identity sum H_n/n^2 = 2 zeta(3)).

question: Find all nonnegative integers $n$ for which $2^{90}+2^{65}+2^n$ is a perfect square.
solution:
Let $N=2^{90}+2^{65}+2^n$. In a perfect square, every prime appears with an even exponent.

\textbf{Case $n\ge66$.} $N=2^{65}\left(2^{25}+1+2^{n-65}\right)$ and the bracket is odd, so $2$ appears in $N$ with the odd exponent $65$. Not a square.

\textbf{Case $n=65$.} $N=2^{90}+2^{66}=2^{66}\left(2^{24}+1\right)$, and $2^{24}+1$ lies strictly between the consecutive squares $\left(2^{12}\right)^2$ and $\left(2^{12}+1\right)^2$. Not a square.

\textbf{Case $n\le64$.} Suppose $N=m^2$ with $m>0$. Since
\[2^{90}<N\le2^{90}+2^{65}+2^{64}<2^{90}+2^{66}+2^{40}=\left(2^{45}+2^{20}\right)^2,\]
we can write $m=2^{45}+t$ with $0<t<2^{20}$. Then $m^2=2^{90}+2^{46}t+t^2$, so
\[2^{46}t+t^2=2^{65}+2^n.\tag{$*$}\]
Write $t=2^vw$ with $w$ odd; then $v\le19$. On the left, $2^{46}t$ is divisible by $2^{46+v}$, while $t^2=2^{2v}w^2$ is divisible by $2^{2v}$ but not by $2^{2v+1}$; since $2v<46+v$, the left side is divisible by $2^{2v}$ but not by $2^{2v+1}$. On the right, $2^{65}+2^n=2^n\left(2^{65-n}+1\right)$ with an odd bracket. Hence $n=2v$. Dividing $(*)$ by $2^{2v}$:
\[2^{46-v}w+w^2=2^{65-2v}+1,\qquad\text{so}\qquad w^2-1=2^{46-v}\left(2^{19-v}-w\right).\]
\begin{itemize}
\item If $w=1$, then $2^{19-v}=1$, so $v=19$ and $n=38$.
\item If $w\ge3$, the left side is positive, so $2^{19-v}-w\ge1$; then $w<2^{19-v}$ and $w^2-1<2^{38-2v}$. But the right side is at least $2^{46-v}>2^{38-2v}$. Contradiction.
\end{itemize}
Finally, $n=38$ works:
\[2^{90}+2^{65}+2^{38}=\left(2^{45}\right)^2+2\cdot2^{45}\cdot2^{19}+\left(2^{19}\right)^2=\left(2^{45}+2^{19}\right)^2.\]
So the only value is $\boxed{n=38}$.
note: The post asks for "the value of n" and for a hint; the record asks for all n >= 0 and proves that 38 is the only one. Checked for n <= 400 with exact integer square roots.

question: Alfred, Brandon, Charles and David are the four participants in a race. In how many different ways can the four finish if it is possible for two or more participants to finish in a tie? (A finish records who finished ahead of whom and who tied with whom.)
solution:
A finish is an ordered list of groups of tied runners. Count by the sizes of the groups.
\begin{itemize}
\item No ties ($1,1,1,1$): $4!=24$.
\item One pair tied, the others separate ($2,1,1$): choose the pair in $\dbinom42=6$ ways, then order the three groups in $3!=6$ ways: $36$.
\item Two tied pairs ($2,2$): split the four into two pairs in $3$ ways, then order the pairs in $2$ ways: $6$.
\item Three tied and one separate ($3,1$): choose the single runner in $4$ ways, then order the two groups in $2$ ways: $8$.
\item All four tied: $1$.
\end{itemize}
The total is $24+36+6+8+1=\boxed{75}$.
note: The poster's answer 75 is correct; the record supplies the explanation. Checked by enumerating all functions from runners to places and keeping those whose places form an initial segment 1, ..., j.

question:
\emph{Descartes' circle theorem} says the following. Suppose four circles are tangent to each other in pairs, at six different points, and let their curvatures be $k_1,k_2,k_3,k_4$, where a circle of radius $r$ has curvature $\dfrac1r$, except that a circle containing the other three gets curvature $-\dfrac1r$. Then
\[k_4=k_1+k_2+k_3\pm2\sqrt{k_1k_2+k_2k_3+k_3k_1}.\]
Three circles with radii $1$, $2$ and $3$ are externally tangent to each other in pairs. Use the theorem to find the radii of the two circles that are tangent to all three, and check the answers with coordinates.
note: The post asks what Descartes' theorem is and for a problem that uses it. The record states the circle theorem and applies it to circles of radii 1, 2, 3 (answers 6/23 and 6), with an independent coordinate check. Near-miss: aops-topic-3265809-q13 (the same three circles, area of the gap).

question:

A student argues: ``In base ten the number is $2\cdot6^3+36X+30+Y$. Since $10_6=6$, we need $Y\equiv0\pmod6$, so $Y=0$ or $6$. $X$ can be anything, so the answer is $2\cdot10=20$.'' Find the errors and give the correct answer.

question: What is the sum of all positive integers less than $200$ that are $1$ more than a prime, $2$ more than twice a prime, and $3$ more than $3$ times a prime? (The three primes may be different.)
solution:
Let $n=p+1=2q+2=3r+3$ with $p,q,r$ prime. Then $n$ is divisible by $2$ and by $3$, so $n=6m$ with $1\le m\le33$, and
\[p=6m-1,\qquad q=3m-1,\qquad r=2m-1\]
must all be prime.
\begin{itemize}
\item If $m$ is odd, $3m-1$ is even, so $3m-1=2$, $m=1$, and then $r=1$ is not prime. So $m$ is even.
\item Modulo $5$: if $m\equiv1$, then $5\mid6m-1$ with $6m-1>5$ (as $m\ge6$); if $m\equiv2$, then $5\mid3m-1$, so $3m-1=5$ and $m=2$; if $m\equiv3$, then $5\mid2m-1$, so $m=3$, which is odd.
\end{itemize}
So $m=2$ or $m$ is even with $m\equiv0$ or $4\pmod5$: $m\in\{2,4,10,14,20,24,30\}$. Checking:
\begin{itemize}
\item $m=2$: $11,5,3$, all prime; $n=12$.
\item $m=4$: $23,11,7$, all prime; $n=24$.
\item $m=10$: $59,29,19$, all prime; $n=60$.
\item $m=14$: $r=27$ is not prime.
\item $m=20$: $p=119=7\cdot17$ is not prime.
\item $m=24$: $p=143=11\cdot13$ is not prime.
\item $m=30$: $179,89,59$, all prime; $n=180$.
\end{itemize}
The sum is $12+24+60+180=\boxed{276}$.
note: Checked by brute force over n < 200.

question: At his usual rate, Bob rows $15$ miles downstream in $5$ hours less than it takes him to return. If he doubles his usual rate, the time downstream is only $1$ hour less than the time upstream. What is the rate of the stream's current, in miles per hour?
solution:
Let $r$ be Bob's usual rowing rate in still water and $c$ the rate of the current (in miles per hour), with $r>c>0$. Then
\[\dfrac{15}{r-c}-\dfrac{15}{r+c}=5,\qquad\dfrac{15}{2r-c}-\dfrac{15}{2r+c}=1.\]
The first equation gives $\dfrac{30c}{r^2-c^2}=5$, so $r^2-c^2=6c$. The second gives $\dfrac{30c}{4r^2-c^2}=1$, so $4r^2-c^2=30c$. Substituting $r^2=c^2+6c$ into the second:
\[4c^2+24c-c^2=30c\quad\Longrightarrow\quad3c^2=6c\quad\Longrightarrow\quad c=2,\]
and then $r^2=16$, $r=4$. The current flows at $\boxed{2}$ miles per hour. (Check: $\dfrac{15}{2}-\dfrac{15}{6}=5$ and $\dfrac{15}{6}-\dfrac{15}{10}=1$.)
note: "Usual rate" is Bob's rowing speed in still water. Checked with exact fractions.

solution:
\textbf{(a)} The minute hand turns $360^\circ$ in $60$ minutes, that is, $6^\circ$ per minute, so after $m$ minutes it is at $6m$ degrees. The hour hand turns $360^\circ$ in $12$ hours $=720$ minutes, that is, $\dfrac12$ degree per minute ($30^\circ$ per hour). At $h$ hours $m$ minutes, $60h+m$ minutes have passed since $12{:}00$, so it is at $\dfrac{60h+m}{2}=30h+\dfrac m2$ degrees. The difference of the two positions is
\[30h+\dfrac m2-6m=30h-\dfrac{11m}{2}\]
degrees, so one of the angles between the hands is $\left|30h-\dfrac{11m}{2}\right|$ degrees and the other is $360^\circ$ minus that; the angle between the hands is the one that is at most $180^\circ$.

\textbf{(b)} $h=9$, $m=48$: $\left|270-264\right|=\boxed{6^\circ}$.

\textbf{(c)} We need $30\cdot2-\dfrac{11m}{2}$ to be a multiple of $360$ with $0\le m<60$. Since $60-\dfrac{11m}2$ lies between $-270$ and $60$, it must be $0$: $m=\dfrac{120}{11}=10\dfrac{10}{11}$. The hands point the same way at $\boxed{10\dfrac{10}{11}\text{ minutes past }2}$ (about $2{:}10{:}55$).
note: The post asks in general how to solve clock-angle problems and where the "clock formula" comes from. The record derives the formula and applies it twice. Checked with exact fractions.

question: Find all pairs of integers $(x,y)$ such that $x(x-31)=y(y-41)$.
note: The post asks for a good method (the poster found the solutions by a method called unoptimal); the record asks for all solutions. Checked by brute force over |x| <= 1000.

solution:
\textbf{(a)} The hour hand goes once around the dial, $360^\circ$, in $12$ hours, which is $12\cdot60=720$ minutes. Turning steadily, it turns $\dfrac{360}{720}=\dfrac12$ degree per minute (equivalently $30^\circ$ per hour, the angle between neighbouring hour marks).

\textbf{(b)} From $1{:}15$ to $3{:}45$ is $150$ minutes, so the hour hand turns $\dfrac{150}{2}=\boxed{75^\circ}$.

\textbf{(c)} At $10{:}15$ the hour hand has moved $10\cdot30+\dfrac{15}{2}=307.5$ degrees from the $12$, and the minute hand $15\cdot6=90$ degrees. The difference is $217.5^\circ$, so the angle between the hands is $360^\circ-217.5^\circ=\boxed{142.5^\circ}$.
note: The post asks why the hour hand moves 1/2 degree per minute; the record asks for the explanation and two applications.

question: Find the value of $\sqrt{90+\sqrt{90+\sqrt{90+\cdots}}}$, that is, the limit of the sequence $a_1=\sqrt{90}$, $a_{n+1}=\sqrt{90+a_n}$.
solution:
If the limit $L$ exists, then $L=\sqrt{90+L}$ with $L\ge0$, so $L^2-L-90=0$, $(L-10)(L+9)=0$ and $L=10$.

To see that the sequence really tends to $10$: first, $0<a_n<10$ for all $n$, since $a_1=\sqrt{90}<10$, and if $a_n<10$ then $a_{n+1}<\sqrt{100}=10$. Next,
\[10-a_{n+1}=\dfrac{100-(90+a_n)}{10+a_{n+1}}=\dfrac{10-a_n}{10+a_{n+1}}<\dfrac{10-a_n}{10},\]
so the distance from $10$ shrinks by more than a factor of $10$ at each step, and $a_n\to10$. The value is $\boxed{10}$.
note: Near-miss: aops-topic-3452431-q01 (the same nested radical with 20, value 5).

solution:
A positive integer $n$ leaves remainder $2$ on division by $4$ and by $21$ exactly when $n-2$ is divisible by $4$ and by $21$, that is (as $4$ and $21$ are coprime) by $\operatorname{lcm}(4,21)=84$. So $n=2,86,170,\dots$.

\textbf{(a)} The smallest is $\boxed{2}$: $2=0\cdot4+2=0\cdot21+2$. This is the trap in the question; the answer is not $86$.

\textbf{(b)} The next one is $2+84=\boxed{86}$.
note: The post asks for advice on careless mistakes and quotes this question ("the smallest number that leaves a remainder of 2 when divided by 4 and 21") as one that confuses the poster. The record asks it in both readings, since 2 itself qualifies.

question:
Real numbers $a,b,c,d,e,f$ are such that all the roots of
\[x^8-4x^7+7x^6+ax^5+bx^4+cx^3+dx^2+ex+f\]
are positive real numbers. Find all possible values of $f$.
solution:
Let the roots, with multiplicity, be $r_1,\dots,r_8>0$. By Vieta's formulas,
\[\sum r_i=4,\qquad\sum_{i<j}r_ir_j=7,\qquad f=r_1r_2\cdots r_8\]
(the degree is even, so the constant term is $+r_1\cdots r_8$). Hence
\[\sum r_i^2=\left(\sum r_i\right)^2-2\sum_{i<j}r_ir_j=16-14=2.\]
By the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, $\left(\sum r_i\right)^2\le8\sum r_i^2$, that is, $16\le16$. So equality holds, which happens only when all $r_i$ are equal: $r_i=\dfrac12$. Therefore $f=\left(\dfrac12\right)^8=\dfrac1{256}$.

This value does occur: $\left(x-\dfrac12\right)^8$ has $x^7$-coefficient $-8\cdot\dfrac12=-4$ and $x^6$-coefficient $\dbinom82\cdot\dfrac14=7$. So the only possible value is $\boxed{f=\dfrac{1}{256}}$.
note: Checked by expanding (x - 1/2)^8 with sympy.

question: A ``red orange'' costs $\$9200$. Glerp wants to buy only a part of one red orange: the part must be between $\dfrac1{921}$ and $\dfrac1{433}$ of an orange, and it must cost less than $\$10$. As a percentage of a whole orange, rounded to the nearest thousandth of a percent, what is the largest part he can take? (Calculators allowed.)
solution:
A part $f$ of an orange costs $9200f$ dollars, so $9200f<10$ means $f<\dfrac{10}{9200}=\dfrac{1}{920}$. Together with $f>\dfrac1{921}$ (the upper bound $\dfrac1{433}$ is then automatic), Glerp can take any part with
\[\dfrac{1}{921}<f<\dfrac{1}{920}.\]
As percentages,
\[\dfrac{100}{921}\%\approx0.10858\%\qquad\text{and}\qquad\dfrac{100}{920}\%\approx0.10870\%.\]
Strictly speaking there is no largest allowed part ($\dfrac1{920}$ itself costs exactly $\$10$), but every part in this range, and $\dfrac1{920}$ too, rounds to the same value. To the nearest thousandth of a percent, the answer is $\boxed{0.109\%}$.
note: Problem 1 of the post; the story is condensed. "Under ten dollars" is strict, so there is no largest part; the record notes that every admissible part (and 1/920 itself) rounds to 0.109%.

\textbf{Stolen.} The multiples of $13$ from $44$ to $60$ are only $52$. It is even, and $8008=2^3\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13$ is divisible by $52=2^2\cdot13$. So $F_S=52$.

\textbf{Touched.} The multiples of $12$ from $70$ to $89$ are $72$ and $84$. Since $5976=2^3\cdot3^2\cdot83$, the number $84=2^2\cdot3\cdot7$ is not a factor (no factor $7$), while $72=2^3\cdot3^2$ is. So $F_T=72$.

The rating is
\[\dfrac{72-52}{72}=\dfrac{20}{72}=\boxed{\dfrac{5}{18}}.\]
note: Problem 2 of the post; the story is condensed. "From 44 to 60" and "from 70 to 89" are read as inclusive (it makes no difference).

question: The gaps between neighbouring bars of a jail window are $6$, $7$, $5.5$, $8$, $8.5$ and $8$ centimetres wide. A person can squeeze through a gap if his thickness is at most $0.5$ centimetre more than the width of the gap. Glerp can squeeze through exactly three of the six gaps. What is the largest possible thickness of Glerp?
solution:
Let Glerp's thickness be $T$ centimetres. He fits through a gap of width $g$ exactly when $T-0.5\le g$, so the gaps he fits through are the widest ones. In increasing order the widths are
\[5.5,\ 6,\ 7,\ 8,\ 8,\ 8.5.\]
He fits through exactly three gaps exactly when he fits through the gaps $8$, $8$, $8.5$ but not through the gap $7$:
\[T-0.5\le8\qquad\text{and}\qquad T-0.5>7,\]
that is, $7.5<T\le8.5$. The largest possible thickness is $\boxed{8.5\text{ cm}}$.
note: Problem 3 of the post; the story is condensed and "people can squeeze down 0.5 centimetres" is made precise (a person fits through a gap if thickness - 0.5 <= gap). Problem 4 of the post (the height of the tip of his hair while walking) is not included: it does not say whether 2.2 cm is the rise above standing height or the whole up-and-down range, nor whether 182 cm includes the hair, and any reading is plain addition.

question: You need $10$ litres of a $15\%$ acid solution, but you only have a $10\%$ acid solution and a $30\%$ acid solution. How many litres of each should you mix?
solution:
Let $x$ litres of the $10\%$ solution be mixed with $10-x$ litres of the $30\%$ solution. The amount of acid must be $15\%$ of $10$ litres, that is, $1.5$ litres:
\[0.1x+0.3(10-x)=1.5\quad\Longrightarrow\quad3-0.2x=1.5\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x=7.5.\]
Use $\boxed{7.5\text{ litres of the }10\%\text{ solution and }2.5\text{ litres of the }30\%\text{ solution}}$.

(Shortcut: $15$ is $5$ above $10$ and $15$ below $30$, so the two solutions are mixed in the inverse ratio $15:5=3:1$, giving $7.5$ and $2.5$ litres. Check: $0.75+0.75=1.5$ litres of acid.)
note: The post asks for advice on mixture problems and quotes this one (from purplemath); the record is that problem.

solution:
\textbf{(a)} Yes. Let $A(x)$ and $B(x)$ be the two polynomials and $D(x)=A(x)-B(x)=px^2+qx+r$, a polynomial of degree at most $2$, with $D(1)=D(2)=D(3)=0$. Then
\[D(2)-D(1)=3p+q=0\qquad\text{and}\qquad D(3)-D(2)=5p+q=0,\]
so $2p=0$, $p=0$, $q=0$, and then $r=D(1)=0$. Thus $D$ is the zero polynomial and $A=B$. (In general, a nonzero polynomial of degree at most $2$ has at most $2$ roots, and $D$ has the three roots $1,2,3$.)

\textbf{(b)} No. For example, $x^2$ and $x^2+(x-1)(x-2)=2x^2-3x+2$ both take the value $1$ at $x=1$ and $4$ at $x=2$, but they are different (at $x=3$ they give $9$ and $11$).
note: Part (b) is added to show why three points are needed.

question: Is $2t^2$ the same as $(2t)^2$? For which real numbers $t$ are the two expressions equal?
solution:
No. In $2t^2$ the exponent applies only to $t$, so $2t^2=2\cdot t\cdot t$, while $(2t)^2=(2t)(2t)=4t^2$. For example, at $t=1$ they are $2$ and $4$.

They are equal exactly when $2t^2=4t^2$, that is, $2t^2=0$, so only for $\boxed{t=0}$.
note: The post only asks whether 2t^2 = (2t)^2; the record adds for which t they are equal.

question: An arrangement of the six letters C, C, C, A, G, N in a row is fixed. Each day, Farley chooses an arrangement of the six letters G, G, G, A, C, N in a row, uniformly at random among all the different arrangements and independently of the other days. The two arrangements \emph{match} at a position if they have the same letter there. On the first day on which the arrangements match in at least $4$ positions, Farley solves all the problems of a contest and stops. What is the expected number of days, including that day?
note: The post's story (Farley and the 2021 USAJMO) is condensed. "Randomly and arbitrarily selects a permutation" is read as uniform over the 120 distinct arrangements, independently each day (uniform orderings of six labelled letters give the same probability), and "for how many days is Farley expected to work" as the expected number of days up to and including the first success. Checked by enumerating all 120 x 120 pairs of arrangements.

question:
Find all residues $x$ modulo $14$ such that $x(x-3)\equiv0\pmod{14}$.

A proposed solution says: ``Either $x$ or $x-3$ must be $0\pmod{14}$, so $x\equiv0$ or $x\equiv3\pmod{14}$.'' Find the error in this solution and give the correct answer.
solution:
\textbf{The error.} The rule ``if a product is $0$, one factor is $0$'' holds modulo a prime, but not modulo the composite number $14$: for example $2\cdot7\equiv0\pmod{14}$ with neither factor $\equiv0$. Indeed $x=7$ gives $7\cdot4=28\equiv0\pmod{14}$, a solution the proposed answer misses.

\textbf{Correct solution.} $14\mid x(x-3)$ exactly when $2\mid x(x-3)$ and $7\mid x(x-3)$.
\begin{itemize}
\item $x$ and $x-3$ have opposite parity, so $x(x-3)$ is always even.
\item $7$ is prime, so $7\mid x(x-3)$ exactly when $x\equiv0$ or $x\equiv3\pmod7$.
\end{itemize}
Modulo $14$ these are $\boxed{x\equiv0,\ 3,\ 7,\ 10\pmod{14}}$.
note: Problem P1 of the post, with its "bogus solution" to correct.
