The post leaves the relative position of the two spheres open, so "only one point P satisfies all the conditions" is not well defined as stated. The record asks to disprove uniqueness with a counterexample (concentric spheres) and to prove that at most two points have the given distances.

solution:
\textbf{(a)} Let $S=1+2+\cdots+n$. Writing the sum forwards and backwards and adding term by term gives $n$ pairs, each with sum $n+1$, so $2S=n(n+1)$ and $S=\dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}$. Factoring out $d$,
\[d+2d+\cdots+nd=d(1+2+\cdots+n)=\dfrac{dn(n+1)}{2}.\]

\textbf{(b)} Here $d=7$ and $nd=700$, so $n=100$:
\[7+14+\cdots+700=\dfrac{7\cdot100\cdot101}{2}=\boxed{35350}.\]

\textbf{(c)} The sum consists of $n$ copies of $a$ plus $d\bigl(0+1+\cdots+(n-1)\bigr)$, so
\[a+(a+d)+\cdots+\bigl(a+(n-1)d\bigr)=na+\dfrac{n(n-1)}{2}\,d=\boxed{\dfrac{n\bigl(2a+(n-1)d\bigr)}{2}},\]
that is, $n$ times the average of the first and last terms. Part (a) is the case $a=d$.
note: The post reports the formula d + 2d + ... + nd = dn(n+1)/2 as a discovery; the record asks to prove it, apply it, and generalise it to any arithmetic series.

question:
The expression
\[(x+y+z)^{2006}+(x-y-z)^{2006}\]
is simplified by expanding it and combining like terms. How many terms are in the simplified expression?
solution:
Let $w=y+z$. By the binomial theorem,
\[(x+w)^{2006}+(x-w)^{2006}=\sum_{k=0}^{2006}\dbinom{2006}{k}x^{2006-k}w^k\bigl(1+(-1)^k\bigr)=2\sum_{k\ \text{even}}\dbinom{2006}{k}x^{2006-k}(y+z)^k.\]
For each even $k$, $(y+z)^k$ expands into the $k+1$ monomials $y^jz^{k-j}$ ($0\le j\le k$), all with positive coefficients. Different values of $k$ give different powers of $x$, so no two of these monomials combine or cancel. Hence the number of terms is
\[\sum_{\substack{k=0\\k\ \text{even}}}^{2006}(k+1)=1+3+5+\cdots+2007=1004^2=\boxed{1008016}.\]

\emph{Remark.} The post wrote $(x+y-z)^{2006}+(x-y-z)^{2006}$. With $u=x-z$ this is $(u+y)^{2006}+(u-y)^{2006}$, which keeps the \emph{even} powers of $y$ (not the odd ones): $2\sum_{j\ \text{even}}\dbinom{2006}{j}y^j(x-z)^{2006-j}$. Each $(x-z)^{2006-j}$ has $2007-j$ terms with nonzero coefficients, so it has $\sum_{j\ \text{even}}(2007-j)=2007+2005+\cdots+1=1004^2$ terms as well.
note: The post copies 2006 AMC 12A Problem 24 (which it links) with a typo, (x+y-z)^2006 instead of (x+y+z)^2006, and the poster thinks the odd powers survive. The record states the AMC problem; the remark shows that the posted expression has the same number of terms. Checked by counting monomials for small even exponents and by the formula.

solution:
\textbf{(a)} Put the right-hand side over the common denominator $n(n+1)$:
\[\dfrac{1}{n}-\dfrac{1}{n+1}=\dfrac{n+1}{n(n+1)}-\dfrac{n}{n(n+1)}=\dfrac{(n+1)-n}{n(n+1)}=\dfrac{1}{n(n+1)}.\]
(In words: two consecutive unit fractions differ by $\dfrac{1}{n(n+1)}$ because their denominators differ by $1$.)

\textbf{(b)} By (a) the sum telescopes:
\[\left(1-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)+\left(\dfrac{1}{2}-\dfrac{1}{3}\right)+\cdots+\left(\dfrac{1}{99}-\dfrac{1}{100}\right)=1-\dfrac{1}{100}=\boxed{\dfrac{99}{100}}.\]
note: The post asks why 1/(n(n+1)) = 1/n - 1/(n+1); the record asks for the proof and adds the standard telescoping application.

solution:
Since no four points are coplanar, no three are collinear, so three points that are pairwise joined do form a genuine triangle.

\textbf{(a)} Split the points into two groups of $n$ and join every point of the first group to every point of the second: $n\cdot n=n^2$ segments. Any three points include two from the same group, and these are not joined, so there is no triangle.

\textbf{(b)} Suppose $m=n^2+1$ segments are drawn and there is no triangle. For a point $P$ let $d(P)$ be the number of drawn segments at $P$.

If $PQ$ is drawn, no point $R$ is joined to both $P$ and $Q$ (otherwise $PQR$ would be a triangle). So the $d(P)-1$ other points joined to $P$ and the $d(Q)-1$ other points joined to $Q$ are disjoint sets among the remaining $2n-2$ points:
\[d(P)+d(Q)\le2n\quad\text{for every drawn segment }PQ.\]
Add this over all $m$ drawn segments. Each point $P$ is an endpoint of $d(P)$ segments, so it contributes $d(P)$ to the left side $d(P)$ times:
\[\sum_{P}d(P)^2\le2n\,m.\]
On the other hand $\sum_Pd(P)=2m$ (each segment has two ends), and by the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality (or QM-AM) over the $2n$ points,
\[\sum_Pd(P)^2\ge\dfrac{\left(\sum_Pd(P)\right)^2}{2n}=\dfrac{4m^2}{2n}=\dfrac{2m^2}{n}.\]
Combining, $\dfrac{2m^2}{n}\le2nm$, so $m\le n^2$, contradicting $m=n^2+1$. Hence the segments form at least one triangle. $\blacksquare$

(This is Mantel's theorem; (a) shows that $n^2+1$ cannot be lowered.)
note: The post collects notes on induction, the pigeonhole principle and inclusion-exclusion and then proves (by induction) that the segments even form at least n triangles. The record asks for the stated problem (at least one triangle) and adds part (a), which shows the bound is sharp; the solution uses a double-counting argument. Checked by brute force over all graphs on 4 and 6 points.

question: Solve $x^2-18x+81=0$. A student applied the quadratic formula and obtained $x=\dfrac{18\pm\sqrt{648}}{2}$. Find the student's mistake.
solution:
The left side is a perfect square: $x^2-18x+81=(x-9)^2$. So the equation is $(x-9)^2=0$, whose only solution is $x=\boxed{9}$ (a double root).

With the quadratic formula, $a=1$, $b=-18$, $c=81$, and the discriminant is
\[b^2-4ac=324-4\cdot1\cdot81=324-324=0,\]
so $x=\dfrac{18\pm\sqrt0}{2}=9$. The student's $648=324+324$ comes from adding $4ac$ instead of subtracting it (a sign error, as if $c$ were $-81$). A zero discriminant always means a single repeated root, which is a good check here because the quadratic is visibly a perfect square.
note: The post asks whether (18 +- sqrt 648)/2 is right; it is not (sign error in the discriminant). Turned into a solve-and-find-the-error question.

question:
Find a closed form for
\[\sum_{i=0}^{n}2^{n+i}\dbinom{n}{i}\]
where $n$ is a positive integer.
solution:
Factor out $2^n$ and use the binomial theorem $(1+x)^n=\sum_{i=0}^n\dbinom nix^i$ with $x=2$:
\[\sum_{i=0}^{n}2^{n+i}\dbinom ni=2^n\sum_{i=0}^n\dbinom ni2^i=2^n(1+2)^n=2^n3^n=\boxed{6^n}.\]
For example, $n=1$ gives $2+4=6$ and $n=2$ gives $4+16+16=36$.
note: Problem A of the post.

question:
Prove or disprove: for every positive integer $n$,
\[1+x+x^2+\cdots+x^{\dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}}=(x+1)(x^2+1)(x^3+1)\cdots(x^n+1).\]
Determine exactly for which positive integers $n$ the identity holds.
solution:
Both sides have degree $\dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}=1+2+\cdots+n$, but they are not always equal.

\textbf{It holds for $n=1$ and $n=2$:} $1+x=x+1$, and $(x+1)(x^2+1)=x^3+x^2+x+1$.

\textbf{It fails for every $n\ge3$.} Substitute $x=1$. The left side has $\dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}+1$ terms, each equal to $1$, so it equals $\dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}+1$; the right side equals $2^n$. For $n=3$ these are $7$ and $8$. For $n\ge3$ we always have $2^n>\dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}+1$: this is true for $n=3$, and if it holds for $n$, then
\[2^{n+1}>n(n+1)+2\ge\dfrac{(n+1)(n+2)}{2}+1,\]
since $n(n+1)+2-\left(\dfrac{(n+1)(n+2)}{2}+1\right)=\dfrac{(n+1)(n-2)}{2}+1>0$. So the two polynomials take different values at $x=1$ and are not equal.

(Another way to see it: expanding the product, the coefficient of $x^k$ counts the subsets of $\{1,2,\dots,n\}$ with sum $k$; for $n\ge3$ the coefficient of $x^3$ is $2$, from $\{3\}$ and $\{1,2\}$, while on the left it is $1$.)

So the statement is \textbf{false}; the identity holds exactly for $\boxed{n=1\text{ and }n=2}$.
note: Problem B of the post (the poster did not know how to solve it). The record asks for exactly which n the identity holds.

solution:
\textbf{(a)} For every number $x$, the pair $(x,12-x)$ satisfies the equation, for example $(1,11)$, $(5,7)$, $(-3,15)$ and $(2.5,9.5)$. One equation in two unknowns has infinitely many solutions; to pin down $x$ and $y$ we need more information, such as a second independent equation or extra conditions.

\textbf{(b)} With $x$ and $y$ positive integers, $x$ can be $1,2,\dots,11$, and then $y=12-x$ is a positive integer. So there are $\boxed{11}$ ordered pairs.

\textbf{(c)} Adding the equations gives $2x=16$, so $x=\boxed{8}$, and then $y=\boxed{4}$.
note: The post asks how to "find the right numbers" for x + y = 12; turned into an exercise showing that one equation does not determine two unknowns, counting the positive integer solutions, and solving with a second equation.

question:
Real numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ satisfy
\[\dfrac{1}{a}+\dfrac{1}{b}+\dfrac{1}{c}=1,\qquad a+b+c=11,\qquad a^2+b^2+c^2=49.\]
Find $a^3+b^3+c^3$.
solution:
Let $p=a+b+c=11$, $q=ab+bc+ca$ and $r=abc$. From $a^2+b^2+c^2=p^2-2q$,
\[49=121-2q,\qquad q=36.\]
From $\dfrac{1}{a}+\dfrac{1}{b}+\dfrac{1}{c}=\dfrac{ab+bc+ca}{abc}=\dfrac {q}{r}=1$, we get $r=36$. Using
\[a^3+b^3+c^3=p^3-3pq+3r,\]
we find
\[a^3+b^3+c^3=1331-3\cdot11\cdot36+3\cdot36=1331-1188+108=\boxed{251}.\]
(Such numbers exist: $a,b,c$ are the roots of $t^3-11t^2+36t-36=(t-2)(t-3)(t-6)$, so they are $2,3,6$ in some order, and indeed $8+27+216=251$.)
note: Checked with sympy; the numbers are 2, 3, 6.

question: How many positive divisors does one million have?
solution: $1000000=10^6=2^6\cdot5^6$. A divisor has the form $2^a5^b$ with $0\le a\le6$ and $0\le b\le6$, so there are $(6+1)(6+1)=\boxed{49}$ divisors.
note: Problem P2 of a set of ten counting and probability questions.

question: How many four-letter strings of letters have vowels in the two middle places and consonants in the two outer places, with no letter repeated? (Use the $26$-letter English alphabet with the $5$ vowels A, E, I, O, U; the other $21$ letters, including Y, are consonants.)
solution:
Choose the outer letters and the middle letters in order: the first letter is any of $21$ consonants and the last any of the remaining $20$; the second letter is any of $5$ vowels and the third any of the remaining $4$. The number of strings is
\[21\cdot5\cdot4\cdot20=\boxed{8400}.\]
note: Problem P3 of the set; "random letters" is read as any letters, and Y is counted as a consonant.

question: What is the largest integer $n$ such that $2^n$ divides $100!$?
solution:
Among $1,2,\dots,100$ there are $\left\lfloor\dfrac{100}{2}\right\rfloor=50$ multiples of $2$, $25$ multiples of $4$, $12$ of $8$, $6$ of $16$, $3$ of $32$ and $1$ of $64$. A number divisible by exactly $2^k$ is counted $k$ times, so the exponent of $2$ in $100!$ is
\[50+25+12+6+3+1=\boxed{97}.\]
note: Problem P4 of the set.

question: In how many ways can the letters of the word PROBABILITY be arranged?
solution:
PROBABILITY has $11$ letters: B and I appear twice each, and P, R, O, A, L, T, Y once each. The number of distinguishable arrangements is
\[\dfrac{11!}{2!\,2!}=\dfrac{39916800}{4}=\boxed{9979200}.\]
note: Problem P6 of the set.

question: Find the greatest integer $n$ for which $12^n$ divides $20!$.
solution:
Since $12^n=2^{2n}3^n$, we need the exponents of $2$ and $3$ in $20!$:
\[v_2(20!)=10+5+2+1=18,\qquad v_3(20!)=6+2=8.\]
We need $2n\le18$ and $n\le8$, so the greatest $n$ is $\boxed{8}$.
note: Problem P8 of the set.

question: In a round-robin tournament, each of six basketball teams plays every other team exactly once. How many games are played in the tournament?
solution: Each game corresponds to a pair of teams, so the number of games is $\dbinom62=\boxed{15}$.
note: Problem P9 of the set; "how many games are required to have one winner" is read as the total number of games of the round robin.

question: In a single-elimination lacrosse tournament, $64$ teams play $6$ rounds and $63$ games. Before the tournament you must predict the winners of all $63$ games (your predictions must be consistent: a team you predict to win a game must be one you predicted to reach it). You score $32$ points for correctly predicting the champion, $16$ points for each correctly predicted winner of a semifinal, and so on, down to $1$ point for each correctly predicted winner of a first-round game; the maximum score is $192$. Knowing nothing about the teams, you decide every prediction by flipping a fair coin. What is the expected number of points you score?
solution:
A game of round $r$ ($r=1,\dots,6$) is worth $2^{r-1}$ points, and there are $2^{6-r}$ such games. Each game of round $r$ is between teams from a fixed group of $2^r$ teams (its part of the bracket), and exactly one of those teams actually wins it.

Your predicted winner of that game is decided by $r$ coin flips (one for each game on its path), so it is equally likely to be any of the $2^r$ teams of the group, whatever the actual results are. Hence you predict that game correctly with probability $\dfrac{1}{2^r}$, and its expected contribution is
\[2^{r-1}\cdot\dfrac{1}{2^r}=\dfrac{1}{2}.\]
By linearity of expectation, summing over all $63$ games,
\[63\cdot\dfrac{1}{2}=\boxed{\dfrac{63}{2}}=31.5\ \text{points}.\]
note: Problem P10 of the set; consistency of the bracket is stated explicitly. Checked by simulation and by exact enumeration on an 8-team bracket.

solution:
The question can only be consistent if the declared value equals the probability of picking a choice that shows this value.
\begin{itemize}
\item If $25\%$ is correct, then (A) and (D) are both correct choices, so the chance of picking a correct choice is $\dfrac{2}{4}=50\%\ne25\%$.
\item If $50\%$ is correct, only (C) is correct, so the chance is $\dfrac{1}{4}=25\%\ne50\%$.
\item If $0\%$ is correct, then (B) is a correct choice, so the chance is $\dfrac{1}{4}=25\%\ne0\%$.
\item If no choice is correct, the chance of being correct is $0\%$; but then (B) states the true value and is correct after all, a contradiction.
\end{itemize}
Every possibility contradicts itself, so the question has no consistent answer. It is a self-referential paradox, like ``this sentence is false''.
note: A well-known self-referential puzzle; the post asks for the chance of being correct, which has no consistent value. Recorded as showing that every choice leads to a contradiction.

question: When $(a+b+c+d+5)^{2020}$ is expanded and like terms are combined, the resulting expression contains exactly $N$ terms that include all four variables $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$, with the power of $a$ at least $5$, the power of $b$ at least $4$, the power of $c$ at least $3$ and the power of $d$ at least $2$. Find $N$ (in terms of a binomial coefficient, and as a number).
solution:
By the multinomial theorem, the expansion is a sum of terms
\[\dfrac{2020!}{p!\,q!\,r!\,s!\,t!}\,5^t\,a^pb^qc^rd^s,\qquad p+q+r+s+t=2020,\]
with nonnegative exponents and positive coefficients. Like terms are those with the same $(p,q,r,s)$ (then $t=2020-p-q-r-s$ is determined), so the terms of the simplified expression correspond exactly to the quadruples $(p,q,r,s)$ of nonnegative integers with $p+q+r+s\le2020$.

We need $p\ge5$, $q\ge4$, $r\ge3$, $s\ge2$. Put $p=5+p'$, $q=4+q'$, $r=3+r'$, $s=2+s'$; then $p'+q'+r'+s'\le2020-14=2006$. Adding a slack variable $t'\ge0$,
\[p'+q'+r'+s'+t'=2006,\]
which by stars and bars has $\dbinom{2006+4}{4}$ solutions. Hence
\[N=\dbinom{2010}{4}=\dfrac{2010\cdot2009\cdot2008\cdot2007}{24}=\boxed{678072034710}.\]
note: Version 1 of the post. Checked by brute force for small exponents.

question:
Let $a\ne0$ and $r\ne1$, and let $S_n=a+ar+ar^2+\cdots+ar^{n-1}$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Show that $S_n=\dfrac{a(1-r^n)}{1-r}$.
\item[(b)] Suppose $|r|<1$. Find $\dfrac{a}{1-r}-S_n$ and explain why $S_n$ gets as close as we like to $\dfrac{a}{1-r}$ as $n$ grows. (This is what is meant by saying that the infinite series $a+ar+ar^2+\cdots$ has sum $\dfrac{a}{1-r}$.)
\item[(c)] For $\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{4}+\dfrac{1}{8}+\cdots$, find the sum and the least $n$ for which the sum of the first $n$ terms is within $0.001$ of it.
\item[(d)] Explain why the series $1+1+1+\cdots$ and $1-1+1-1+\cdots$ ($r=1$ and $r=-1$) have no sum in this sense.
\end{enumerate}
solution:
\textbf{(a)} Multiply $S_n$ by $r$ and subtract:
\[S_n-rS_n=(a+ar+\cdots+ar^{n-1})-(ar+ar^2+\cdots+ar^n)=a-ar^n,\]
so $S_n=\dfrac{a(1-r^n)}{1-r}$ for $r\ne1$.

\textbf{(b)} By (a),
\[\dfrac{a}{1-r}-S_n=\dfrac{a}{1-r}-\dfrac{a-ar^n}{1-r}=\boxed{\dfrac{ar^n}{1-r}}.\]
When $|r|<1$, the powers $|r|^n$ become smaller than any positive number as $n$ grows (each step multiplies by the fixed factor $|r|<1$), so the difference $\left|\dfrac{a}{1-r}-S_n\right|=\dfrac{|a|\,|r|^n}{|1-r|}$ becomes as small as we like. An infinite series has a sum when its partial sums approach a single number; here that number is $\dfrac{a}{1-r}$. No one adds infinitely many numbers one by one: the ``sum'' is the limit of the finite sums.

\textbf{(c)} Here $a=r=\dfrac{1}{2}$, so the sum is $\dfrac{\dfrac{1}{2}}{1-\dfrac{1}{2}}=\boxed{1}$, and $1-S_n=\dfrac{1}{2^n}$ by (b). We need $\dfrac{1}{2^n}\le0.001$, i.e.\ $2^n\ge1000$; since $2^9=512$ and $2^{10}=1024$, the least such $n$ is $\boxed{10}$.

\textbf{(d)} For $r=1$ the partial sums $1,2,3,\dots$ grow without bound. For $r=-1$ they are $1,0,1,0,\dots$, which keep jumping between two values and approach no single number. In neither case do the partial sums approach a number, so there is no sum. (The formula $\dfrac{a}{1-r}$ needs $|r|<1$.)
note: The post asks how an infinite series can have a sum; turned into an exercise deriving the partial-sum formula and the limit a/(1-r), with an example and two series without a sum.

solution:
\textbf{(a)} If $a=b$, then $a^6$ and $b^6$ are the same number raised to the same power: $a^6=a\cdot a\cdot a\cdot a\cdot a\cdot a=b\cdot b\cdot b\cdot b\cdot b\cdot b=b^6$, replacing each factor $a$ by the equal number $b$.

\textbf{(b)} $a=1$, $b=-1$: $1^6=1=(-1)^6$, but $1\ne-1$.

\textbf{(c)} Factor:
\[a^6-b^6=(a^3-b^3)(a^3+b^3)=(a-b)(a+b)(a^2+ab+b^2)(a^2-ab+b^2).\]
Now $a^2+ab+b^2=\left(a+\dfrac {b}{2}\right)^2+\dfrac{3}{4}b^2$ and $a^2-ab+b^2=\left(a-\dfrac {b}{2}\right)^2+\dfrac{3}{4}b^2$ are positive unless $a=b=0$. So if $a^6=b^6$ and not $a=b=0$, then $(a-b)(a+b)=0$, i.e.\ $a=b$ or $a=-b$; and if $a=b=0$ this holds too. Conversely, $a=\pm b$ gives $a^6=(\pm b)^6=b^6$. $\blacksquare$
note: Problem P1 of the "prove the obvious" post; parts (b) and (c) about the converse were added to make the exercise substantive.

question: Prove that $\sqrt{11}$ is irrational.
solution: Suppose $\sqrt{11}=\dfrac {p}{q}$ with positive integers $p,q$ and the fraction in lowest terms. Then $p^2=11q^2$, so the prime $11$ divides $p^2$ and hence divides $p$ (a prime dividing a product divides one of the factors). Write $p=11k$. Then $121k^2=11q^2$, so $q^2=11k^2$, and in the same way $11$ divides $q$. Now $11$ divides both $p$ and $q$, contradicting that $\dfrac {p}{q}$ is in lowest terms. Hence $\sqrt{11}$ is irrational. $\blacksquare$
note: Problem P2 of the "prove the obvious" post.

question:
Evaluate
\[\dfrac{1}{8}+\dfrac{1}{15}+\dfrac{1}{24}+\dfrac{1}{35}+\dfrac{1}{48}+\dfrac{1}{63}+\dfrac{1}{80}+\dfrac{1}{99}.\]
solution:
The denominators are not in arithmetic progression (their differences are $7,9,11,\dots$), but each is one less than a square: $8=3^2-1=2\cdot4$, $15=3\cdot5$, $\dots$, $99=9\cdot11$. So the terms are $\dfrac{1}{k(k+2)}$ for $k=2,3,\dots,9$, and
\[\dfrac{1}{k(k+2)}=\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{k}-\dfrac{1}{k+2}\right).\]
The sum telescopes, leaving the first two positive and the last two negative parts:
\[\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{3}-\dfrac{1}{10}-\dfrac{1}{11}\right)=\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{5}{6}-\dfrac{21}{110}\right)=\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{275-63}{330}=\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{212}{330}=\boxed{\dfrac{53}{165}}.\]
note: The poster says the denominators are in arithmetic progression; they are not (they are k(k+2), with differences 7, 9, 11, ...). Checked with exact fractions.

question: Factor $x^2y+xy^2+x^2+2xy+y^2+x+y$ completely.
solution:
Group the terms by degree:
\[x^2y+xy^2+x^2+2xy+y^2+x+y=xy(x+y)+(x+y)^2+(x+y).\]
Every group contains the factor $x+y$:
\[=(x+y)(xy+x+y+1)=(x+y)\bigl(x(y+1)+(y+1)\bigr)=\boxed{(x+y)(x+1)(y+1)}.\]
(Check at $x=1$, $y=2$: the original is $2+4+1+4+4+1+2=18$ and $(3)(2)(3)=18$.)
note: Problem 1 of a factorisation marathon; no other problems are in the post.

question: A fair coin is flipped $6$ times. What is the expected length of the longest run of consecutive tails? (If no tails appear, the longest run has length $0$.)
solution:
Let $L$ be the length of the longest run of tails. Since $L=\sum_{k\ge1}[L\ge k]$ (the number of $k=1,2,\dots$ with $L\ge k$),
\[E[L]=\sum_{k=1}^{6}P(L\ge k)=\sum_{k=1}^{6}\left(1-\dfrac{c_k}{64}\right),\]
where $c_k$ is the number of sequences of $6$ flips with no run of $k$ tails.

\textbf{Counting $c_k$.} Let $f_k(m)$ count sequences of length $m$ with no run of $k$ tails. For $m<k$ every sequence works, so $f_k(m)=2^m$. For $m\ge k$, a valid sequence starts with $j$ tails ($0\le j\le k-1$), then a head, then any valid sequence of length $m-j-1$:
\[f_k(m)=f_k(m-1)+f_k(m-2)+\cdots+f_k(m-k).\]
\begin{itemize}
\item $k=1$: only HHHHHH, so $c_1=1$.
\item $k=2$: $1,2,3,5,8,13,21$, so $c_2=21$.
\item $k=3$: $1,2,4,7,13,24,44$, so $c_3=44$.
\item $k=4$: $1,2,4,8,15,29,56$, so $c_4=56$.
\item $k=5$: $64-3=61$ (the runs of $5$ or $6$ tails are TTTTTH, HTTTTT, TTTTTT).
\item $k=6$: $64-1=63$.
\end{itemize}
The numbers $64-c_k$ are $63,43,20,8,3,1$, so
\[E[L]=\dfrac{63+43+20+8+3+1}{64}=\dfrac{138}{64}=\boxed{\dfrac{69}{32}}\approx2.16.\]
note: Question 1 of the post. Checked by enumerating all 64 sequences.

question:
A fair coin is flipped $n$ times, and $L_n$ is the length of the longest run of consecutive tails. For $k\ge1$ let $f_k(m)$ be the number of sequences of $m$ flips with no run of $k$ consecutive tails.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Show that $f_k(m)=2^m$ for $0\le m<k$ and $f_k(m)=f_k(m-1)+f_k(m-2)+\cdots+f_k(m-k)$ for $m\ge k$.
\item[(b)] Show that
\[E[L_n]=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\left(1-\dfrac{f_k(n)}{2^n}\right).\]
\item[(c)] Use (a) and (b) to compute $E[L_3]$ and $E[L_4]$.
\end{enumerate}
solution:
\textbf{(a)} If $m<k$, no sequence of length $m$ contains $k$ tails in a row, so all $2^m$ sequences count. Let $m\ge k$. A sequence with no run of $k$ tails cannot start with $k$ tails, so it starts with exactly $j$ tails followed by a head, for some $0\le j\le k-1$ (here $j+1\le k\le m$, so the head fits). The rest is a sequence of length $m-j-1$ with no run of $k$ tails, and conversely every such choice gives a valid sequence, different choices giving different sequences. So $f_k(m)=\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}f_k(m-1-j)$.

\textbf{(b)} For every outcome, $L_n=\sum_{k=1}^{n}[L_n\ge k]$, where $[L_n\ge k]$ is $1$ if $L_n\ge k$ and $0$ otherwise (the longest run is at most $n$). Taking expectations, $E[L_n]=\sum_{k=1}^nP(L_n\ge k)$. The event $L_n\ge k$ means that some run of $k$ tails occurs, whose complement has $f_k(n)$ of the $2^n$ equally likely sequences. So $P(L_n\ge k)=1-\dfrac{f_k(n)}{2^n}$, which gives the formula.

\textbf{(c)} For $n=3$: $f_1(3)=1$, $f_2(3)=5$ (from $1,2,3,5$), $f_3(3)=7$, so
\[E[L_3]=\dfrac{(8-1)+(8-5)+(8-7)}{8}=\boxed{\dfrac{11}{8}}.\]
For $n=4$: $f_1(4)=1$, $f_2(4)=8$, $f_3(4)=13$ (from $1,2,4,7,13$), $f_4(4)=15$, so
\[E[L_4]=\dfrac{15+8+3+1}{16}=\boxed{\dfrac{27}{16}}.\]
(There is no simple closed form in $n$; the formula in (b) with the recursion in (a) is the standard way to compute $E[L_n]$. For $n=6$ it gives $\dfrac{69}{32}$.)
note: Question 2 of the post asks for "the expected value ... if n coins are flipped"; there is no simple closed form, so the record asks to derive the general formula (sum of complementary probabilities with a k-step recursion) and to apply it to n = 3 and 4. Checked by enumeration for n up to 12.

question: If $x=3y$ and $y=3x+1$, what is the value of $x$?
solution:
Substitute $x=3y$ into the second equation: $y=9y+1$, so $-8y=1$ and $y=-\dfrac{1}{8}$. Then
\[x=3y=\boxed{-\dfrac{3}{8}}.\]
(Check: $3x+1=-\dfrac{9}{8}+1=-\dfrac{1}{8}=y$.)

question:
Find the sum of all real numbers $x$ such that
\[x=\sqrt{9x+\dfrac{88}{\sqrt{x-11}+2\sqrt{x-10}+\sqrt{x-7}}}.\]
solution:
The square roots require $x\ge11$; on this range the denominator $D(x)=\sqrt{x-11}+2\sqrt{x-10}+\sqrt{x-7}$ is positive. Since the right side is a nonnegative square root, the equation is equivalent (for $x\ge11$) to squaring both sides:
\[x^2=9x+\dfrac{88}{D(x)},\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad x^2-9x=\dfrac{88}{D(x)}.\]
\textbf{$x=11$ is a solution:} $D(11)=0+2\cdot1+2=4$, so the right side is $\dfrac{88}{4}=22$, and $11^2-9\cdot11=22$.

\textbf{It is the only one.} For $x>11$, the left side $x^2-9x=x(x-9)$ is larger than at $x=11$ (both factors are positive and increasing), so $x^2-9x>22$. Each square root in $D(x)$ increases with $x$, so $D(x)>4$ and $\dfrac{88}{D(x)}<22$. Hence the two sides cannot be equal for $x>11$.

The only solution is $x=11$, so the sum of all solutions is $\boxed{11}$.
note: Checked numerically on a fine grid for 11 <= x <= 10^4.

question: In how many ways can $8$ distinct grapes be distributed into $3$ distinct bowls so that at least one bowl is empty?
solution:
Each grape goes into one of the $3$ bowls, so there are $3^8=6561$ distributions in all. Count those with at least one empty bowl by inclusion-exclusion: a given bowl is empty in $2^8$ distributions, and two given bowls are both empty in $1$ distribution, so
\[3\cdot2^8-3\cdot1=768-3=\boxed{765}.\]
(Equivalently, $6561$ minus the $5796$ distributions with no empty bowl.)
note: Checked by enumerating all 3^8 distributions.

question: Four fair dice are tossed, and the numbers on top are all different. Given this, find the probability that at least $3$ of the four numbers have the same parity.
solution:
Given that the four numbers are different, the set of numbers shown is equally likely to be any of the $\dbinom64=15$ four-element subsets of $\{1,\dots,6\}$ (each subset arises from $4!$ equally likely ordered outcomes). The die has three odd faces $1,3,5$ and three even faces $2,4,6$, so four different numbers cannot all have the same parity. At least $3$ have the same parity when the set has $3$ odd and $1$ even number ($1\cdot3=3$ sets) or $3$ even and $1$ odd ($3$ sets). The probability is
\[\dfrac{6}{15}=\boxed{\dfrac{2}{5}}.\]
note: Question 1 of the post. Checked by enumerating all 6^4 outcomes.

question: Four fair dice are tossed, and the numbers on top are all different. Given this, find the probability that the sum of the four numbers is greater than $15$.
solution: Given that the four numbers are different, the set of numbers shown is equally likely to be any of the $\dbinom64=15$ four-element subsets of $\{1,\dots,6\}$ (each subset arises from $4!$ equally likely ordered outcomes). The four numbers have sum $21-(\text{sum of the two missing numbers})$, so the sum exceeds $15$ exactly when the two missing numbers have sum less than $6$: $\{1,2\},\{1,3\},\{1,4\},\{2,3\}$. That is $4$ subsets, and the probability is $\boxed{\dfrac{4}{15}}$.
note: Question 2 of the post. Checked by enumerating all 6^4 outcomes.

solution:
\textbf{(a)} By the binomial theorem,
\[11^n=(10+1)^n=\sum_{k=0}^n\dbinom nk10^{\,n-k}1^k=\sum_{k=0}^n\dbinom nk10^{\,n-k}.\]
So $11^n$ is the number whose ``digits'' are the entries of row $n$, the first entry in the $10^n$ place, the next in the $10^{n-1}$ place, and so on. For $n\le4$ every entry is at most $9$, so these really are the decimal digits, which explains $1,11,121,1331,14641$.

\textbf{(b)} For $n\ge5$ some entries are $10$ or more, so the sum in (a) still equals $11^n$, but the entries overlap into neighbouring places and must be carried. For row $5$:
\[1\cdot10^5+5\cdot10^4+10\cdot10^3+10\cdot10^2+5\cdot10+1=100000+50000+10000+1000+50+1=161051=11^5.\]
Row $6$ is $1,6,15,20,15,6,1$, so
\[11^6=10^6+6\cdot10^5+15\cdot10^4+20\cdot10^3+15\cdot10^2+6\cdot10+1=\boxed{1771561}.\]
note: The post asks whether the powers of 11 in Pascal's triangle are a coincidence (it numbers the rows from 1); the record uses the usual numbering from row 0 and asks for the binomial-theorem explanation and 11^6 from row 6.

question:
Prove that if $a$ and $b$ are positive real numbers with $a^2+b^2=5$, then
\[a^3+b^6\ge9.\]
When does equality hold?
solution:
By AM-GM on the three positive numbers $a^3$, $a^3$, $8$,
\[a^3+a^3+8\ge3\sqrt[3]{a^3\cdot a^3\cdot8}=6a^2,\qquad\text{so}\qquad a^3\ge3a^2-4,\]
with equality when $a^3=8$, i.e.\ $a=2$. By AM-GM on $b^6$, $1$, $1$,
\[b^6+1+1\ge3\sqrt[3]{b^6}=3b^2,\qquad\text{so}\qquad b^6\ge3b^2-2,\]
with equality when $b^6=1$, i.e.\ $b=1$. Adding,
\[a^3+b^6\ge3(a^2+b^2)-6=15-6=9.\]
Equality holds exactly when $a=2$ and $b=1$, which indeed satisfy $a^2+b^2=5$ and give $8+1=9$. $\blacksquare$

(The constants $8$ and $1$ are chosen so that the equality cases $a=2$, $b=1$ of the two AM-GM steps match the point where the minimum is attained.)
note: Checked numerically along the whole arc a^2 + b^2 = 5.
The post includes the "bonus" with side 2x, which is part (b). The region asked for includes the inside of the big circle, as the post states.

question: Find $\displaystyle\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\dfrac{3^i+5^i}{8^i}$.
solution:
Split the sum into two geometric series with ratios $\dfrac{3}{8}$ and $\dfrac{5}{8}$, both less than $1$ in absolute value, so both converge:
\[\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\left(\dfrac{3}{8}\right)^i+\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\left(\dfrac{5}{8}\right)^i=\dfrac{1}{1-\dfrac{3}{8}}+\dfrac{1}{1-\dfrac{5}{8}}=\dfrac{8}{5}+\dfrac{8}{3}=\boxed{\dfrac{64}{15}}.\]
note: The poster found the answer by summing decimals and asked for a better method.

solution:
\textbf{(a)} By the quadratic formula the solutions are $\dfrac{-b+\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}$ and $\dfrac{-b-\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}$. The square roots cancel when we add them, so their sum is $-\dfrac {b}{a}$ and their average is
\[\boxed{-\dfrac{b}{2a}}.\]
(This also holds when $b^2-4ac<0$, for the two complex solutions; and it is Vieta's formula $x_1+x_2=-\dfrac {b}{a}$. Geometrically, $x=-\dfrac {b}{2a}$ is the axis of symmetry of the parabola $y=ax^2+bx+c$, halfway between its $x$-intercepts.)

\textbf{(b)} Any pair of claimed solutions must have average $-\dfrac {b}{2a}$ (and product $\dfrac {c}{a}$), which is quick to test without substituting. For $2x^2-7x+3=0$, $-\dfrac {b}{2a}=\dfrac{7}{4}$.
\begin{itemize}
\item $3$ and $\dfrac{1}{2}$: the average is $\dfrac{7}{4}$, and the product $\dfrac{3}{2}$ equals $\dfrac {c}{a}=\dfrac{3}{2}$, so these are the solutions; indeed $2x^2-7x+3=(2x-1)(x-3)$.
\item $3$ and $-\dfrac{1}{2}$: the average is $\dfrac{5}{4}\ne\dfrac{7}{4}$, so this pair is wrong (a sign error).
\end{itemize}
The average alone can miss some errors (for example $1$ and $\dfrac{5}{2}$ also average $\dfrac{7}{4}$), which is why checking the product as well is useful.
note: The post's two questions (the average of the solutions, and how this helps to check solutions) are combined into one record with parts (a) and (b); part (b) adds a concrete check.

question: Three fair dice are rolled. Find the sum of all values $x$ such that the probability that the sum of the three dice equals $x$ is $\dfrac{1}{8}$.
solution:
There are $6^3=216$ equally likely outcomes, and $\dfrac{1}{8}=\dfrac{27}{216}$, so we need the sums that occur in exactly $27$ ways.

\textbf{Sum $10$.} The number of solutions of $a+b+c=10$ with $1\le a,b,c\le6$: putting $a=a'+1$ etc., $a'+b'+c'=7$ with $0\le a',b',c'\le5$. Without the upper bound there are $\dbinom92=36$ solutions; those with some variable at least $6$ have that variable equal to $6$ or $7$ and the other two summing to $1$ or $0$: $3\cdot(2+1)=9$. So sum $10$ occurs in $36-9=27$ ways.

\textbf{Symmetry.} Replacing each die value $v$ by $7-v$ turns a sum $s$ into $21-s$, so sums $s$ and $21-s$ occur equally often; hence sum $11$ also occurs $27$ times.

\textbf{No other sums.} The numbers of ways for the sums $3,4,\dots,10$ are
\[1,3,6,10,15,21,25,27,\]
increasing, and by symmetry the sums $11,\dots,18$ give $27,25,\dots,1$. So exactly the sums $10$ and $11$ have probability $\dfrac{1}{8}$, and the answer is $10+11=\boxed{21}$.
note: The poster's answer 21 is right; the record adds the check that no other sum has probability 1/8. Checked by enumerating all 216 outcomes.

question: How many different four-digit numbers can be formed by rearranging the four digits of $2020$?
solution: The digits are $2,2,0,0$. They can be arranged in $\dfrac{4!}{2!\,2!}=6$ ways, but a four-digit number cannot start with $0$; the arrangements starting with $0$ are those of $2,2,0$ in the last three places, $3$ of them. That leaves $6-3=\boxed{3}$ numbers: $2002$, $2020$ and $2200$.

question: For numbers $a$ and $b$, a \emph{move that adds $(a,b)$} takes a particle from a point $(c,d)$ to the point $(c+a,d+b)$. A particle moves by these rules: if the move that brought it to its current position added $(p,q)$, then its next move adds either $(p-1,q)$ or $(p,q-1)$, and neither coordinate of an added vector may ever be negative. Particle $A$ starts at $(0,0)$ and its first move takes it to $(3,4)$. It keeps moving by the rules until no further move is possible, and at that moment it is at a point $(r,r)$. What is $r$?
solution:
The first move adds $(3,4)$. Each later move adds a vector whose coordinates sum to one less than those of the vector before it, so the added vectors have coordinate sums
\[7,\ 6,\ 5,\ 4,\ 3,\ 2,\ 1,\ 0 .\]
The last of these is a move adding $(0,0)$ (made after a move adding $(1,0)$ or $(0,1)$); after it no move is possible, because $(-1,0)$ and $(0,-1)$ are not allowed. Before that a move is always possible, since a vector $(p,q)\ne(0,0)$ has a positive coordinate that can be lowered by $1$.

The final position is the sum of all the added vectors, so its two coordinates add up to
\[7+6+5+4+3+2+1+0=28,\]
whichever choices are made. If the final point is $(r,r)$, then $2r=28$, so $r=\boxed{14}$.

Such a path exists: for example the added vectors
\[(3,4),\ (3,3),\ (2,3),\ (2,2),\ (2,1),\ (1,1),\ (1,0),\ (0,0)\]
have $x$-coordinates summing to $3+3+2+2+2+1+1+0=14$ and $y$-coordinates summing to $4+3+3+2+1+1+0+0=14$. (Other choices end at other points of the line $x+y=28$, from $(6,22)$ to $(18,10)$.)
note: FTW problem quoted in the post (no contest source given). The post asks for a fast solution; the record gives the invariant x + y = 28 and an explicit path to (14, 14). Checked by enumerating all move sequences.

solution:
\textbf{(a)} Let $S=a+ar+\cdots+ar^{n-1}$. Then $rS=ar+ar^2+\cdots+ar^n$, and subtracting,
\[(r-1)S=ar^n-a,\qquad S=\dfrac{a(r^n-1)}{r-1}.\]
The mean is the sum divided by the number of terms:
\[\boxed{\text{mean}=\dfrac{a(r^n-1)}{n(r-1)}}.\]
(For $r=1$ all terms equal $a$ and the mean is $a$.) So there is a formula, but it is just ``sum divided by count'' with the geometric-series formula for the sum.

\textbf{(b)} Here $a=3$, $r=2$ and $1536=3\cdot2^9$, so $n=10$. The mean is
\[\dfrac{3(2^{10}-1)}{10\cdot1}=\dfrac{3\cdot1023}{10}=\boxed{\dfrac{3069}{10}=306.9}.\]
note: The post asks whether there is a formula for the mean of a geometric sequence; it is turned into deriving the formula a(r^n - 1)/(n(r - 1)) with an example. Checked with exact fractions.

solution:
\textbf{(a)} The numbers $7y+9z$ in increasing order are $0,7,9,14,16,18,21,23,25,27,\ldots$, with remainders mod $5$ equal to $0,2,4,4,1,3,1,3,0,2,\ldots$. The first number in each remainder class is
\[k=0:\ 0,\qquad k=1:\ 16=7+9,\qquad k=2:\ 7,\qquad k=3:\ 18=9+9,\qquad k=4:\ 9 .\]
(Every number below $16$ of the form $7y+9z$ is one of $0,7,9,14$, with remainders $0,2,4,4$, and $17$ is not of that form; so these really are the smallest.)

\textbf{(b)} A number $N$ can be written as $5x+7y+9z$ exactly when $N$ is at least the smallest number $m_k$ of part (a) in its remainder class $k$: then $N=m_k+5x$ with $x\ge0$; and if $N<m_k$, every $7y+9z\le N$ is smaller than $m_k$, so it lies in a different remainder class and $N-(7y+9z)$ is not a multiple of $5$.

So in each class the largest impossible number is $m_k-5$ (or none if $m_k=0$): these are $11$, $2$, $13$ and $4$. The largest is $\boxed{13}$. Check: $13$ is not $5x+7y+9z$ (the candidates $13-0$, $13-7=6$, $13-9=4$ are not multiples of $5$), while $14=7\cdot2$, $15=5\cdot3$, $16=7+9$, $17=5+5+7$, $18=9\cdot2$, and every larger number is one of these plus a multiple of $5$.

\textbf{(c)} The number $23$ is the largest number that cannot be made from $5$ and $7$ \emph{alone}. Allowing $9$ as well makes more numbers possible, for example $16=7+9$, $18=9+9$ and $23=5+9+9$, which cannot be made from $5$ and $7$ alone. So the largest impossible number can only go down, and here it drops to $13$. The third number has to be used in the calculation, as in (a) and (b).
note: The post asks how to use the Chicken McNugget theorem for three numbers and describes a heuristic based on the two smaller numbers. It is turned into the residue-class method for 5, 7, 9 (answer 13) and why 23 is wrong. Near-miss: aops-topic-2506266-q01 (the same question for 6, 10, 15) and aops-topic-2839235-q01 (6, 9, 20). Checked by brute force.

question: An $8\times7$ rectangle (width $8$, height $7$) has a $3$-$4$-$5$ right triangle drawn in each corner, with its right angle at the corner of the rectangle and its legs along the sides of the rectangle. The two lower triangles have their legs of length $4$ along the bottom edge of the rectangle, and the two upper triangles have their legs of length $3$ along the top edge. A circle is tangent to the hypotenuse of each of the four triangles. The diameter of the circle is $\dfrac {m}{n}$, where $m$ and $n$ are relatively prime positive integers. Find $m+n$.
note: Purple Comet 2015 Middle School Problem 20 (the post gives the source; the figure was only linked, so the record describes the configuration in words). Checked with exact coordinates: centre (4, 25/7), radius 20/7, tangency points on the segments.

question: A rectangular prism has as its vertices the eight points $(x,y,z)$ with $x\in\{0,24\}$, $y\in\{0,12\}$ and $z\in\{0,12\}$, namely $(0,0,0)$, $(0,0,12)$, $(0,12,0)$, $(0,12,12)$, $(24,0,0)$, $(24,0,12)$, $(24,12,0)$ and $(24,12,12)$. A sphere of radius $2$ is chosen at random from all spheres of radius $2$ that lie entirely inside the prism (that is, its centre is chosen uniformly from all possible centres). What is the probability that the point $(21,6,6)$ lies inside the chosen sphere?
note: "Chosen at random" is made precise as a uniformly random centre among all admissible centres. Checked the cap volume by integration and the probability by Monte Carlo.

question: Integers $a$ and $b$ satisfy $7a+5b=35$. Find the remainder when $a$ is divided by $5$.
solution:
Since $5b$ and $35$ are multiples of $5$, so is $7a=35-5b$. As $\gcd(7,5)=1$, $5$ must divide $a$. Hence the remainder is $\boxed{0}$.

(Indeed all solutions are $a=5t$, $b=7-7t$ for integers $t$, for example $(a,b)=(0,7),(5,0),(10,-7)$.)
note: Checked by listing the integer solutions with |a| <= 100.

question: Jamie, Linda and Don bought bundles of roses at a flower shop, all paying the same price per bundle. They took the bundles to a fair, where all three sold bundles at the same fixed price per bundle, higher than the shop's price. At the end of the fair they gave their unsold bundles away. Jamie bought $20$ bundles, sold $15$ and made a profit of $\$60$. Linda bought $34$ bundles, sold $24$ and made a profit of $\$69$. Don bought $40$ bundles and sold $36$. How many dollars of profit did Don make? (Profit is money received minus money paid.)
solution:
Let the shop price be $c$ dollars per bundle and the fair price $s$ dollars per bundle. Then
\[15s-20c=60,\qquad 24s-34c=69.\]
The first equation gives $3s-4c=12$, so $24s-32c=96$. Subtracting the second equation, $2c=27$, so $c=13.5$, and then $3s=12+54=66$, so $s=22$.

Don received $36\cdot22=792$ dollars and paid $40\cdot13.5=540$ dollars, so his profit was $\boxed{252}$ dollars.

Check: Jamie $15\cdot22-20\cdot13.5=330-270=60$ and Linda $24\cdot22-34\cdot13.5=528-459=69$.
note: The post (titled for its wordiness) gives no source. "A fixed price" is read as the same selling price for all three; profit counts the cost of every bundle bought. Checked with exact fractions.

question: Real numbers $x$ and $y$ are chosen independently and uniformly at random with $-1<x<4$ and $-4<y<2$. What is the probability that the product $xy$ is positive? Express your answer as a common fraction.
solution:
The point $(x,y)$ is uniform in a $5\times6$ rectangle of area $30$. The product is positive when $x$ and $y$ have the same sign: $0<x<4,\ 0<y<2$ (area $4\cdot2=8$) or $-1<x<0,\ -4<y<0$ (area $1\cdot4=4$). The lines $x=0$ and $y=0$ have area $0$. So the probability is
\[\dfrac{8+4}{30}=\boxed{\dfrac{2}{5}}.\]
note: The record is problem 1 of a forum-made mock MATHCOUNTS Target round (no official source). Checked with exact areas and Monte Carlo.

question: A runner covered $40$ miles in exactly $6$ hours. His speed was $12$ miles per hour for the first $5$ miles, $7$ miles per hour for the next $10$ miles and $6$ miles per hour for the next $15$ miles. Running at a constant speed over the final $10$ miles, what was his speed on that stretch? Express your answer as a common fraction.
solution:
The first $30$ miles took
\[\dfrac{5}{12}+\dfrac{10}{7}+\dfrac{15}{6}=\dfrac{35}{84}+\dfrac{120}{84}+\dfrac{210}{84}=\dfrac{365}{84}\text{ hours}.\]
That leaves $6-\dfrac{365}{84}=\dfrac{504-365}{84}=\dfrac{139}{84}$ hours for the last $10$ miles, so his speed was
\[\dfrac{10}{\ \dfrac{139}{84}\ }=\boxed{\dfrac{840}{139}}\text{ miles per hour}\approx6.04\text{ mph}.\]
note: The record is problem 4 of a forum-made mock MATHCOUNTS Target round (no official source). The irrelevant "he runs 40 miles each day" is dropped, and constant speed on the last stretch is stated.

question: A baseball pitcher throws his fastball at $100$ miles per hour from $60$ feet away from home plate. How many seconds does the ball take to reach home plate? Express your answer to the nearest hundredth of a second. ($1$ mile $=5280$ feet.)
solution:
$100$ miles per hour is
\[\dfrac{100\cdot5280}{3600}=\dfrac{440}{3}\approx146.67\text{ feet per second}.\]
So $60$ feet take $\dfrac{60}{\ \dfrac{440}{3}\ }=\dfrac{180}{440}=\dfrac{9}{22}\approx0.409$ seconds, which is $\boxed{0.41}$ seconds to the nearest hundredth.

question: Jamie draws a path on the coordinate plane. He starts at $(0,0)$ and repeatedly draws a segment of length $1$ either to the right or up, each with probability $\dfrac{1}{2}$, independently. What is the probability that his path passes through the point $(4,4)$? Express your answer as a common fraction.
solution:
After $k$ segments the path is at a point whose coordinates add up to $k$. So the path passes through $(4,4)$ exactly when, after $8$ segments, it is at $(4,4)$, i.e. exactly $4$ of the first $8$ segments go right. All $2^8=256$ sequences of $8$ moves are equally likely, and $\dbinom84=70$ of them have $4$ moves right. The probability is
\[\dfrac{70}{256}=\boxed{\dfrac{35}{128}}.\]

question: I am a three-digit number. My tens digit is five more than my ones digit, and my hundreds digit is eight less than my tens digit. What number am I?
solution: Let the digits be $h$ (hundreds), $t$ (tens) and $u$ (ones). Then $t=u+5$ and $h=t-8$. Since $h\ge1$ (a three-digit number), $t\ge9$, so $t=9$. Then $h=1$ and $u=4$, and the number is $\boxed{194}$.
note: Riddle 3 of the post; riddles 1 and 2 repeat earlier records and are aliased.

question:
Compute
\[\dfrac{1}{1\cdot2}+\dfrac{1}{2\cdot3}+\dfrac{1}{3\cdot4}+\cdots+\dfrac{1}{99\cdot100}.\]
solution:
For every positive integer $n$,
\[\dfrac{1}{n}-\dfrac{1}{n+1}=\dfrac{(n+1)-n}{n(n+1)}=\dfrac{1}{n(n+1)}.\]
So the sum telescopes:
\[\left(1-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)+\left(\dfrac{1}{2}-\dfrac{1}{3}\right)+\cdots+\left(\dfrac{1}{99}-\dfrac{1}{100}\right)=1-\dfrac{1}{100}=\boxed{\dfrac{99}{100}}.\]
note: The post is a solution to "MATHCOUNTS Challenge #1" (the problem statement itself is not quoted); the record is the computation it solves, checked with exact fractions.

question: The number $2^{59}-7^{33}$ is negative. Find the units digit of its absolute value, $7^{33}-2^{59}$.
solution:
Powers of $2$ end in $2,4,8,6$, repeating with period $4$; since $59=4\cdot14+3$, $2^{59}$ ends in $8$. Powers of $7$ end in $7,9,3,1$, repeating with period $4$; since $33=4\cdot8+1$, $7^{33}$ ends in $7$.

Also $7^{33}>4^{33}=2^{66}>2^{59}$, so $2^{59}-7^{33}<0$ and its absolute value is $7^{33}-2^{59}$. A number ending in $7$ minus a smaller number ending in $8$ ends in $17-8=9$ (one is borrowed). So the units digit is $\boxed{9}$.

(Subtracting the units digits the other way, $8-7=1$, ignores that the difference is negative: for instance $8-17=-9$.)
note: Problem 1 of a forum-made mock MATHCOUNTS Sprint round (no official source). As posted ("units digit of 2^59 - 7^33") the number is negative; the record asks for the units digit of its absolute value (9, not the tempting 1).

question: How many zeros are at the end of $32!$?
solution:
Each trailing zero comes from a factor $10=2\cdot5$, and $32!$ has more factors $2$ than factors $5$. The number of factors $5$ in $32!$ is
\[\left\lfloor\dfrac{32}{5}\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor\dfrac{32}{25}\right\rfloor=6+1=7,\]
so $32!$ ends in $\boxed{7}$ zeros.

question: Simplify $\dfrac{\sqrt{48}}{\sqrt9}+\dfrac{\sqrt{54}}{\sqrt8}$.
solution:
We have $\dfrac{\sqrt{48}}{\sqrt9}=\dfrac{4\sqrt3}{3}$ and $\dfrac{\sqrt{54}}{\sqrt8}=\sqrt{\dfrac{54}{8}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{27}{4}}=\dfrac{3\sqrt3}{2}$. So the sum is
\[\dfrac{4\sqrt3}{3}+\dfrac{3\sqrt3}{2}=\dfrac{8\sqrt3+9\sqrt3}{6}=\boxed{\dfrac{17\sqrt3}{6}}.\]

question: Pump A can fill a tank in $30$ minutes, pump B can fill it in $50$ minutes, and pump C can fill it in $75$ minutes. How many minutes will it take all three pumps working together to fill the tank?
solution:
In one minute the pumps fill $\dfrac{1}{30}$, $\dfrac{1}{50}$ and $\dfrac{1}{75}$ of the tank, together
\[\dfrac{5}{150}+\dfrac{3}{150}+\dfrac{2}{150}=\dfrac{10}{150}=\dfrac{1}{15}\]
of the tank. So they need $\boxed{15}$ minutes.

question: Walter has $5$ bottles of juice; each bottle contains either cranberry juice or orange juice, and he has at least two bottles of each kind. Every bottle contains at least $12$ oz and at most $20$ oz of juice, and altogether he has $80$ oz. One of his orange-juice bottles contains $16$ oz. What is the largest possible ratio of the total amount of cranberry juice to the total amount of orange juice? Express your answer as a common fraction.
solution:
Let $O$ be the total amount of orange juice; then there are $80-O$ ounces of cranberry juice, and the ratio $\dfrac{80-O}{O}=\dfrac{80}{O}-1$ is largest when $O$ is smallest.

With two orange bottles, one holds $16$ oz and the other at least $12$ oz, so $O\ge28$; with three orange bottles $O\ge16+12+12=40$. So $O\ge28$.

$O=28$ is possible: orange bottles of $16$ and $12$ oz, and three cranberry bottles holding $52$ oz in total, for example $20,20,12$ oz (each between $12$ and $20$). The largest ratio is
\[\dfrac{52}{28}=\boxed{\dfrac{13}{7}}.\]

question: The square of a number $n$ is eight more than twice $n$. Find all possible values of $n$.
solution: We need $n^2=2n+8$, i.e. $n^2-2n-8=0$, which factors as $(n-4)(n+2)=0$. So $n=\boxed{4\text{ or }-2}$. (Check: $16=8+8$ and $4=-4+8$.)

question: What is the sum of all positive multiples of $7$ that are less than $200$ and whose digits add up to $10$?
solution:
A number and its digit sum leave the same remainder when divided by $9$, so a number with digit sum $10$ is $\equiv1\pmod 9$. We need $n\equiv0\pmod7$ and $n\equiv1\pmod9$; since $28=7\cdot4=9\cdot3+1$, this means $n\equiv28\pmod{63}$. Below $200$ the candidates are $28$, $91$ and $154$, and their digit sums are $10$, $10$ and $10$. (The condition $n\equiv1\pmod9$ is only necessary, so each candidate had to be checked.) The sum is
\[28+91+154=\boxed{273}.\]
note: Problem 10 of a forum-made mock MATHCOUNTS Sprint round (no official source). Checked by brute force over all multiples of 7 below 200.

question: At sunrise the temperature in a town was $50$ degrees Fahrenheit, and at noon it was $72$ degrees Fahrenheit. If the temperature rose steadily by $4$ degrees every hour, at what time was sunrise?
solution: The temperature rose $72-50=22$ degrees, which takes $\dfrac{22}{4}=5.5$ hours at $4$ degrees per hour. Five and a half hours before noon is $\boxed{6\!:\!30\text{ a.m.}}$

question: A train travels at $45$ miles per hour and a plane at $200$ miles per hour. The train leaves $5$ hours before the plane. At the moment when the plane has travelled $700$ miles, how many miles has the train travelled?
solution: The plane has flown for $\dfrac{700}{200}=3.5$ hours, so the train has been travelling for $3.5+5=8.5$ hours and has covered $45\cdot8.5=\boxed{382.5}$ miles.

question: Two different integers are chosen at random from $\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}$, all pairs equally likely. What is the probability that they have no common prime factor? Express your answer as a common fraction.
solution: There are $\dbinom62=15$ pairs. Two numbers from $1$ to $6$ share a prime factor only if they share $2$ or $3$ ($5$ divides only one of them). Pairs sharing $2$: $\{2,4\},\{2,6\},\{4,6\}$; pairs sharing $3$: $\{3,6\}$. That is $4$ pairs, so $11$ pairs have no common prime factor (pairs with $1$ count, since $1$ has no prime factors). The probability is $\boxed{\dfrac{11}{15}}$.
note: Problem 13 of a forum-made mock MATHCOUNTS Sprint round (no official source).

question: A water bottle is $\dfrac{3}{4}$ full. Jill drinks $\dfrac{2}{5}$ of the water in it, and then Joe drinks $\dfrac{1}{3}$ of the water left after Jill. What fraction of a full bottle of water is still in the bottle? Express your answer as a common fraction.
solution:
After Jill, $\dfrac{3}{5}$ of the water is left: $\dfrac{3}{4}\cdot\dfrac{3}{5}=\dfrac{9}{20}$ of a bottle. After Joe, $\dfrac{2}{3}$ of that is left:
\[\dfrac{9}{20}\cdot\dfrac{2}{3}=\boxed{\dfrac{3}{10}}\]
of a full bottle.

question:
Arty places his $5$ brushes, coloured red, yellow, green, blue and black, in a row on a table, in positions $1$ to $5$ counted from the left. The following are true.
\begin{itemize}
\item The yellow brush is not at either end and not in the centre.
\item The position of the blue brush is not a prime number.
\item The black brush is somewhere between the red brush and the yellow brush.
\item The green brush is farther from the blue brush than any other brush is, and of all the other brushes, the red one is the closest to the green brush.
\end{itemize}
Which brushes are to the right of the black brush?
solution:
Yellow is in position $2$ or $4$, and blue is in position $1$ or $4$ (the non-primes among $1,\ldots,5$).

\textbf{Blue in position $4$.} The brush farthest from position $4$ is in position $1$, so green is in position $1$, and red, being closest to green, is in position $2$. Then yellow must be in position $2$ or $4$, both taken: impossible.

\textbf{Blue in position $1$.} Green is farthest from blue, so green is in position $5$, and red, closest to green, is in position $4$. Yellow is then in position $2$, and black, between red and yellow, is in position $3$. All conditions hold.

The order is blue, yellow, black, red, green, so the brushes to the right of black are the $\boxed{\text{red and green brushes}}$.
note: Problem 15 of a forum-made mock MATHCOUNTS Sprint round (no official source). The clue "the green brush is farthest away from blue, and closest to red" is made precise: green is the brush farthest from blue, and red is the brush nearest to green. Checked over all 120 orders.

question: What is the sum of all distinct roots of the equation $x^5+5x^4+10x^3+10x^2+5x+1=0$?
solution: By the binomial theorem the left side is $(x+1)^5$, so the only root is $x=-1$ (with multiplicity $5$). The sum of the \emph{distinct} roots is $\boxed{-1}$. (Vieta's formula $-5$ counts the root five times.)

question: Jeff the coat boy takes coats at a party, numbering them $1,2,3,\ldots$ in the order they arrive. Every $2$nd coat (coats $2,4,6,\ldots$) is black, every $5$th coat (coats $5,10,15,\ldots$) is an overcoat, and every $7$th coat (coats $7,14,21,\ldots$) is leather; a coat may have several of these properties. So far there have been exactly $9$ overcoats and $6$ leather coats. What are the possible numbers of black coats so far?
solution:
Let $n$ be the number of coats so far. There are $\left\lfloor\dfrac {n}{5}\right\rfloor$ overcoats and $\left\lfloor\dfrac {n}{7}\right\rfloor$ leather coats. From $\left\lfloor\dfrac {n}{5}\right\rfloor=9$ we get $45\le n\le49$, and from $\left\lfloor\dfrac {n}{7}\right\rfloor=6$ we get $42\le n\le48$. So $n\in\{45,46,47,48\}$.

The number of black coats is $\left\lfloor\dfrac {n}{2}\right\rfloor$, which is $22$, $23$, $23$, $24$ for these four values. So the number of black coats is $\boxed{22,\ 23\text{ or }24}$; the given information does not determine it.
note: Problem 21 of a forum-made mock MATHCOUNTS Sprint round (no official source). Ill-posed as posted ("how many black coats are there?"): 45 to 48 coats are all consistent, giving 22, 23 or 24 black coats. The record asks for all possible numbers.

question: Find the sum of the two roots of the equation $x^2-14x+4=23$.
solution: The equation is $x^2-14x-19=0$. Its discriminant $196+76=272$ is positive, so it has two real roots, and by Vieta's formulas their sum is $\boxed{14}$. (They are $7\pm\sqrt{68}=7\pm2\sqrt{17}$.)

question: Call a positive integer \emph{Jefrozen} if it satisfies $x^2-12x+36>40$ and has exactly $6$ positive divisors. What is the smallest Jefrozen number?
solution:
The inequality is $(x-6)^2>40$. For positive integers this means $x-6\ge7$ (as $6^2=36<40<49=7^2$), i.e. $x\ge13$; the other branch $x-6\le-7$ gives no positive $x$.

Now check $13,14,\ldots$ for exactly $6$ divisors: $13$ and $17$ are prime ($2$ divisors), $14=2\cdot7$ and $15=3\cdot5$ have $4$, $16=2^4$ has $5$, and $18=2\cdot3^2$ has $(1+1)(2+1)=6$. The smallest Jefrozen number is $\boxed{18}$. (The number $12$ also has $6$ divisors, but $(12-6)^2=36<40$.)

question: Charlie, Evan and Gary take turns rolling a fair six-sided die, in that order, starting with Charlie and repeating the cycle. The first player to roll a $4$ wins and the game ends. How much greater is Charlie's probability of winning than Gary's? Express your answer as a common fraction.
solution:
Let $q=\dfrac{5}{6}$. A full round without a $4$ has probability $q^3=\dfrac{125}{216}$, and after it the game starts afresh. Charlie wins on his first roll with probability $\dfrac{1}{6}$, so
\[P(\text{Charlie})=\dfrac{1}{6}\left(1+q^3+q^6+\cdots\right)=\dfrac{\dfrac{1}{6}}{1-q^3}=\dfrac{\dfrac{1}{6}}{\dfrac{91}{216}}=\dfrac{36}{91}.\]
Gary wins only after Charlie and Evan both miss, so $P(\text{Gary})=q^2\cdot P(\text{Charlie})=\dfrac{25}{36}\cdot\dfrac{36}{91}=\dfrac{25}{91}$. (Similarly Evan wins with probability $\dfrac{30}{91}$, and the three add up to $1$.) The difference is
\[\dfrac{36}{91}-\dfrac{25}{91}=\boxed{\dfrac{11}{91}}.\]
note: Problem 28 of a forum-made mock MATHCOUNTS Sprint round (no official source).

question: A supermarket is having a sale. All food is discounted by $25\%$, all toys by $20\%$, and everything else by $10\%$. Of the store's products, $80\%$ are food and $5\%$ are toys. Averaged over all products (each product counted once), by what percent is a product discounted?
solution:
The remaining $100\%-80\%-5\%=15\%$ of the products are discounted by $10\%$. The average discount is the weighted average
\[0.80\cdot25\%+0.05\cdot20\%+0.15\cdot10\%=20\%+1\%+1.5\%=\boxed{22.5\%}.\]

question: Using exactly six zeros, and any of the symbols $+$, $-$, $\times$, $\div$, the factorial sign $!$ and parentheses (but no other digits), write an expression whose value is $720$.
note: Riddle 2 of the post.

solution:
\textbf{(a)} If $A+B=99$ or $A\times B=99$ with positive integers $A,B$, then $A,B\le99$, so together they have at most $4$ digits, not $10$.

\textbf{(b)} From $A=99B$ we get $10B\le A<100B$, so $A$ has one or two more digits than $B$. If $B$ has $m$ digits, the total number of digits is $2m+1$ or $2m+2$; it equals $10$ only for $2m+2=10$, i.e. $B$ has $4$ digits and $A$ has $6$.

The digit sums $S(A)$ and $S(B)$ add up to $0+1+\cdots+9=45$. Since $9\mid99B=A$, also $9\mid S(A)$, and then $9\mid45-S(A)=S(B)$.

\textbf{(c)} $5013\cdot99=501300-5013=496287$, so $496287\div5013=\boxed{99}$. The digits used are $4,9,6,2,8,7$ and $5,0,1,3$: each of $0,\ldots,9$ exactly once. (Here $S(A)=36$ and $S(B)=9$, as (b) predicts.)

(A computer search over all ways of splitting the ten digits into two numbers shows that this is the only solution, and that the sign $-$ is also impossible.)
note: Riddle 3 of the post ("using 0-9 once, get 99 with one math symbol, concatenation allowed"). The open-ended riddle is made precise with the four basic signs, and the record asks for the impossibility of + and x, the structure of a division solution and a check of the solution 496287 / 5013 (found by computer; unique, and - is impossible, by exhaustive search). Riddles 4-6 are word riddles and are not included.

question:
Define $f$ by $f(0)=1$ and, for every integer $x\ge1$,
\[f(x)=\dfrac{f(x-1)+1}{x+1}.\]
Compute $\dfrac{0!+1!+2!+3!+4!+5!+6!+7!}{f(7)}$.
solution:
We claim that
\[f(x)=\dfrac{0!+1!+\cdots+x!}{(x+1)!}\qquad\text{for all }x\ge0.\]
For $x=0$ the right side is $\dfrac{0!}{1!}=1=f(0)$. If the formula holds for $x-1$, then
\[f(x)=\dfrac{1}{x+1}\left(\dfrac{0!+1!+\cdots+(x-1)!}{x!}+1\right)=\dfrac{0!+1!+\cdots+(x-1)!+x!}{(x+1)\cdot x!}=\dfrac{0!+1!+\cdots+x!}{(x+1)!},\]
so by induction it holds for all $x$. (For example $f(1)=1$, $f(2)=\dfrac{2}{3}$, $f(3)=\dfrac{5}{12}$.)

Hence
\[\dfrac{0!+1!+\cdots+7!}{f(7)}=8!=\boxed{40320}.\]
note: Checked with exact fractions.

question: Find the sum of the squares of all real numbers $x\ne0$ for which both $x+\dfrac{1}{x}$ and $9x-x^2$ are integers.
solution:
Let $x+\dfrac{1}{x}=a$ and $9x-x^2=b$ be integers. The first condition gives $x^2=ax-1$, so
\[b=9x-x^2=9x-ax+1=(9-a)x+1 .\]
\textbf{Case $a\ne9$.} Then $x=\dfrac{b-1}{9-a}$ is rational. Write $x=\dfrac {p}{q}$ in lowest terms with $q>0$. Then $x+\dfrac{1}{x}=\dfrac{p^2+q^2}{pq}$ is an integer, so $p\mid p^2+q^2$, hence $p\mid q^2$; as $\gcd(p,q)=1$, this forces $p=\pm1$. Likewise $q\mid p^2$ forces $q=1$. So $x=1$ or $x=-1$, and both work: $1+1=2$, $9-1=8$, and $-1-1=-2$, $-9-1=-10$.

\textbf{Case $a=9$.} Then $x^2-9x+1=0$, so $x=\dfrac{9\pm\sqrt{77}}{2}$, and for both roots $x+\dfrac{1}{x}=9$ and $9x-x^2=1$ are integers.

So the numbers are $1$, $-1$ and the two roots $x_1,x_2$ of $x^2-9x+1=0$. By Vieta's formulas $x_1+x_2=9$ and $x_1x_2=1$, so $x_1^2+x_2^2=81-2=79$. The required sum is
\[1+1+79=\boxed{81}.\]
note: "All numbers x" is read as all nonzero real x. Checked: the four numbers satisfy both conditions, and a search over rationals p/q with |p|, q <= 60 finds only 1 and -1 in the case a != 9.

question:
Let
\[A=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2: x^4+y^2\le1\},\qquad B=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2: x^6+y^4\le1\}.\]
Show that $A\subseteq B$, and that $A\ne B$.
solution:
Let $(x,y)\in A$. Since $x^4\ge0$ and $y^2\ge0$, we have $x^4\le1$ and $y^2\le1$, so $x^2\le1$ and $y^2\le1$. Therefore
\[x^6=x^4\cdot x^2\le x^4\qquad\text{and}\qquad y^4=y^2\cdot y^2\le y^2,\]
and hence $x^6+y^4\le x^4+y^2\le1$, i.e. $(x,y)\in B$. So $A\subseteq B$.

The sets are not equal: the point $(0.9,\,0.8)$ has
\[x^6+y^4=0.531441+0.4096=0.941041\le1,\qquad x^4+y^2=0.6561+0.64=1.2961>1,\]
so it lies in $B$ but not in $A$. $\blacksquare$
note: The post asks to show that A is a subset of B; the record proves the inclusion and adds that it is strict.

question:
In a geometric sequence of real numbers, the sum of the first $2$ terms is $7$ and the sum of the first $6$ terms is $91$. The sum of the first $4$ terms is

$\textbf{(A)}\ 28\qquad\textbf{(B)}\ 32\qquad\textbf{(C)}\ 35\qquad\textbf{(D)}\ 49\qquad\textbf{(E)}\ 84$
solution:
Let the terms be $a,ar,ar^2,\ldots$ and $S_n$ the sum of the first $n$ terms. Grouping the terms in pairs,
\[S_6=a(1+r)+ar^2(1+r)+ar^4(1+r)=S_2\,(1+r^2+r^4).\]
So $7(1+r^2+r^4)=91$, i.e. $r^4+r^2-12=0$, $(r^2+4)(r^2-3)=0$, and since $r$ is real, $r^2=3$. Then
\[S_4=S_2(1+r^2)=7\cdot4=28,\]
answer $\boxed{\textbf{(A)}\ 28}$. (Both $r=\sqrt3$ and $r=-\sqrt3$ are possible, with $a=\dfrac{7}{1+r}$; they give the same sums.)
note: The post names AHSME 1981 as the source; the problem number is not given. Checked numerically for r = sqrt 3 and r = -sqrt 3.

question:
A rectangular garden $60$ feet long and $20$ feet wide is enclosed by a fence. To make the garden larger, while using the same fence, its shape is changed to a square. By how many square feet does this enlarge the garden?

$\textbf{(A)}\ 100\qquad\textbf{(B)}\ 200\qquad\textbf{(C)}\ 300\qquad\textbf{(D)}\ 400\qquad\textbf{(E)}\ 500$
note: The post names the 1999 AMC 8 as the source; the problem number is not given. Near-miss: aops-topic-3129090-q01 (a 50 by 10 garden).

solution:
\textbf{(a)} There are $\dbinom{n+1}{r+1}$ ways to choose a committee of $r+1$ people from $n+1$ people numbered $1,2,\ldots,n+1$. Sort the committees by the largest number $m$ in them; $m$ is at least $r+1$. Write $m=k+1$ with $r\le k\le n$. Once $m=k+1$ is fixed, the other $r$ members are any $r$ of the $k$ people numbered $1,\ldots,k$, which can be chosen in $\dbinom kr$ ways. Every committee is counted exactly once, so
\[\binom{n+1}{r+1}=\sum_{k=r}^{n}\binom kr .\]

\textbf{(b)} A path from $(0,0)$ to $(n-r,\,r+1)$ has $n+1$ steps, of which $r+1$ go up, so there are $\dbinom{n+1}{r+1}$ paths. Look at the last step up in a path: it goes from some point $(j,r)$ to $(j,r+1)$ with $0\le j\le n-r$, and after it all steps go right. So the path consists of an arbitrary path from $(0,0)$ to $(j,r)$, followed by one step up and then $n-r-j$ steps right. There are $\dbinom{j+r}{r}$ paths from $(0,0)$ to $(j,r)$, and different $j$ give different paths. With $k=j+r$ (so $r\le k\le n$),
\[\binom{n+1}{r+1}=\sum_{j=0}^{n-r}\binom{j+r}{r}=\sum_{k=r}^{n}\binom kr. \qquad\blacksquare\]
(In Pascal's triangle the terms $\dbinom rr,\ldots,\dbinom nr$ lie along a diagonal and $\dbinom{n+1}{r+1}$ just below and to the side of its end, which gives the ``hockey stick'' shape.)
note: The post asks for the block-walking and committee-forming proofs of the hockey stick identity; the record asks for both. Checked numerically for n <= 30.

solution:
\textbf{(a)} $\gcd(2,100)=2\ne1$. In fact no power $2^k$ with $k\ge2$ can be $\equiv1\pmod{100}$, since it is divisible by $4$ while $1$ is not. So we split $100=4\cdot25$ into coprime factors.

\textbf{(b)} \emph{Modulo $4$:} $2^{56}\equiv0$, so $2^{56}+7\equiv3\pmod 4$.

\emph{Modulo $25$:} $\gcd(2,25)=1$ and $\varphi(25)=20$, so $2^{20}\equiv1\pmod{25}$ and $2^{56}=\left(2^{20}\right)^2\cdot2^{16}\equiv2^{16}$. Also $2^{10}=1024\equiv-1\pmod{25}$, so $2^{16}=2^{10}\cdot2^6\equiv-64\equiv11\pmod{25}$. Hence $2^{56}+7\equiv18\pmod{25}$.

\emph{Combining:} the numbers $\equiv18\pmod{25}$ below $100$ are $18,43,68,93$, with remainders $2,3,0,1$ modulo $4$. Only $43$ is $\equiv3\pmod4$, so by the Chinese remainder theorem $2^{56}+7\equiv43\pmod{100}$, and its last two digits are $\boxed{43}$ (whose digit sum is $7$, as the post says).
note: The post asks how Euler's theorem and Fermat's little theorem give last digits, with the example 2^56 + 7 (answer 43, digit sum 7 as stated). Checked: 2^56 = 72057594037927936.

question: Find all primes $p\ge7$ such that $2^{p-7}\equiv1\pmod p$.
solution:
Since $p$ is an odd prime, Fermat's little theorem gives $2^{p-1}\equiv1\pmod p$. If $2^{p-7}\equiv1\pmod p$, then
\[1\equiv2^{p-1}=2^6\cdot2^{p-7}\equiv64\pmod p,\]
so $p\mid63=3^2\cdot7$. With $p\ge7$ this leaves $p=7$, and indeed $2^{0}=1\equiv1\pmod7$. The only prime is $\boxed{p=7}$.
note: Checked for all primes below 10^5.

question: Factor $2x^2(x+y)-y(x+y)^2$ completely.
solution:
Expanding,
\[2x^2(x+y)-y(x+y)^2=2x^3+2x^2y-x^2y-2xy^2-y^3=2x^3+x^2y-2xy^2-y^3.\]
Group the terms in pairs:
\[x^2(2x+y)-y^2(2x+y)=(2x+y)(x^2-y^2)=\boxed{(2x+y)(x-y)(x+y)}.\]
Check with $x=2$, $y=1$: the original expression is $8\cdot3-1\cdot9=15$ and $(5)(1)(3)=15$.
note: The post asks how to factor such expressions; the record factors the given one. Checked symbolically.

solution:
\textbf{(a)} Place the balls in the order $1,2,\ldots,2020$. Ball $1$ can go into any of the $3$ boxes. For $k\ge2$, the only condition involving ball $k$ and the balls before it is that ball $k$ is not in the same box as ball $k-1$; so ball $k$ has exactly $2$ choices, whatever happened before. Every valid distribution arises exactly once, so the number of ways is
\[\boxed{3\cdot2^{2019}}.\]

\textbf{(b)} From the distributions in (a) remove those that leave a box empty. All the balls cannot go into one box (balls $1$ and $2$ would be together). If exactly two boxes are used, the balls must alternate between them, since consecutive balls are in different boxes: once the box of ball $1$ is chosen, everything is determined. There are $3$ choices of the pair of boxes and $2$ choices of the box of ball $1$, so $6$ such distributions. Hence the number of ways is
\[\boxed{3\cdot2^{2019}-6}.\]
note: The post does not say whether a box may stay empty; the record asks for both readings (part (b): every box used). The boxes are distinguishable. Checked by brute force for up to 8 balls (3 * 2^(n-1) and 3 * 2^(n-1) - 6).

question: A completely filled, valid Sudoku grid (every row, column and $3\times3$ box contains each of $1,\ldots,9$ exactly once) has the entries of three of its cells erased. Prove that there is only one way to fill in the three empty cells so that the grid is again a valid Sudoku.
solution:
The original entries give one valid completion. Suppose $G$ and $H$ are two different valid completions, and let $D$ be the set of cells where they differ. Then $D$ is a nonempty set of at most $3$ cells, all among the erased ones.

\textbf{Claim.} Every row that contains a cell of $D$ contains at least two cells of $D$, and likewise for every column.

Indeed, in a row the entries of $G$ are $1,\ldots,9$ in some order, and so are those of $H$. If the row contained only one cell $c$ of $D$, then $G$ and $H$ would agree on the other $8$ cells of the row, so the entry in $c$ would be the one number missing from those $8$ cells, both in $G$ and in $H$; so $G$ and $H$ would agree at $c$, a contradiction. The same argument works for columns.

Now take a cell $c_1\in D$. By the claim its row contains another cell $c_2\in D$, in a different column, and the column of $c_1$ contains another cell $c_3\in D$, in a different row. The column of $c_2$ must also contain a second cell $c_4\in D$, different from $c_2$. The cell $c_4$ is neither $c_1$ nor $c_3$, because those lie in the column of $c_1$, not in that of $c_2$. So $c_1,c_2,c_3,c_4$ are four different cells of $D$, contradicting $|D|\le3$.

Hence two different completions cannot exist, and the completion is unique. $\blacksquare$
note: "Any Sudoku puzzle which has three missing numbers" is read as a valid completed grid with three cells erased. Only the row and column rules are needed. Checked by brute force on a sample grid (every choice of 3 erased cells has one completion).

solution:
\textbf{(a)} We have
\[\dfrac{1}{T_n}=\dfrac{2}{n(n+1)}=2\left(\dfrac{1}{n}-\dfrac{1}{n+1}\right),\]
so the sum telescopes:
\[\sum_{n=1}^{j}\dfrac{1}{T_n}=2\left(1-\dfrac{1}{j+1}\right)=\boxed{\dfrac{2j}{j+1}}.\]
\textbf{(b)} The partial sums $\dfrac{2j}{j+1}=2-\dfrac{2}{j+1}$ increase and tend to $2$ as $j\to\infty$. So the series converges, and its sum is $\boxed{2}$.
note: Near-miss: aops-topic-3426332-q01 (the series starting from 1/3, sum 1). Checked with exact fractions for j <= 50.

question: A positive integer $n$ leaves remainder $a$ when divided by $3$, remainder $b$ when divided by $5$, and remainder $c$ when divided by $7$. Find the remainder when $n$ is divided by $105$, given that $4a+3b+2c=30$.
solution:
The remainders satisfy $0\le a\le2$, $0\le b\le4$, $0\le c\le6$, so $4a+3b+2c\le8+12+12=32$.
\begin{itemize}
\item $a=2$: $3b+2c=22$. Since $2c\le12$, $3b\ge10$, so $b=4$ and $c=5$.
\item $a=1$: $3b+2c=26$ needs $3b\ge14$, so $b\ge5$: impossible.
\item $a=0$: $3b+2c=30$ needs $3b\ge18$: impossible.
\end{itemize}
So $n\equiv2\pmod3$, $n\equiv4\pmod5$, $n\equiv5\pmod7$. The first two say $n\equiv-1\pmod{15}$, so $n$ is one of $14,29,44,59,74,89,104$ modulo $105$; their remainders modulo $7$ are $0,1,2,3,4,5,6$, and only $89$ leaves remainder $5$. Hence the remainder is $\boxed{89}$.
note: Source as given in the post title (Junior Regional Olympiad, Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, 2014, Grade 7, Problem 4). Checked by brute force over n < 105.

question: In how many ways can a $2\times5$ rectangle be covered, without overlaps, by $1\times2$ dominoes and $1\times1$ squares? (Dominoes may be placed horizontally or vertically; the rectangle's cells are fixed, so tilings that differ by a rotation or reflection of the whole rectangle count as different.)
solution:
Let $a_n$ be the number of tilings of a $2\times n$ rectangle, and let $b_n$ be the number of tilings of a $2\times n$ rectangle with one extra cell attached to the right end of its top row (the top row has $n+1$ cells, the bottom row $n$). By symmetry $b_n$ also counts the shape with the extra cell on the bottom row. Set $a_0=1$, $b_0=1$.

\textbf{Recursion for $b_n$.} The extra cell is covered either by a square (leaving a $2\times n$ rectangle: $a_n$ ways) or by a horizontal domino together with the last top cell of the rectangle (leaving a shape whose bottom row is one cell longer: $b_{n-1}$ ways). So $b_n=a_n+b_{n-1}$.

\textbf{Recursion for $a_n$.} Look at the two cells of the last column.
\begin{itemize}
\item They are covered by two squares or by one vertical domino: $2a_{n-1}$ ways.
\item Both are covered by horizontal dominoes: $a_{n-2}$ ways.
\item One is covered by a horizontal domino and the other by a square: what is left is a $2\times(n-2)$ rectangle with one extra cell in one row, $b_{n-2}$ ways, and there are $2$ choices of which row has the domino: $2b_{n-2}$ ways.
\end{itemize}
So $a_n=2a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}+2b_{n-2}$ for $n\ge2$, with $a_1=2$.

\textbf{Computing.}
\begin{align*}
a_2&=2\cdot2+1+2\cdot1=7, & b_1&=a_1+b_0=3,\\
a_3&=2\cdot7+2+2\cdot3=22, & b_2&=7+3=10,\\
a_4&=2\cdot22+7+2\cdot10=71, & b_3&=22+10=32,\\
a_5&=2\cdot71+22+2\cdot32=228.
\end{align*}
So there are $\boxed{228}$ ways.
note: The post asks for a solution by recursive counting; the record gives one. Checked by brute-force enumeration of tilings for 2 x n, n <= 6.

solution:
\textbf{(a)} $(a_1+\cdots+a_k)^n$ is a product of $n$ factors, each equal to $a_1+\cdots+a_k$. Multiplying out, we choose one term $a_i$ from each factor and multiply the choices; the expansion is the sum of all $k^n$ such products. A choice gives $a_1^{m_1}\cdots a_k^{m_k}$ exactly when $a_1$ is chosen from $m_1$ of the factors, $a_2$ from $m_2$ of them, and so on. Such a choice is the same as a word of length $n$ (the $i$th letter tells which term is chosen from the $i$th factor) containing $m_1$ letters $a_1$, \ldots, $m_k$ letters $a_k$. The number of these words is
\[\binom{n}{m_1}\binom{n-m_1}{m_2}\cdots\binom{m_k}{m_k}=\dfrac{n!}{m_1!\,(n-m_1)!}\cdot\dfrac{(n-m_1)!}{m_2!\,(n-m_1-m_2)!}\cdots=\dfrac{n!}{m_1!\,m_2!\cdots m_k!}.\]
Collecting equal products gives the stated coefficient. For $k=2$ this is the binomial theorem, since $\dfrac{n!}{m!\,(n-m)!}=\dbinom nm$. $\blacksquare$

\textbf{(b)} The product index is $f$, but the factor $m_k!$ does not depend on $f$; as written, $\prod_{f=1}^k m_k!=(m_k!)^k$. The correct expression is $\prod_{f=1}^k m_f!=m_1!\,m_2!\cdots m_k!$.

\textbf{(c)} Here $n=7$ and the exponents are $2,1,3,1$, so the coefficient is
\[\dfrac{7!}{2!\,1!\,3!\,1!}=\dfrac{5040}{12}=\boxed{420}.\]
note: The post presents the multinomial theorem ("Super Binomial Theorem") with a proof; it is turned into proving it, spotting the index typo m_k! in the post's formula, and an example. Near-miss: aops-topic-2538293-q01 (three variables, coefficient of x^2 y^3 z in (x+y+z)^6). Checked with sympy.

question: All arrangements of the eight letters of the word VENHANCE are listed in alphabetical order and numbered $1,2,3,\ldots$; thus ACEEHNNV is number $1$ and VNNHEECA is number $10080$. What number does EVANCHEN have?
solution:
The letters are A, C, E, E, H, N, N, V (two Es and two Ns), so there are $\dfrac{8!}{2!\,2!}=10080$ arrangements. Count the arrangements that come before EVANCHEN.
\begin{itemize}
\item Starting with A or with C: the other $7$ letters contain two Es and two Ns, $\dfrac{7!}{2!\,2!}=1260$ each, so $2520$.
\item Starting with E, second letter before V: the second letter is A, C, E or H (leaving $6$ letters with two Ns: $\dfrac{6!}{2!}=360$ each) or N (leaving $6$ different letters: $6!=720$). Total $4\cdot360+720=2160$.
\item Starting EVA (A is the smallest remaining letter, so nothing starts EV with a smaller third letter), fourth letter before N: C, E or H, each leaving $4$ letters with two Ns: $\dfrac{4!}{2!}=12$, so $36$.
\item Starting EVAN, then C is the smallest remaining letter; starting EVANC, sixth letter before H: only E, leaving $2$ letters H, N: $2$ arrangements.
\item EVANCH is followed by E and N, and EVANCHEN is the first of these.
\end{itemize}
So $2520+2160+36+2=4718$ arrangements come first, and EVANCHEN is number $\boxed{4719}$.
note: The post's "8 letters ... given a letter corresponding to the position" is read as the position in the alphabetical list. Checked by generating all 10080 arrangements.

question: Prove that for every positive integer $x$, the number $10^{10^x}$ leaves remainder $4$ when divided by $7$.
solution:
Since $7$ is prime and does not divide $10$, Fermat's little theorem gives $10^6\equiv1\pmod 7$. So $10^N$ modulo $7$ depends only on $N$ modulo $6$.

Now $10\equiv4\pmod6$ and $4^2=16\equiv4\pmod 6$, so $4^x\equiv4\pmod6$ for every $x\ge1$, i.e. $10^x\equiv4\pmod 6$. Write $10^x=6m+4$. Then
\[10^{10^x}=\left(10^6\right)^m\cdot10^4\equiv10^4\equiv3^4=81\equiv4\pmod7. \qquad\blacksquare\]
note: Checked with pow(10, 10**x, 7) for x <= 6.

question: Factor $x^2+4x-12$.
solution:
We need two numbers with product $-12$ and sum $4$: they are $6$ and $-2$. So
\[x^2+4x-12=\boxed{(x+6)(x-2)}.\]
Check: $(x+6)(x-2)=x^2-2x+6x-12=x^2+4x-12$.

\textbf{(a)} Expanding and using $ab+bc+ca=1$,
\[(1-a)(1-b)(1-c)=1-(a+b+c)+(ab+bc+ca)-abc=2-(a+b+c+abc).\]
So
\[a+b+c+abc=2-(1-a)(1-b)(1-c)<2,\]
because each factor $1-a$, $1-b$, $1-c$ is positive.

\textbf{(b)} Take $c=t$ with $0<t<1$, and $a=b=s$ with $s^2+2ts=1$, i.e. $s=\sqrt{t^2+1}-t=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{t^2+1}+t}$. Then $0<s<1$ and $ab+bc+ca=s^2+2st=1$, and by (a)
\[a+b+c+abc=2-(1-s)^2(1-t).\]
As $t\to1$, the factor $1-t\to0$ while $(1-s)^2<1$, so the value tends to $2$. Together with (a), the values come arbitrarily close to $2$ but never reach it: there is $\boxed{\text{no largest value; the supremum is }2}$.

(If the interval were $(0,1]$, then $c=1$ would be allowed; the condition becomes $a+b+ab=1$, and the value is exactly $2$, which is then the maximum.)
note: Ill-posed as posted ("find the largest value"): on the open interval (0, 1) the value is always below 2 and approaches 2, so there is no maximum. The record asks to prove the bound and that it is not attained. Checked numerically on random admissible triples.

question:
Real numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ satisfy
\[3ab+6a+2b+4=8,\qquad 2bc+3b+4c+6=10,\qquad 6ac+9a+4c+6=15.\]
Find all possible values of
\[6abc+9ab+12ac+4bc+18a+6b+8c+12.\]
solution:
Each left side factors:
\[3ab+6a+2b+4=(3a+2)(b+2),\quad 2bc+3b+4c+6=(b+2)(2c+3),\quad 6ac+9a+4c+6=(3a+2)(2c+3).\]
With $X=3a+2$, $Y=b+2$, $Z=2c+3$ the system is $XY=8$, $YZ=10$, $ZX=15$, and the target expression is
\[(3a+2)(b+2)(2c+3)=XYZ\]
(expand $(3ab+6a+2b+4)(2c+3)$ to check). Multiplying the three equations, $(XYZ)^2=8\cdot10\cdot15=1200$, so $XYZ=\pm\sqrt{1200}=\pm20\sqrt3$.

Both signs occur. With $X=2\sqrt3$, $Y=\dfrac{4}{\sqrt3}$, $Z=\dfrac{5\sqrt3}{2}$ we get $XY=8$, $YZ=10$, $ZX=15$ and $XYZ=20\sqrt3$; replacing $X,Y,Z$ by $-X,-Y,-Z$ keeps the three products and gives $XYZ=-20\sqrt3$. In each case $a=\dfrac{X-2}{3}$, $b=Y-2$, $c=\dfrac{Z-3}{2}$ are real. So the possible values are $\boxed{20\sqrt3\text{ and }-20\sqrt3}$.
note: The post asks for "the value", but the system has two real solutions with values 20 sqrt 3 and -20 sqrt 3 (with a, b, c > 0 only the first). The record asks for all values. Checked numerically for both solutions.

solution:
Write each number in lowest terms $\dfrac {a}{b}$, and a candidate as $\dfrac {p}{q}$ in lowest terms.

\textbf{(a)} $\dfrac {p}{q}\div\dfrac {a}{b}=\dfrac{pb}{qa}$ is an integer exactly when $a\mid p$ and $q\mid b$: if $qa\mid pb$, then $q\mid pb$ with $\gcd(q,p)=1$ gives $q\mid b$, and $a\mid pb$ with $\gcd(a,b)=1$ gives $a\mid p$; the converse is clear. So $\dfrac {p}{q}$ is a common multiple exactly when $p$ is a multiple of every numerator and $q$ divides every denominator. The smallest choice is
\[\dfrac{\operatorname{lcm}(2,9,6,3)}{\gcd(5,4,7,8)}=\dfrac{18}{1}=\boxed{18}.\]
Check: $18$ divided by the four numbers gives $45$, $8$, $21$, $48$.

\textbf{(b)} In the same way $\dfrac {a}{b}\div\dfrac {p}{q}=\dfrac{aq}{bp}$ is an integer exactly when $p\mid a$ and $b\mid q$. The largest common divisor is
\[\dfrac{\gcd(2,9,6,3)}{\operatorname{lcm}(5,4,7,8)}=\boxed{\dfrac{1}{280}}.\]
Check: the four numbers divided by $\dfrac{1}{280}$ give $112$, $630$, $240$, $105$.
note: The post asks for the LCM and GCD of four fractions without defining them; the record states the usual definition (integer multiples) and derives lcm(numerators)/gcd(denominators) and gcd(numerators)/lcm(denominators). solution:
From the list: the words with exactly two As are Amazing, Daydream, Extraordinary, Marriage and Vacation ($5$ words; no word has more than two), and the words beginning with S are Sadness, Scars, Shame, Silly, Sing, Smile, Sparkle, Special, Sunny, Sunset and Sweet ($11$ words). ``Laugh'' has one A and does not begin with S, and no word with two As begins with S, so the three groups do not overlap.

\textbf{(a)} The three words must be ``Laugh'', one of the $5$ two-A words and one of the $11$ S-words, in one of $3!=6$ orders. So the probability is
\[\dfrac{6\cdot1\cdot5\cdot11}{88^3}=\dfrac{330}{681472}=\boxed{\dfrac{15}{30976}}\approx0.00048.\]

\textbf{(b)} There are $\dbinom{88}{3}=109736$ equally likely sets of three words, of which $1\cdot5\cdot11=55$ are favourable. The probability is
\[\dfrac{55}{109736}=\boxed{\dfrac{5}{9976}}\approx0.00050.\]
